Abstract

We present Denario, an AI multi-agent system designed to serve as a scientific research assis-
tant. Denario can perform many different tasks, such as generating ideas, checking the literature,
developing research plans, writing and executing code, making plots, and drafting and reviewing a
scientific paper. The system has a modular architecture, allowing it to handle specific tasks, such as
generating an idea, or carrying out end-to-end scientific analysis using Cmbagent as a deep-research
backend. In this work, we describe in detail Denario and its modules, and illustrate its capabilities by
presenting multiple Al-generated papers generated by it in many different scientific disciplines such as
astrophysics, biology, biophysics, biomedical informatics, chemistry, material science, mathematical
physics, medicine, neuroscience and planetary science. Denario also excels at combining ideas from
different disciplines, and we illustrate this by showing a paper that applies methods from quantum
physics and machine learning to astrophysical data. We report the evaluations performed on these
papers by domain experts, who provided both numerical scores and review-like feedback. We then
highlight the strengths, weaknesses, and limitations of the current system. Finally, we discuss the
ethical implications of Al-driven research and reflect on how such technology relates to the philosophy
of science. We publicly release the code at this URL. A Denario demo can also be run directly on
the web at this URL, and the full app will be deployed on the cloud.

1 Introduction

Modern science has been built on the rules of the scientific method [1]. This empirical and iterative
method begins by formulating an idea or hypothesis, which represents the foundation for the entire
research endeavor. This initial idea might arise from a variety of sources: a theoretical question, an
unexplained phenomenon, an unexpected result in prior work, or a curiosity-driven exploration of a
dataset or simulation. The hypothesis can aim to explain an observed behavior in nature, test the
validity of a theoretical model, or uncover new patterns or relationships within existing data.

Once the idea is identified, it is often refined through collaboration discussions, preliminary literature
reviews, and feasibility assessments. Researchers seek to understand the broader context of the problem,
what has already been studied, and where the current knowledge gaps lie. This step is crucial for ensuring
that the proposed work is novel, feasible, and impactful.

Next, a detailed plan is developed to execute the project and investigate the proposed idea. This stage
involves identifying the necessary data, selecting or designing appropriate methodologies, and outlining
the sequence of steps required for the analysis. Depending on the nature of the research, this may include
data collection or simulation, data preprocessing and cleaning, implementing algorithms or analytical
models, and performing statistical or computational analyses. Along this process, scientists may use
lower-dimensional representations of the data, e.g., via plots or diagrams, to help interpret intermediate


results and to communicate findings effectively. The ultimate goal of this phase is to systematically
explore the hypothesis, extract meaningful insights, and arrive at scientifically sound conclusions.

Finally, a scientific paper or report is written describing in detail the problem or hypothesis, the
methods used, the results obtained, and the conclusions reached, describing how the research has advanced
knowledge and its connections with previous works.

Each of the above steps is a highly sophisticated task that requires extensive time for highly skilled
domain experts. Because of this, the generation of a scientific paper can take from months to years.
Unfortunately, a significant fraction of that time is consumed on tasks such as literature search, learning
new methods, debugging code, and writing text. These are tasks where recent advances in Artificial
Intelligence (AI), such as large language models and AI agents, can help. Thus, developing AI tools
that can assist scientists with some or all of the tasks involved in the generation of new knowledge can
accelerate scientific discovery by enabling scientists to formulate new hypotheses and test those faster
than in the traditional method.

In this work, we introduce and describe Denario, an AI multi-agent system designed to serve as a
scientific research assistant. Denario can generate ideas, check the literature to evaluate the novelty of
those, develop research plans, write and execute code, make plots, and draft and review scientific papers.
It can also perform end-to-end scientific research by carrying out, sequentially, all the above tasks. We
evaluate the capabilities and limitations of Denario by generating paper drafts from a very diverse set of
disciplines, from biology to astrophysics, and reporting the positive and negative aspects of these papers,
as judged by domain experts. Hoping to be a tool that can accelerate scientific discovery, we also make
Denario publicly available.

We want to stress that Denario is not the first attempt at building tools to help researchers perform
end-to-end research. The idea of having machines perform research is much older. For instance, the robot
scientist (also known as Adam) [2] was able to formulate hypotheses, plan and run experiments (physically
via robotics), interpret the results, and repeat the cycle. Adam was designed to study functional genomics
and was the first machine to generate scientific knowledge independently of humans. The same group
later developed Eve [3], another robot scientist tailored towards drug discovery. Another early important
work is the Automated Statistician [4], which was able to perform a detailed statistical analysis of some
data and provide a report about its findings. More recently, lots of recent work on AI assistants for
research has been done by many different teams, such as Sakana Al-scientist [5, 6], Google co-scientist
[7], Al-cosmologist [8], Curie [9], and Agent laboratory [10].

We note that lots of works are also developing tools to help scientists with increasingly sophisticated
tasks. For instance, AutoWEKA was developed to identify the best machine learning model to tackle a
particular problem [11]. ResearchAgent [12] was able to formulate new hypotheses and design experiments
by checking their novelty with the literature. [13] created a self-driving lab to re-engineer enzymes without
human intervention, while [14] created a virtual lab with several Al-scientist experts in different areas
capable of creating nanobodies. Another example is AstroAgents [15], a multi-agent system designed to
test and consolidate many different hypotheses about the origins of life on Earth. Recent works have also
shown that AI systems can write expert-level scientific software and discover new algorithms [16, 17, 18].
Other works are exploring the capabilities of agentic systems via graphs [19, 20]. We also note that
AgentRxiv [21] is a framework for Agents to learn from previous works.

While some of these technologies have the potential to accelerate scientific discovery —for instance,
[22] designed an autonomous system combining AI with robotics to discover new materials a lot of serious
debates about human standards for validation sparked [23]. These are very important considerations and
we discuss them in detail, for the case of Denario. Furthermore, given the ethical considerations raised
by such a technology, we devote a paper section to discuss ethical aspects, along with how this technology
fits within the philosophy of science.

We note that in scientific research, there is usually a tradeoff between depth and breadth, given a fixed
amount of time to carry out a task or study. We believe that Al systems like Denario can help researchers
explore a wide range of possibilities, at a more superficial level, while researchers can go deeper into the
most interesting or promising ones. We emphasize that the goal of Denario is not to automate science,
but to develop a research assistant that can accelerate scientific discovery. By making Denario publicly
available and user-friendly, we hope it will become a standard tool that benefits the scientific community
in their enterprises.

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce the different pieces that made our system,
such as LLMs, AI agents, and agentic orchestration. In Sec. 3 we describe in detail the different modules
in Denario and show the different ways to run the system in Sec. 4. In Sec. 5, we show different Al-
generated papers from many different disciplines and discuss the positive and negative aspects of those.


We then present in Sec. 6 some of the observed failure modes of Denario together with advantages,
limitations, and future directions. We discuss the ethical considerations that systems like Denario raise
and how the technology powering is seen from the philosophy of science in Sec. 7. We conclude in Sec.
8.

2 Al multi-agent systems

Denario is an Al multi-agent framework designed to function as a scientific research assistant. It is built
with AG2 and LangGraph, and designed to assist in different stages of the research process. It can also
execute multiple tasks sequentially, enabling it to perform end-to-end scientific research.

The system is composed of several modules, each focused on a specific task. Within each module, there
are agents—autonomous or semi-autonomous computational entities that perceive their environment,
process information, and take actions to achieve defined goals. Some of these are Al agents, which
leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform specialized tasks. Agents can communicate and
collaborate to solve complex problems, while orchestration manages their interactions—determining task
order, information flow, and overall coordination. The system takes some input text and returns one or
several outputs depending on how Denario is run. We show a cartoon representation of the system in
Fig. 1.

In this section, we describe the different components relevant to setting the agents, including the LLM
models and the orchestration.

which can exchange messages among them (blue arrows outside modules). The modules are composed of
multiple agents (bots icons), that can communicate with each other (blue arrows inside modules).

2.1 Large Language Models

The majority of the agents in Denario are Al-agents that typically call Large Language Models (LLMs)
[24], including multi-modal ones, with a very specialized prompt that may depend on the output of other
agents. Denario allows the user to choose among many different models, including:

e gpt-5, gpt-5-mini, gpt-4o, gpt-4.1, gpt-4.1-mini, 0o3-mini from OpenAl,

e gemini-2.5-pro, gemini-2.5-flash, gemini-2.0-flash from Google,


e claude-3-7-sonnet, claude-4-Opus, claude-4.1-0Opus, claude-4.5 from Anthropic.

We note that Denario is not limited to these LLMs, and new models, or models from other providers,
can easily be incorporated into the system. Our choice of models has so far been made based on trial
and error rather than systematic evaluation. For example, for coding, our primary models of choice
are gemini-2.5-pro, gpt-4.1, and o3-mini. For critiquing and reviewing, our default choice is Claude
models or reasoning models from OpenAl

2.2 Multi-Agent Orchestration and Strategy

In Denario, the agent orchestration is carried out with two different frameworks: AG2' and LangGraph”.
Some modules (e.g. idea module) are implemented in both frameworks, while others (e.g. analysis
module) are only implemented in one framework. Some modules implemented in AG2 follow the Planning
& Control strategy as implemented in Cmbagent that we describe below.

2.2.1 Orchestration

eo AG2. AG2 is an open-source AgentOS that supports advanced agentic Al applications and research.
It offers an agentic abstraction that unifies AI foundation models like LLMs, non-LLM tools and
human inputs, and intuitive conversation programming to orchestrate multiple agents. Stronger
agents or agentic systems can be composed recursively using primitive agents and basic conversation
patterns like sequential chats, group chats, nested chats. This modular architecture also enables
rich agentic design patterns such as advanced tool use, structured context, conditional handoffs,
dynamic updates, dynamic task decomposition and team building, guardrails, and many other
extensions. All agents using AG2 are part of Cmbagent [25, 26, 27], an open source and publicly
available? multi-agent system designed to perform a variety of scientific research-related tasks.

e LangGraph. LangGraph is based on LangChain* and is an open-source Python framework de-
signed to orchestrate agents through directed graphs. In LangGraph, the graph nodes represent
callable units, such as agents, functions, and tools. The edges between nodes represent the way the
flow of the computation is carried out. Another important component of LangGraph is the graph
state, an object (typically a Python class) passed through the different nodes and enabling agent
communication, memory, coordination, etc. LangGraph supports both static and dynamic graphs.
For instance, depending on the outcome of an agent, one may want to call a particular agent. Loops
and interrupts are also allowed in LangGraph.

2.2.2 Planning and Control Strategy

Planning & Control, a fundamental concept in robotics, refers to strategies for orchestrating decision-
making and action execution. The basic idea is that during the planning phase, a complex task is
decomposed into smaller, manageable subtasks, and a strategy is defined for achieving them. During the
control phase, these subtasks are executed, with monitoring and adjustments as needed to ensure the
overall goal is achieved. Some modules in Denario follow this strategy, as implemented in Cmbagent. We
now briefly describe the Cmbagent Planning & Control implementation and refer the reader to [26] for
further details. The strategy is illustrated in figure 2.

In Cmbagent, during the planning phase, the main task is broken down into sub-tasks, and an agent
is assigned to each of them. During control, the agent responsible for a sub-task executes its instructions
until completion. Once a sub-task is complete, a control agent records its status and proceeds to the next
sub-task, continuing until the entire plan is complete.

The Planning stage starts with a call to a plan setter agent, whose task is to select the set of
agents that should be involved during the session. This function call stores into the context detailed
instructions for the plan (namely, the agents and description of agents that should be involved) and
ends on the next agent target, which is the planner agent. Then, the elaboration of a plan is done via
a two-agent conversation where a planner agent suggests plans and a plan reviewer agent suggests
recommendations on the plan. Recommendations and suggested plans are recorded in the context via
function calls, including the number of steps in the plan. This information is injected into each agent’s

system message before reply. The number of review rounds, 7 eviews, iS @ hyperparameter of our system,
and we generally set it to one’. Once the number of rounds of recommendation Nn eviews is reached, the
final plan is recorded into the context, and the Planning stage ends. The response of the planner is a
list of subtasks, where each subtask consists of three fields:

e sub_task: the sub-task to be performed
e sub_task_agent: the name of the agent in charge of the sub-task.

e bullet points: A bullet-point list describing the specific actions the subtask is expected to per-
form.

The number of subtasks is constrained from the prompt of the planner and plan_reviewer agents,
which are instructed to produce a plan with, at most, ngeps steps, another tunable hyperparameter of
our system. Typically, our plans contain between 3 and 8 steps’.

The Control stage is orchestrated by a control agent. The plan obtained from the Planning stage
is injected into the system message of the control agent and it replies by calling the record_status
function. This function updates the context variable dictionary to record the current step being executed,
whether it is completed, failed, or in progress, whether some new plots or new code have been produced,
whether some code execution has failed, and, depending on this information, which agent to transfer to
next. The control agent records two types of termination signals: whether the number of times a code
execution has failed exceeds the maximum number of failures allowed by the user, or whether the final
step of the plan has been carried out successfully. In the former, the session aborts before the main task
has been solved, and in the latter, the session ends positively with the full plan completely executed.
Upon reception of a termination signal, control agent transfers to a terminator agent to end the session
smoothly.

Given the fact that the system may fall into an infinite loop (e.g., trying unsuccessfully to fix a bug),
we set a hard limit to the maximum number of messages exchanged between the agents, n,ounds- BY

default, we set this to n.oungs = 500. The system will fail if more than n,oungs are exchanged. We note
the system can fail for many other reasons, including limits on API calls set on the provider platforms,
or occasional exceptions/errors that are not fully dealt with.

3 Architecture

Denario is built as a modular system, allowing the user to execute a single or a combination of modules.
Each module is an ATI agentic system designed to carry out a specific scientific task. Figure 3 illustrates
the overall workflow and architecture of Denario.

Figure 3: This scheme shows the architecture of Denario. The green hexagons represent the different
modules in Denario. These modules are agentic systems that can 1) generate an idea for a research
project, 2) check the literature to validate the novelty of the idea, 3) develop a plan to carry out the
project, 4) implement the plan by writing and executing code, making plots, and describing the results,
5) write a scientific paper discussing the research and showing the plots, and 6) review the paper. Orange
arrows indicate the input to the modules, while the green arrows show the output of them. The output
of the modules are shown in the blue boxes. For details about the output, see Table 1. At the top,
in magenta, there is the input description, where the user describes the data, postulates the problem...
etc. We note that Denario is fully modular, and human input can be added at any point. For instance,
Denario can be run as a standalone program and generate a paper from the input text file (by running
the idea, methods, analysis, and paper modules sequentially), or can also be used as a standalone tool to
create plots and results from an input text, idea, and methods provided by the user.

For most of the modules, Denario requires an input text guiding the system’s behavior. This text
can contain the description of the data to be used together with some computational constraints. It can
also simply contain a description of a problem to be solved. For some research applications, it can also
be relevant to specify that the data can (or should) be generated by the agents. The six main modules
in Denario can perform these tasks (see Table 1 for a summary):

e Idea module. This module is in charge of generating an idea for a project. This module only
requires the input text file to be run. After calling this module, Denario will print out the idea
and save it in a markdown file called idea.md. The agents in charge of this module are described
in Section 3.2.

e Literature module. This module is in charge of checking the literature to figure out if an idea is
original or there are existing works that have carried it out. The input to this module is the input
text together with the idea.md file. This module will then check the literature and and write a
report on whether the idea is new or not. The report will be saved to a file called literature .md.
The agents in charge of this module are described in Section 3.3.

Table 1: This table shows the different modules contained in Denario along with their tasks, inputs,
and outputs. input .md contains a description of the data or problem of interest and is provided by the
human researcher in markdown format. idea.md contains the project idea, literature.md a report on
whether the idea is new, methods .md the research methodology, results.md the research analysis, Plots
is a folder containing the plots and referee.md contains a referee report. paper.pdf is the scientific
paper in pdf format. Files between parentheses are optional.

eo Methodology module. This module is in charge of generating a detailed plan to carry out the
idea. To be run, it needs the input description text file and the idea.md file with the description of
the idea. We note that idea.md can be generated by the previous module or provided by the user.
After executing this module, Denario generates a detailed plan outlining the steps and methods
needed for the project. Denario stores this generated text in a file called methods.md. The agents
in this module are described in Section 3.4

e Analysis module. This module is in charge of implementing the research plan. It requires the
input text, together with the idea.md and methods.md files (generated by previous modules or
provided by the user). By calling this module, Denario will carry out the research plan, usually
translating into writing and running code, making plots, etc. The output of this module is a file,
results.md, with the outcome of the analysis, together with the plots generated. The agents
behind this module are described in Section 3.5.

eo Paper module. This module is in charge of writing a scientific paper. This module requires the
input text along with the idea.md, methods.md, results.md, and all plots. As above, these files
can be the outcome of the modules or can be provided by the user. By calling this module, Denario
writes a scientific paper and saves the .tex, .bib, and .pdf files. The agents behind this module are
described in Section 3.6.

eo Review module. This module is in charge of reviewing a scientific paper. The input to this
module is a pdf with the scientific paper along with an input description (optional). This module
will review the paper and provide a report about the positive and negative aspects of the draft.
The output of this module is a referee report that will be saved on a file called referee.md. The
agents behind this module are described in Section 3.7.

We emphasize that Denario is designed in a modular way. By calling sequentially all the above
modules, Denario will perform end-to-end scientific research from an input text (e.g. from a description
of a dataset). However, the user can also just run one (or several) of the modules to perform a specific
task. For instance, given a well-defined idea and research plan (provided by the user), the user can run
the analysis module to write code and create plots. We now discuss in detail the architecture and agents
involved in each module of Denario.

3.1 Input Text

All modules in Denario accept an input text. This input text usually contains a description of the data
to be analyzed or the problem to be solved. This text is later used by the modules to generate ideas,


develop research plans, analyze the data, or check the literature. How well the system behaves depends
critically on this text. We now outline a few guidelines on how to write the input text:

If the project to carry out consists of analyzing some data, and the structure of the dataset is not
well described, the analysis module will fail, as the code it will write will likely not be appropriate
to read the data properly. We recommend that the user describe the data or the problem with as
much detail as possible in the input text. For instance, if the project is about analyzing a tabular
dataset, it is important to write what the data is about and some context. Besides, it is important
to describe in detail what the different columns and rows are, and specify things like units, ranges
(if available), etc.

If the goal is not to analyze some data but instead to solve some problem, it is very important to
describe in detail the problem, connections with previous works, and some details about the steps
to carry out if known.

It is also very important to write explicitly the location of the data (with absolute paths if possible);
otherwise, the system will not be able to find the location of the data.

When used in end-to-end mode, Denario sometimes may generate papers with very few plots. One
can fix this by writing in the input text to generate many plots for each step. Sometimes, the
system may generate many similar plots, which will make the paper more like a research note than
an actual paper. For this, the user can add some text like this: Join plots that are similar.

We have also seen cases where Denario fails to read the data, and to continue, it will create its own
synthetic one. To avoid these situations, we usually write in the input text Do not create dummy
data..

One can also set computational constraints in the input text so that the system is aware of what
resources it has when performing the analysis. Examples of this are: You have access to 1 GPU
and 10 CPUs; use all the resources when training neural networks.

We have observed cases where the system is not able to use a particular library (perhaps because it
does not know about its documentation or because its API has recently changed). In these cases,
the user can explicitly write Do not use X library to perform this analysis to avoid that situation.

On the other hand, if the user has some piece of code, or a library, that may not be known to LLMs,
the user can add instructions about its usage in the input text so that the system learns how to use
it when analyzing the data.

In many occasions, it is necessary to iterate over the input text in order to guide the system in
a particular direction or to improve the quality of the generated papers. In this case, the user
should add details about previous experiments, or directions where the analysis is wanted, in order
to achieve the desired outcome.

If arXiv URL’s are provided in the input text description, Denario automatically downloads the pdf
of the corresponding papers. The pdf’s are OCR’ed with mistral ocr lattest and the resulting
markdown versions are stored in the local repository. Then, the full markdown versions are sent to
03-mini for summarization and the summary of the papers are appended to the initial input text,
providing the necessary contextual information for the subsequent LLM agents. (In the GUI this
is done with the Enhance data description button, see Fig. 9.)

We refer the reader to the example papers repository’ for a comprehensive list of examples, across
disciplines, of input text used for different papers.

3.2

Idea module

The goal of this module is to generate research ideas given some input text (e.g. describing some dataset).
We note that recent work [28] has suggested that Al-generated ideas may be more novel (according to
human evaluators), than human-generated ideas. The input to this module is the input text (see Fig. 3)
and the output of it is a file called idea.md that stores the generated idea. We now describe in detail
how this module works.

"https: //github.com/AstroPilot-AI/DenarioExamplePapers

10


Input Text

— esa =? Research

IDEA MAKER < IDEA HATER

Criticizes and

Figure 4: The Idea module is a propose-critique block consisting of two agents: idea maker and
idea hater. The system first calls the idea maker agent, that will generate an idea given the input text.
Next, the idea is sent to the idea hater, who will critique the generated idea. The idea maker will then
take the input text, the generated idea, and the critique and will improve the idea. This process is then
repeated several times until the final idea is generated.

A critical part of scientific research is the generation and refinement of ideas. In any ambitious project,
it’s not enough to simply work on a fixed plan — creativity and adaptability are needed to explore the
best possible directions. However, creativity must be balanced by careful critique to ensure ideas are
realistic, impactful, and tightly connected to the available data. To systematize this process, our pipeline
includes specialized agents dedicated to idea generation (idea maker) and idea critique (idea hater).

In this pipeline, the idea maker agent generates creative and feasible research project ideas based on
the input text and any feedback from the idea hater agent. Its goal is to propose diverse approaches
for extracting new information, considering the current plan, task, and instructions. However, simply
generating ideas is not enough — to ensure that only the strongest, most relevant ideas move forward,
each proposal must undergo careful evaluation. This is where the idea hater agent steps in, critically
reviewing each idea for feasibility, scientific value, and relevance to the dataset. By identifying weaknesses
and suggesting improvements, the idea hater ensures that no idea is accepted blindly without scrutiny.
Figure 4 provides a schematic of the conversation between the idea maker and idea hater agents. This
loop can be repeated as many times as requested.

This setup mirrors the natural human process of idea development, where individuals brainstorm
concepts and refine them through feedback and discussion. Just like in human teams, iteration is key:
the idea maker improves its proposals based on the critiques received from the idea hater, leading
to a cycle of continuous refinement. This multi-agent dialogue helps distill raw ideas into well-formed,
robust research directions, ultimately ensuring that the final projects are both innovative and grounded
in realistic scientific practice. The concept of multi-agent systems to produce ideas has been motivated
by previous works such as [29], who used reinforcement learning between agents, and [30], who showed
that a large team of agents produced better ideas than a single agent. In its current version, Denario
has two different implementations (see Section 2.2) for this module:

e Fast idea. In this case, a single idea is generated by the idea maker agent and then improved
(or completely changed) after receiving feedback from the idea hater agent. The final idea is
obtained after three iterations of the two agents, followed by a further iteration from the idea maker
agent. This implementation is fast (around 15 seconds with gemini-2.0-flash) and is written in
LangGraph.

e Planning & Control idea. This implementation is carried out with Cmbagent using the planning
and control strategy. The instructions passed to the Planning agents are:

Idea Generation Planning Instructions

Given these datasets and information, make a plan according to the following instructions:

. Ask idea maker to generate 5 new research project ideas related to the datasets.

. Ask idea hater to critique these ideas.

. Ask idea maker to select and improve 2 out of the 5 research project ideas given the output
of the idea hater.

11


4. Ask idea hater to critique the 2 improved ideas.

5. Ask idea maker to select the best idea from the two.

6. Ask idea maker to report the best idea as a scientific paper title, accompanied by a 5-sentence

description.

The goal of this task is to generate a research project idea based on the data of interest. Don’t
suggest performing any calculations or analyses here. The only goal of this task is to obtain the
best possible project idea.

During the Planning stage, the planner and plan reviewer design the plan for the idea maker and
idea hater agents to generate an idea, given the input text needed for the module. To illustrate this
implementation, we show below the first two steps of an idea generation plan created by using as input
text a description of the Perovskite database [31]:

Idea Generation Plan Example (First 2 Steps Only)

Sub-task: Generate 5 new research project ideas related to the perovskite dataset.
Agent: idea maker
Instructions:

Review the dataset description and attributes.

Propose 5 innovative and feasible research project ideas based on the dataset’s scope
and potential.

Ensure the ideas are diverse and cover different aspects of the dataset.

Consider focusing on different aspects such as material composition relationships, fab-
rication parameters, device architecture correlations, stability factors, and performance
optimization based on the 95 attributes in the dataset.

Sub-task: Critique the 5 research project ideas.
Agent: idea hater
Instructions:

e Evaluate the feasibility, originality, and potential impact of each idea.
e Identify weaknesses or limitations in the ideas.
e Suggest improvements or recommend discarding weak ideas.

e Evaluate each idea’s scientific novelty and whether it leverages the unique comprehen-
sive nature of this manually curated dataset with 42,4004 devices.

As seen in this example, with this approach, the idea maker and idea hater agents receive explicit
instructions specific to the data or problem of interest. This could potentially improve the quality of the
generated ideas. However, this approach is time-consuming and incurs a significant cost. With our default
LLM choices (we use gpt-4o and claude-3-7-sonnet for idea maker and idea hater, respectively),
Planning takes ~1 minute and costs ~ $0.20, while Control takes ~3 minutes and costs ~ $0.90. This
amounts to ~ $1 and ~ 4 minutes per generated idea, to be contrasted with the 15 seconds of the fast
method that comes at no or significantly lower cost with gemini-2.0-flash.

The reason behind the two different implementations of this module is to provide the user more
flexibility when using Denario. For instance, a new user may prefer to use the fast idea implementation
to get results quicker, while in full production mode, the user may prefer a more robust approach by
using the curated idea generation.

As stated above, this module will generate an idea and store it in a file called idea.md. This file is
later used as input for other modules. We emphasize that the user can use the idea module to generate
an idea, or can provide the idea directly by writing it to the idea.md file.

12


3.3 Literature module

The goal of the literature module is to search the literature to determine whether an idea, in combination
with the input text, is new or not. This module takes as input the input text together with the idea
(usually in the form of the idea.md file). The module then searches the literature for papers similar to
the proposed idea and evaluates whether the project idea is new or not. The input text is taken into
consideration when evaluating the idea. We do this because in some research areas, standard techniques
applied to new datasets may be seen as novel research. For instance, even if graph neural networks are
very standard in deep learning, they may not have been applied to cosmological datasets, and this may be
seen as novel in the cosmology research area. The module returns a file, literature .md, that contains a
report on whether the idea is new or not. Denario provides two different implementations of this module:

Input text Idea
NOVELTY \
AGENT
Ba NEY - |b
SUMMARY SEMANTIC
AGENT SCHOLAR

Literature report AGENT

Figure 5: This diagram shows the semantic scholar implementation of the literature module. The module
takes as input the input text and the idea. These files are then passed to a novelty agent whose task is
to determine if the idea is new or not. This agent can output 1) idea new, 2) idea not new, or 3) query.
The agent will choose the later if it does not enough information to make a yes/no decision. In that case,
it will generate a query that will be sent to the semantic scholar agent who will search the literature
with it. This agent will then retrieve a series of papers (including titles and abstracts) and will send
this information back to the novelty agent. This process is repeated several times until the relevant
literature is well sampled. If no relevant papers are found after a number of iterations, the novelty agent
will conclude that the idea is new. Once the novelty agent has determined that the idea is new/not
new, all the papers found, the queries, and the responses will be sent to a summary agent that will write
a report stating why the idea is new (or not new) and the most relevant papers.

oe Semantic scholar. In this implementation, carried out with LangGraph, we follow the workflow
introduced in [5]. The module consist of two agents that collaborate to determine whether an
idea, together with the associated data description, is new or has already been carried out. First,
the novelty agent is presented with the idea, the data description, and with titles and abstracts
of papers already found. The goal of this agent is then to determine whether, with the given
information, the paper is new, is not new, or whether it does not have enough information to reach
a conclusion. If it determines that the paper is new, or not new, all the information is sent to
another agent to summarize the results and to write a report. This report will be placed on a file
called literature.md. If the novelty agent determines that it does not have enough information,
then it can call the semantic scholar agent which can make a query using Semantic Scholar®.
This other agent will then make an API call to Semantic Scholar, using the query sent by the
novelty agent, and obtain papers (titles, abstracts, URLs, etc) that will be sent back to the

8https://www.semanticscholar.org/


novelty agent for evaluation. This procedure is repeated several times up to a maximum number,
where the module will determine that the idea is new as it has not found relevant papers after
multiple iterations. We show a scheme about the workflow of this implementation in Fig. 5.

FuturHouse’s Owl. For this implementation, we just make use of the Owl agent developed by
FutureHouse.” This is a specialized agent designed to search the literature and provide an answer
to the question: Has anyone implemented this idea before? We refer the reader to the FuturHouse
documentation!’ for details about this agent.

Denario contains both implementations to allow the user to choose among the two, or perhaps better,

to run both of them to get to "independent” opinions. This module will generate the literature report,
located in the literature.md file. We note that in the current implementation, this file is not used by
any other module. We do this intentionally so that a human evaluator decides whether the idea is truly
new /original or not.

The methods module is responsible for producing a detailed plan, or methodology, to carry out the

e Planning & Control methods. This mode uses the Planning é Control strategy of Cmbagent,

15


These instructions are appended to the default instructions of the researcher agent. We further
constrain nsgeps = 4 (maximum 4 steps in the plan). With the default models, at the time of writing this
paper, Planning typically costs around $0.20 and takes around 1 minute, while Control takes around 1.5
minutes per step at a cost of around $0.10 per step. Thus, with Planning & Control, the total cost of
designing the methodology is around $0.50 and takes around 4 minutes. This is to be contrasted with the
Fast mode that takes around 15 seconds at no cost to produce the methodology with gemini-2.0-flash.
We note that using gemini-2.5-pro for the fast implementation has a small cost (around ~ $0.10) and
will take around 90 seconds, but typically will produce a much more detailed plan to help run the analysis
pipeline.

As in the case of the idea module, we provide two different implementations to the user to enhance
their range of options when executing this module. We note that the curated implementation may not
necessarily yield a better research plan, while its cost and execution time will be significantly higher than
the fast option when run with gemini-2.5-pro. However, we recommend the user try both options for
the particular case study.

3.5 Analysis module

The goal of this module is to implement the analysis outlined in the methodology. This is done with
Cmbagent [25, 26, 27]. The inputs to this module are the input text, the project idea, and the methodology
(either created by earlier modules or supplied directly). The output of the module is 1) a report on the
results obtained, located in a file called results.md, and 2) a folder called Plots that contains all plots
generated. In the current version of Denario, the analysis module relies exclusively on Cmbagent and
its Planning & Control strategy for “Deep Research” orchestration, similar in nature to the workflows of
agentic tools like Claude Code or Cursor agent mode. See Fig. 2 for an illustration of this strategy.
For the Planning phase, we append the instructions reported hereafter to the planning agents.

Analysis Generation Planning Instructions

{research _idea}

{methodology}

Given these datasets, project idea and methodology, we want to perform the project analysis and
generate the results, plots and insights.

The goal is to perform the in-depth research and analysis.
The plan must strictly involve only the following agents: {involved_agents_ str}.
The goal here is to do the in-depth research and analysis, not an exploratory data analysis.

The final step of the plan, carried out by the researcher agent, must be entirely dedicated to writing
the full Results section of the paper or report. If this research project involves code implementa-
tion, this final step should report on all the qualitative and quantitative results, interpretations of
the plots and key statistics, and references to the plots generated in the previous steps. The final
result report will be what will be passed on to the paper writer agents, so all relevant information
must be included in the final report (everything else will be discarded).

As we store the full idea and methodology in the context variable dictionary, the planning instructions
contain these explicitly. The context variable involved agents str is a string with the names of the
agents involved for the analysis generation, which by default are the engineer and researcher agents
of Cmbagent. We append the following instructions to these two agents.

Analysis Generation Appended Engineer Instructions

{research _idea}

{methodology}

Given these datasets, and information on the features and project idea and methodology, we
want to perform the project analysis and generate the results, plots and key statistics. The goal
is to perform in-depth research and analysis. This means that you must generate the results,
plots, and key statistics.

Warnings for computing and plotting:
- make sure dynamical ranges are well captured (carefully adjust the limits, binning, and log or
linear axes scales, for each feature).

For histograms (if needed):
-Use log-scale for features with values spanning several orders of magnitude.

GENERAL IMPORTANT INSTRUCTIONS: You must print out in the console ALL the
quantitative information that you think the researcher will need to interpret the results. (The
researcher does not have access to saved data files, only to what you print out!) Remember that
the researcher agent can not load information from files, so you must print ALL necessary info
in the console (without truncation). For this, it may be necessary to change Pandas (if using it)
display options.

The engineer agent is in charge of writing Python code analysis pipelines. The engineer agent call
triggers a nested chat (similar to self-debug [32]), of which only the output is kept. This allows for long
sessions without hitting LLM provider API token limits. A failed code execution may trigger different
transitions. If the number of failed executions is lower than ngs, the module would generally transit
back to the engineer agent for another attempt. If the failure is caused by a missing Python package,
the system will send a request to an installer agent, which runs a bash pip install command before
attempting the code execution again. If the number of failed executions equals ng,js, a transition to the
terminator agent is triggered and the session ends.

Given the planning instructions reported above, the engineer agent is generally in charge of the bulk
of the analysis, while the researcher agent is called in the final step of the workflow to report on the
results. For Denario, we append the researcher’ system message with the following instructions:

Analysis Generation Appended Researcher Instructions

{research _idea}
{methodology}

At the end of the session, your task is to generate a detailed /extensive discussion and inter-

pretation of the results. If quantitative results were derived you should provide interpretations
of the plots and interpretations of the key statistics, including reporting meaningful quantitative
results, tables and references to material previously generated in the session. The results should
be reported in full (not a summary) and in academic style. The results report/section should be
around 2000 words.

The final result report will be what will be passed on to the paper writer agents, so all relevant
information must be included in the final report (everything else will be discarded).

Each step during control, with gemini-2.5-pro or gpt-4.1 as engineer and researcher, costs around
$0.30, amounting to around $2 for a plan in 6 steps. The time needed to run this module depends
critically on the amount of data, the technique used to analyze it, and the available computational
resources. For simple analyses with less than 1 Gigabyte of data, the typical time is ~30 minutes on a
personal computer. The user can (and should) specify which computational resources are ready to be
committed to the analysis.

3.6 Paper module

This module is in charge of writing a scientific paper or report. In its current form, it should be seen as
a paper draft more than a publication-ready paper. This module is entirely written in LangGraph (but
for the keyword search, which uses Cmbagent). The module takes as input the input text, the project
idea, the project methodology, and the project results. As for the other modules, these files can be either
provided by the user or generated by previous modules. The output of this module is a set of LaTeX files
together with associated pdfs. A scheme showing the workflow of this subsystem is shown in Fig. 7. We
note that the user has multiple options available when running this module, such as the LLM to use, the

journal of the paper, and whether the paper includes citations or not'!.
Input Files
SEE NW
‘ SECTION AGENTS ———» PLOTS — » REFINING ——» CITATIONS

ye 1 Abctract AGENT AGENT AGENT
. Strac
a — RB —_— N= | | 2. Introduction | | |
3. Method , ,
PREPROCESS KEYWORDS 4. Reclte Paper Preliminar Paper Captions Paper Final

AGENT AGENT 5. Conclusion

Figure 7: This scheme shows the workflow of the paper writing module. Each node represents an agent
(or a group of agents) in charge of a task. The preprocess agent is in charge of reading the input files
and performing some basic operations, such as identifying duplicated plots. Later, a series of agents will
identify keywords and write different sections of the paper draft. Next, an agent will process the plots,
generating captions for them and outputting a preliminary version of the paper draft. Next, an agent
will refine the results section to improve references to the plots and to polish the writing on it, generating
a second version of the paper draft. Next, an agent will place citations in different sections of the paper,
producing a third and fourth final version of the paper draft.

The process starts with an preprocess agent reading the input files, which will be kept in memory
until it has finished writing the entire paper. We note that it is easy to include more files in case the
paper writing requires more information. For instance, the user may provide an additional file with details
about the data, references, literature report, etc. The preprocess agent performs other tasks, such as
counting the number of plots, identifying and removing repeating plots, and creating temporary files.

Next, given the texts read above, another agent will select a set of keywords that characterize the
paper (see Section 3.6.1). After that, another agent will choose a title for the paper and write the abstract.
Next, several agents will write the paper’s different sections: 1) Introduction, 2) Methods, 3) Results,
and 4) Conclusions. For each section, an agent is passed the input texts and asked to write the assigned
section for the paper. We note that the sections are written sequentially, with each section passed to the
next agent to improve the coherence throughout the paper. We perform self-reflections for some sections
to improve the quality of the generated text.

Once these sections are written, another agent is asked to take all the plots available and generate
captions for them. This is achieved by using the multimodal capabilities of the underlying LLM. We note
that the captions are generated taking into account the input files to improve the context and coherence
of the captions. Next, another agent is tasked with inserting the figures and their generated captions
into the results section. This is done in batches of 7 figures'?, as the LLM tends to forget inserting some
figures when there are many figures in the prompt. At this point, the system will generate a first LaTeX
file, compile it, and generate the corresponding pdf.

After this, another agent is asked to rewrite and polish the results section so that the text describes
and refers to the added figures. Next, version 2 of the paper, with the polished results section, will be
generated. We do this because we have observed the module failing at this point and we use these versions
as checkpoints in case we need to rerun the module.

This module can be run with the option to add citations to the paper. If run in that mode, the text
inside the different sections is passed through a Perplexity agent in order to get citations (with arXiv

For research notes or similar, the user may not find it useful to spend time and money adding citations. Given the cost,
we tend to add citations only to the papers that have been reviewed and filtered by human experts.

12This is in principle a hyperparameter. We have noticed that with current LLMs, including more than 10 figures tends
to result in errors, omissions, etc

18


IDs) to the relevant sentences. We use the Perplexity API with the sonar-reasoning-pro model for
this. A script is then used to fetch the BibTeX information from arXiv, which is appended to the LaTeX.
At this point, version 3 of the paper is generated and saved to file. Finally, another agent is asked to
make a final pass through the different sections of the paper in order to improve the clarity of the text
and to fix LaTeX errors. After this, version 4 of the paper is produced.

We note that while multiple agents are always checking for LaTeX errors, and some agents are de-
signed to take the LaTeX errors and fix the text, we find that mistakes can still occur, and that may
cause problems with the document compilation. E.g. misplaced citations, tables not displayed properly,
problems with symbols like _ and &, and %. For that reason, the paper writing module does not produce
a single version of the paper but four different ones, as progress is made. If a problem arises, and the
agents themselves are not able to fix it, then, a human can try to fix it manually from of these checkpoints.

3.6.1 Keyword Search module

Cmbagent provides a method to get the keywords which best characterize a given input text, such as the
abstract of a paper. The Denario Paper module makes use of this functionality to find the correspondent
keywords of the project by passing as input text the idea and methodology. There are three keyword
lists that can be searched by this method:

e UNESCO Nomenclature. This taxonomy has three levels for classifying science and technology
domains, subfields and specific areas. We do the keyword search in four steps. First, the keyword
agent is provided with the list of domains (2-digit codes) and is asked to select at most 3 domains.
Second, for each selected domain, the keyword agent is asked to select at most 3 subfields. Third,
for each subfields, the keyword agent is asked to select 3 specific areas. Domains, subfields and
specific areas are aggregated into one list and in the last step the agent is asked to select the NV
most relevant keywords where N is the number of keywords requested by the user. The original
UNESCO document is publicly available.'® In principle, this list of keywords is broad enough to
be used in all scientific domains. Nevertheless, it is from 1988 and recent technical vocabulary is
sometimes lacking.

eo AAAI Keywords. Here, the keyword agent is provided with the full list of AAAI (The Association
for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence) keywords and asked to select the N most relevant
keywords where N is the number of keywords requested by the user. The AAAI list of keywords is
publicly available.'* This list is relevant for Al-focused research and is updated yearly.

eo AAS Keywords. The keyword agent is provided with the full AAS (American Astronomical
Society) list of keywords and asked to select the N most relevant keywords where N is the number
of keywords requested by the user. This list should only be used for astrophysics related papers,
and can be consulted in the AAS journal page.’

3.7 Review module

This module is in charge of reviewing the generated paper and providing a report about what is good,
interesting, and innovative in the paper, but also about the bad things, flaws, etc. The input to it is
a pdf document together with the input text (optional). The module will then break down the paper
into a set of images, one image for each page, that will be passed to a multi-modal agent along with the
input text (usually gemini-2.5-pro). The agent will then review the paper and write a report about it,
highlighting the good but also the bad things. The report will be placed in a file called referee.md.

The purpose of this module is to help humans review and filter papers. While some of the recom-
mendations we have seen from executing this module are related to ways to describe and connect things,
the module is also able to provide much more in-depth suggestions, such as logical flaws or underlying
assumptions that invalidate reasoning or conclusions. The report generated by this module can be used
to improve the quality of the generated papers via human intervention or automatic agent refinement.
The prompt used for this module is found below.

4 Usage
In its current form, Denario can be run in two different ways:

e Python API
e Graphical User Interface (GUI)

20


The Python API can be run in Python scripts or Jupyter notebooks, while the GUI can be run either
locally or through a web application. In the following subsections we detail the usage of each case.

4.1 Python API

The main entrypoint of Denario is its Python API, which allows the user to call the different modules.
For that, the user firstly needs to install the software locally. Denario is publicly available on GitHub'®
and pypi,’” and can be easily installed by running the command: pip install denario. We refer the
reader to the documentation'® for further details on how to install the package. A typical Python script
to perform end-to-end research is this:

from denario import Denario, Journal

# Initiate Denario by setting the working directory
den = Denario(project_dir="project_dir")

# Set the input text with data description

input_text = """

Analyze the experimental data stored in /path/to/data.csv using sklearn and pandas.
This data includes time-series measurements from a particle detector.

nun

den.set_data_description(input_text)

# Generate a research idea from the input text
den.get_idea()

# check whether the idea is new or not
den.check_idea()

# Generate a research plan to carry out the idea
den.get_method()

# Follow the research plan, write and execute code, make plots, and summarize the results
den.get_results()

# Write a paper for the APS journal
den.get_paper (journal=Journal. APS)

# Review the paper
den.referee()

The Python APT also allows to set research idea and methods provided by the user:

# Set the idea given by a text file in the project folder
den.set_idea()

# or providing an input string
den.set_idea("Write a research idea here")

# Similarly, set the methods given by a text file in the project folder (or providing an input string)
den.set_method()

It is possible to select between the different backends, Cmbagent and the default fast method based
on LangGraph for idea and method generation:

# Generate an idea using the fast method based on the LangGraph implementation (default option)
den.get_idea(mode="fast")

# Generate an idea using the Cmbagent backend
den.get_idea(mode="cmbagent")

The code above can be executed in several ways. For example, the lines can be saved in a Python script
and run using python script.py. Alternatively, the code can be executed interactively in environments
such as a Jupyter notebook or Google Colab. For more details on the implementation and syntax of the
Python API, please refer to the Denario documentation'®.

way to experiment with Denario, we also provide users with the option to run it as a web application. In
this case, no installation is needed and the user can start using Denario immediately. On the other hand,
the free resources available to the user (e.g., data storage, CPUs, GPUs) may be limited. We currently

5 End-to-end research examples

In this section, we illustrate the capabilities of Denario by showing and discussing multiple papers fully
generated by it. To demonstrate the versatility of the system, we show papers generated on a very diverse
set of disciplines, including astrophysics, biology, biophysics, biomedical informatics, chemistry, material
science, mathematical physics, medicine, neuroscience, and planetary science. Furthermore, Denario can
also be used for interdisciplinary research. We illustrate this by showing a paper that applies techniques
from deep learning and quantum physics to cosmological data in Sec. 5.13.

Most of the generated papers have little to none human intervention in the generation process, besides
providing and adjusting the input prompts and data. Some of them have been tested varying the input
prompt with different levels of detail. For instance, in the paper discussed in Sec. 5.12 we showcase
a human-in-the-loop example, where the prompt is iteratively improved using Cmbagent and human
feedback.

In each of the subsections below, we provide details about the data used, the input text, the generated
paper and briefly discuss the positive and negative aspects of the generated paper. The reader can find all
generated files, plots, text, etc for all papers below and many more at the example papers repository”.

5.1 Mathematical Physics. High-level analysis and abstraction of complex
structures: the physics of non-linear PDEs

A central challenge of research in physics lies in interpreting complex results and reducing them to a
framework from which general principles can be drawn. It is this capacity for abstraction that enables
scientific advancement. The problem we posed Denario to solve is the following: we would like to
understand the structure of the solutions to the Burgers equation in fluid dynamics for different values
of the viscosity v and initial conditions. In 1-dimension, the Burgers equation is:

ou ou ou

ot | Yor = Yor? (1)

5.1.1 Background: PINNs

Our tool to solve the Burgers equation is a neural network algorithm called PINNs (physics-informed
neural networks) in its implementation in the package neurodifeqq®®. The PINN will find a space of
solutions for different values of the viscosity and initial conditions. This creates a so-called latent space.

Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), first introduced in the works of Dissanayake and Phan-
Thien [33] and Lagaris et al. [34], have emerged as a powerful tool for solving partial and ordinary
differential equations (PDEs/ODEs). Raissi et al. [35] proved this approach to be valid on a wide variety
of challenging physical problems, while other researchers have made significant advancements in applying
neural networks to PDEs and ODEs, including notable examples such as [36, 37, 38]. In this paradigm,
one typically trains a distinct neural network for each unknown function in the governing equations. The
training process involves minimizing a loss function that encodes the squared residuals of these differential
equations, thereby embedding the physics directly into the learning objective.

In the PINNs setup, we use one NN for every unknown function appearing in the differential equations.
We call these objects VV (z#) and they represent the approximate solution given by the NNs for different
points along the independent variable and possibly different values of parameter or boundary conditions
(all of them are represented by x#). The training process involves minimizing the loss function, typically
defined as the residuals of the differential equations squared, summed across all the sample points of the
input domain:

https: //huggingface.co/spaces/astropilot-ai/Denario
2?https://github.com/AstroPilot-AI/DenarioExamplePapers
23https://github.com/NeuroDiffGym/neurodiffeq

23


L =) (Dy"N(2")* + ALada (2)
batch
where D represents a differential operator that will depend on the differential equations that we are
considering. Here L,q4q represents any additional contribution to the loss that can be added to give extra
information to the model during training. The weight of this piece is controlled by A.

While traditional numerical methods often outperform PINNs in terms of computational efficiency
and accuracy, recent developments in PINNs are offering unique advantages. One key benefit is the ability
of PINNs to learn the parametric dependence of the solutions to different initial or boundary conditions,
or even different values of parameters appearing in the equations. In contrast with traditional numerical
methods, this allows us to train the model on a wide range of different parameters at once, whereas a
traditional solver must be rerun for different values of initial/boundary conditions or parameters. This
eventually will make a PINNs setup much more efficient compared with a numerical method, since
obtaining a solution for a particular value of a parameter just requires the evaluation of the model. This
efficient evaluation permits us to treat otherwise untreatable problems. One of which is the so-called
inverse problem [39, 40]. This consists of recovering a free-form function or parameter appearing on the
differential equations just by considering boundary data. This capability is extremely useful for this work,
since we will use it to recover the viscosity of Burger's equation by considering the initial and final time
configuration of a solution. Another key advantage of PINNs is their capability of learning a general high-
dimensional space of functions called the latent space. The final solution would just be a combination of
these functions in a certain way. This latent space will, in general, depend on the independent variables
of the problem, but it can also be learned for more parameters, like different boundary conditions or
different values of a parameter appearing in the equations. In this work, we learn a latent space of
Burger's equation for different values of the viscosity v in the so-called Multihead training. We will
explain this framework in the following subsection.

Although we have presented the two main advantages that we are going to exploit throughout this
work of using PINNs instead of traditional numerical methods, there exist many more. PINNs are mesh-
free, allowing for obtaining a solution at any point lying inside the training set. Moreover, they can also
be used to find new solutions on stiff regimes using their ability to transfer learning [40].

5.1.2 Multihead training

Multihead (MH) training consists of breaking the neural network into two pieces: the body, which
will learn a higher-dimensional representation (latent space) of the solutions depending on the values
of different parameters or boundary conditions; and the head, which will take care of learning how to
project from this latent space to the actual solution. This setup has already been proven useful to transfer
learn solutions of differential equations to stiffer regimes. However, we use MH training to explore the
functions of the latent space when the head is forced to present a linear response. This will tell us valuable
information about the functional “basis” that the model is learning to solve the problem.
The NN gives us the final solution 1» (2#) composed of two parts

e Body: this itself is going to be a NN which is going to learn a high-dimensional space called the latent
space of solutions. We will denote it as H;(x*), where ¢ runs from 1 to the total dimensionality of this
space. In general, this NN must be large enough such that it can learn a proper representation of the
solutions in this higher-dimensional space. In general, this body will take as inputs the independent
variable plus variations of parameters or different boundary conditions of the equations, denoted
by a#. After passing them through the model, it will return us the latent space H;(z*), which will
be composed of d components.

e Head: this component is also going to be a NN and will take care of processing the latent space
component and combine them on a particular way such that the final result is going to be the
desired approximate solution to the differential equation VV (x). In general, this model is much
smaller than the body, since only a few operations on the latent space will be required to produce
the final solution. Generally, the head will take the latent space of dimension d, and combine its
components such that the final output is dimension 1. We will have one head for each of the values
of the free parameter or boundary conditions that we are considering. Thus, each of them will learn
a particular set of weights and biases that will project down the latent space to the solution for a
particular value of the parameters and boundary conditions chosen.

24


At the end, the solution can be expressed as
PVN 2") = heady [H;(z)]

where head denotes the response of the head, and W the set of its weights and biases.

The model is trained as follows. Once one approximated solution is obtained, we can compute its loss
function just by evaluating the residues of the differential equations squared (2). The total loss will be
the sum of each of the individual losses across all the heads. We can then train the model by optimizing
this loss function. At the end, the model will solve simultaneously all specified differential equations
problems. It is important to note that, since the body is shared across all NNs, it will capture global
properties of the solutions for different values of free parameter or boundary conditions.

5.1.3 Latent space structure with Denario

Our question to Denario then was to find the structure of the latent space generated by training on
Burger's equation for different initial conditions and values of the viscosity. The reason behind it was
that the structure of the latent space might reveal the actual physics determining the structure of the
solutions to this equation. So we asked Denario to explore the structure of the latent space of solutions,
having given it the following results: we provided an array that contained the latent space solutions as a
function of v, space, and time. The input text passed to Denario was this:

Input text

We haved PINNSs to solve a Burger equation in 2 dimensions for a fixed value of the viscosity with
multihead set for different initial conditions. The latent space is located in this file

/Users/fvillaescusa/Documents/Software/Denario/Project\_turbulence/data\_for\_Paco\_turbulence\
_bundle.npy

To read the data, you can do:

import numpy as np

fin = ’/Users/fvillaescusa/Documents/Software/Denario/Project_turbulenceV1/
data_for_Paco_turbulence_bundle.npy’

data = np.load(fin)

data is now a [101,103,25,13] matrix, where the first axis represents the x-coordinate, the second
axis is time, and the third component represents the viscosity. The fourth axis is organized as
follows: - first three components are the mesh of space, time and the viscosity, respectively - the
rest (10 last components) the latent space

Perform a detailed study of the latent space structure. We are interested in knowing if there is
some pattern or simple way to describe its properties.

We have run Denario end-to-end from the above prompt to generate a final article. The generated pa-
per, titled Geometric Structure of PINN Latent Space for Burger’s Equation: Low-Dimensional Manifolds
and Initial Condition Encoding, can be found in the Appendix A.1. In this paper, Denario performed a
detailed analysis of the given latent space of Burger’s equation. It applied common techniques of dimen-
sionality reduction on the provided data set, mainly Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and subspace
similarity measures. Although this analysis is quite standard, it includes some points that were surprising.
The first one was a detailed analysis of the centroids of the manifolds, computing their PCA individually
and discovering that there was only one dominant component when varying the viscosity. Then, it per-
formed a similar analysis on the 3-dimensional principal subspaces for each value of the viscosity. This
analysis included subspace similarity between these manifolds and the dot products of these vectors. The
conclusion was that these manifolds were almost parallel to each other, and that they described up to
97.67% of the variance. At last, it analyzed the global structure of the latent space using the previously
mentioned techniques. It concluded that the PINN is learning a 3-dimensional manifold to describe a
solution for each value of the viscosity. Variations of this parameter are encoded as translations of this
3-dimensional space across a 1-dimensional sub-manifold. We would also like to remark that Denario
produced unexpected results at one point. Throughout the whole paper, it is remarked that the data
is obtained for different initial conditions. However, this is not true, and the index that was treated as
different initial conditions corresponded to different values of the viscosity. This confusion was due to a

25


misleading prompt on our side. In this respect, Denario showed robustness in that it followed the prompt
instructions and did not simply try to repeat what is in the literature.

As a summary, we would like to remark on the analysis that Denario has performed on the data, not
as a novel and groundbreaking job, but as a tool for researchers to unveil future directions that are worth
investigating in detail.

5.2 Planetary Science. Mapping Size and Compositional Gradients in the
Asteroid Belt

The asteroid belt preserves a fossil record of the solar system’s formation and dynamical evolution. We
compiled a dataset of over 35,000 main-belt asteroids, integrating orbital parameters, diameters, and
spectral types. These data were obtained from a wide range of sources, including the Lowell dataset [41],
the Asteroid Lightcurve Database (LCDB) [42], DAMIT [43], mp3c [44], and the Python tool classy
[45]. We then asked Denario to analyze the data. The input text we used was this:

Input text

We have some data about asteroids. The data is located in /mnt/ceph/users/fvillaescusa/As-
troPilot/Asteroids/data

Each asteroid is identified by a unique number. For example, 1 corresponds to the first discovered
asteroid, Ceres.

All CSV files share a common structure:
eo Column 1: Asteroid identification number
e Column 2: Corresponding physical or orbital property

These files are recommended to be opened with the Python package ”pandas”.
File Descriptions:

e asteroid_name.csv: number + name of the asteroid
asteroid_diameter.csv: number + diameter of the asteroid in kilometers

asteroid semimajor_axis.csv: number + semimajor axis of the orbit in astronomical units

(AU)
asteroid_eccentricity.csv: number + eccentricity of the orbit

asteroid_inclination.csv: number + inclination of the orbit in degrees
asteroid_arg_peri.csv: number + argument of periapsis of the orbit in degrees
asteroid long asc node.csv: number + longitude of ascending node of the orbit in degrees
asteroid _spin_period.csv: number + spin period of the asteroid in hours

asteroid _obliquity.csv: number + obliquity of the asteroid in degrees (Obliquity is defined
as the angle between the spin vector and the orbital angular momentum vector.)

asteroid_type.csv: number + spectral type of the asteroid

asteroid _family.csv: number + family name of the asteroid (The family name corresponds
to the largest member of the family)

asteroid age.csv: number + age of the asteroid in gigayears (Gyr)

Please come up with an interesting project for a PhD thesis. Use state-of-the-art methods to
analyze the data. For every step, make lots of plots and save the data you generate, as it may be
used for other steps. When writing the code, write some lines to indicate whether the execution
was successful or not. Join plots that are similar. Do not create dummy data. You have access to
128 cpus; for computationally heavy tasks, try to use all of them.

26


The generated paper, titled The Spatial Architecture of the Main Asteroid Belt: Size, Composition,
and Dynamical Gradients, can be found in the Appendix A.2. By applying density estimation, clustering
(DBSCAN and GMM), and predictive modeling, Denario mapped spatial variations in size and com-
position, identified asteroid families, and examined the influence of Jupiter’s resonances on the belt’s
structure. A particular strength of the paper lies in its ability to automate the quantification of compo-
sitional gradients across the belt. This paper reveals an important compositional trend: the dominant
composition shifts from S-type in the inner solar system to C-type in the outer solar system. By mapping
the changing fractions of spectral types as a function of semimajor axis, it offers an accessible, up-to-date
reference that will be useful for researchers studying planetesimal formation and solar system evolution.
The clustering analyses also effectively reproduce known asteroid families, confirming the AI’s capacity
to extract meaningful dynamical structures from complex data.

However, while these results are scientifically sound, they are not fundamentally new. The compo-
sitional gradient and dynamical families are well-established in the literature. The observed trend of
increasing average asteroid size with distance from the Sun is also correctly noted as likely driven by
observational bias rather than a genuine physical gradient. One area for improvement is the depth of
interpretation. While Denario correctly applied clustering and density estimation, it stops at describing
known structures without critically assessing the potential for new dynamical groupings that might hint
at unrecognized collisional families or early migration signatures. This illustrates a broader limitation: al-
though AI can uncover patterns efficiently, it currently lacks the domain intuition to pose new hypotheses
or recognize subtle, novel features without human input.

Similarly, the paper’s predictive modeling using only orbital data yielded limited success, appropriately
acknowledging the role of stochastic collisional histories. But it could have gone further by discussing how
including additional parameters—such as albedo, spin state, or detailed spectral data—might improve
model performance. On the other hand, in its current form, Denario is not designed to do this kind of
critical thinking, so perhaps it is not a surprise that it does not perform well here.

It is also worth noting the experience with another Al-generated paper (not included here, but available
in the example papers repository?*), which focused on spin-orbit coupling effects. In that case, Denario
produced a figure that appeared to show features not previously discussed in the literature. However,
Denario itself did not recognize or highlight these potentially novel patterns, and other figures in that
paper were poorly prepared, limiting its usefulness. This example underscores both the promise and the
current limitations of AI approaches: when handling large, complex datasets, Al can be more efficient
than humans at surfacing candidate phenomena, but human expertise is essential to interpret, validate,
and refine these discoveries. With careful collaboration, such human—AT iteration could focus attention
on these features in subsequent analyses, potentially leading to truly novel scientific breakthroughs.

Overall, while this paper does not claim any fundamentally new discovery, that is not a significant flaw.
It demonstrates that Denario can systematically confirm and clearly document established knowledge,
producing scientifically valuable and well-visualized results in an efficient, reproducible manner. As the
era of big data arrives with observatories like Very Large Telescope (VLT) [46], the Large Synoptic Survey
Telescope (LSST) [47], and The Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) [48], tools like Denario will become
indispensable in planetary and exoplanetary science—helping researchers sift massive datasets, probe
early solar system conditions, and advance our understanding of the origins of life both here and beyond.

5.3 Medicine and Health Services Research. Assessment of Fertility Clinic
Outcomes in the United States

Health services research is a multidisciplinary field that studies healthcare utilization, access, delivery,
and financing, with the goal of improving the quality, efficiency, and equity of healthcare. Combining
insights from medicine, public health, economics, and statistics, health services research aims to inform
decisions by providers, payers, policymakers, and patients.

To evaluate Denario’s capability to design and perform a project in this field, we used the publicly
available datasets from the National ART Surveillance System?®. These annual datasets, published in
the United States by the CDC (US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention), contain clinic-level
aggregated data on the utilization and success rates of approximately 98% of all assisted reproductive
technology (ART) services in the United States. Originally mandated by the US Congress to provide
transparency and information to patients seeking fertility treatments, these datasets have been extensively
used to evaluate the quality, efficiency, and distribution of fertility services.

More specifically, we provided Denario with the three most recent years available for NASS (2020-
