The generated paper, titled Characterizing the Variability and Correlates of U.S. ART Clinic Perfor-
mance During the COVID-19 Pandemic (2020-2022), can be found in the Appendix A.3. In this paper,
Denario characterized the year-to-year variability in success and efficiency metrics of ART clinics, such
as live birth rates per retrieval and average retrievals per live birth, stratified by patient age and egg
source (own vs. donor). The dataset was evaluated using standard statistical analyses, such as the coef-
ficient of variation, to analyze fluctuations in success rates, ordinary least squares regression models, and
Spearman correlation to characterize associations between variability and clinic volume. While the anal-
yses were relatively straightforward and would likely need to be redone using other statistical tools, the
contextualization and characterization of the research question were remarkable. Despite the recognized
importance of inter-clinic variability in outcomes, little attention has been given to the characterization
of year-to-year intra-clinic fluctuations in ART clinic performance, particularly in the context of a major
systemic shock like the COVID-19 pandemic. Denario contextualized the research by not only evaluating
an overlooked topic in the literature, but also by realizing the impact of the global pandemic on healthcare
systems through disruptions like clinic closures, supply chain issues, and shifts in patient behavior.

The final manuscript generated by Denario had some limitations on the presentation of the results
and in the citations to the literature. The results and overall content of the manuscript were signif-
icantly more technical than the standard in the field, which generally focuses more on the discussion
and implications of the results. Statistical analyses were limited to standard tools such as ordinary least
squares and correlations, which (as recognized in the manuscript) would need to be re-evaluated given

29


the distributional properties of the variability measures. Another limitation was the fact that Denario
used only open-access manuscripts available at preprint repositories, such as the arXiv. While the use of
preprint repositories is a common practice in most technical areas, including economics, their use is still
limited in the field of health services research and most areas of medicine. For this reason, the references
included in the final manuscript generated by Denario were not necessarily applicable and were, at best,
marginally relevant to the sentence in which they are used.

Nonetheless, despite the limitations described above, the research conducted by Denario was genuinely
engaging and interesting, highlighting an understudied topic in the area and contextualizing it in a
novel way. This manuscript not only identifies promising directions for future investigation but also
includes methodology and results that would be useful resources for researchers in the field to further
their investigations.

5.4 Chemistry. Molecular dynamics simulations of self-assembling peptides

Self-assembling peptides (SAPs) are promising candidates for biomedical applications such as tissue
engineering, wound healing, and drug delivery. Their modular structure and biocompatibility make them
especially attractive for engineering soft materials with targeted functions. Understanding the relationship
between structure and properties in SAPs is key to unlocking this potential. To investigate this, we tasked
Denario with analyzing a 1200 ns all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) trajectory containing 30 copies of
a known self-assembling pentapeptide: KYFIL. We conducted the study over three rounds?®, each time
increasing the level of contextual information provided in the input text.

In the first round, we instructed Denario on which Python tools to use for trajectory analysis but gave
no domain-specific context. Denario correctly identified the system as a protein but misinterpreted it as
a single large molecule rather than 30 individual peptides. As a result, it analyzed residues in isolation,
failing to recognize that they were equivalent across different peptide chains. This led to an overemphasis
on per-residue metrics like dihedral angles or motif detection, rather than ensemble behaviors across
peptides. Consequently, key phenomena like peptide aggregation and clustering were missed.

In the second round, we added a system description and a research abstract to provide context. With
this information, Denario identified more appropriate analyses related to self-assembly, such as contact
mapping and cluster size distributions. While the outputs were more relevant, they remained conventional
and did not go beyond standard MD analysis pipelines. However, the automation of routine essential
tasks was already a valuable outcome.

In the third round, we explicitly posed hypotheses and research questions. Specifically, we suggested
modeling peptide clusters as graphs and proposed several graph-theoretical analyses, along with practical
motivations for each. The input text we used for this round is this:

Input text

We have data from a molecular dynamics numerical simulation. The data is located in /mnt/-
ceph/users/fvillaescusa/AstroPilot /Project chemist1/data. This trajectory contains an all atom
molecular dynamics simulation of 30 copies of the self-assembling pentapeptide, K-Y-F-I-L. The
simulation starts with the peptides fully separated and over the course of the simulation the
peptides form noncovalent interactions with one another to form an aggregate.

Motivation: The development of biomaterials that mimic the native extracellular matrix (ECM)
of brain tissue represents a promising frontier for neural repair and regeneration. Injectable
hydrogels made of short, self-assembling peptides offer a promising platform for the delivery
and directed differentiation of therapeutic stem cells. Despite the growing interest in this
field, the rational design of self-assembling peptide sequences remains largely empirical. Our
research aims to address this gap by computationally modeling a library of rapidly assembling
pentapeptides for injectable delivery (RAPID)-a family of C-terminally amidated, five-residue
peptides engineered to self-assemble into shear-thinning, self-healing hydrogels. These RAPID
hydrogels have demonstrated the potential to improve cell survival upon minimally invasive
delivery. To better understand the mechanisms behind assembly behavior, we examined KYFIL,
a pentapeptide known to self-assemble, using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to determine
the molecular scale behaviors that distinguish gelling from non-gelling sequences.

261n other words, we generated papers from slightly different prompts.

Considerations:

e In order to understand how the simulated system compares to experiments, we need to
understand how the system behaves at equilibrium (or as close to equilibrium as possible).
Therefore, we are most interested in measuring quantities starting from about 100ns into the
trajectory until the end of the trajectory (as opposed to the beginning of the trajectory).

eo We are interested in making graphs that are either a function of time or averaged over long
time intervals. We are not interested in measurements that are averaged over small time
intervals or representative of a single snapshot.

Research Questions:
e You can consider the peptides aggregates as two different types of graphs:

— First, a graph where each peptides is a node and an edge between nodes represents the
binary property of whether or not those two nodes have a heavy atom contact

— Second, where the aggregates are a hierarchical graph, where the coarse grained graph
is the same as above, but each peptide is additionally made up of a fine grained graph
where every amino acid is a node

eo With these two graph definitions we can measure graph theoretical properties, which tell us
about the overall structure of the graph

— We can construct the graph laplacian and calculate eigenvectors and eigenvalues
— We can calculate the Fiedler vector

— Are there other interesting graph theoretical quantities to explore?
eo We would want to know how do these properties:

— Look on average?
— Fluctuate about that average?

— Change dynamically over time?
eo We would like these properties to tell us:

— How densely packed are the clusters?

— Can this approach be used to predict whether a cluster will split or be long lived?

31



— What are different ways that we can measure peptide clusters or aggregates?

x Our current definition is that a cluster is a set of nodes where none of the nodes
is fully disconnected from any of the other nodes. But one challenge with this
is that the number of clusters varies widely as clusters form and uniform over
the simulation. Is there a way to combine this measurement with some graph
theoretical definition of graph density in order to construct a more stable order
parameter?

Use state-of-the-art methods to analyze the data. For every step, make lots of plots and save the
data you generate, as it may be used for other steps. When writing the code, write some lines
to indicate whether the execution was successful or not. Take into account that all the things
print on screen will be passed to a LLM, thus, only write essential information and don’t print
unnecessary information. Join plots that are similar. Do not create dummy data. You have access
to 128 cpus on a linux machine; for very computationally heavy tasks, try to use all of them.

With this guidance, Denario performed novel, domain-relevant analyses that had not been previously
utilized in the field of peptide self-assembly—and executed them efficiently. The generated paper, titled
Dynamic Multiscale Graph Analysis Reveals Structural Signatures of Peptide Aggregate Stability and
Splitting can be found in the Appendix A.4. These results showed that, for Denario to exhibits its full
capability, a very detailed and extensive description of the data is needed, and in some cases, guidance
over the research direction.

Overall, Denario demonstrated a clear progression in capability based on the depth of contextual
input. With minimal context, it could automate standard analyses; with targeted hypotheses, it extended
into novel analytical territory. While Denario didn’t independently generate insights a human expert
wouldn’t have, it significantly accelerated the exploration of both standard and creative research avenues.

5.5 Astrophysics. Properties of recent high-mass binary black hole merger
from gravitational wave data

We provided Denario with publicly available gravitational wave posteriors [49] from multiple waveform
models for a recently announced gravitational wave event GW231123 [50]. GW231123 is the most mas-
sive confident black hole merger detected till now and has implications for the formation channels of
astrophysical black holes. However, there is a significant disagreement between properties of the event as
predicted by different waveform models (see their description in the prompt below). This was the mo-
tivation for us to perform an exploratory study with Denario regarding the high-dimensional posterior
dataset from multiple models.
The input text we used for this paper is this:

Input text

Below is a description of the models used for the five files mentioned above:

eo NRSur7dg4 is a time-domain waveform model that has been directly calibrated using Nu-
merical Relativity simulations of binary black hole mergers. This model is particularly well-
suited for events with short gravitational wave signals, such as GW231123, as it is designed
to accurately capture the dynamics of the late inspiral, merger, and ringdown phases.

IMRPhenomXO4a, on the other hand, is a phenomenological model that operates in the
frequency domain. It combines post-Newtonian (PN) approximations during the inspiral
phase with a numerical relativity calibration near the merger. This model provides a more
global approximation of binary black hole waveforms and is specifically tailored for events
that can be characterized over a wider range of frequencies.

SEOBNRv5PHM Domain: Time-domain, effective-one-body (EOB) Form: Co-precessing to
inertial frame Key: Efficient inspiral-merger-ringdown with higher modes Calibrated to: NR
+ perturbation theory, high accuracy (unfaithfulness < 3% in 99.8% of cases)

IMRPhenomXPHM Domain: Frequency-domain, phenomenological Form: ”Twisting-up”
non-precessing multipoles into precessing frame Key: Multipolar, fast, calibrated to wave-
form catalogs

IMRPhenomTPHM Domain: Time-domain, phenomenological Form: Time-based twisting-
up using Euler angles + improved ringdown precession treatment Key: Avoids stationary
phase, accurate and computationally efficient

The generated paper, titled Physics-Informed Discrepancy Decomposition and Robust Astrophysical
Inference for GW231123, can be found in the Appendix A.5. In this paper, Denario performed the
exploratory data analysis very well. Without an explicit mention of which tool(s) would be the best to

33


use, Denario identified dimensionality reduction tools like UMAP (which have not been widely used in
the previous gravitational wave literature) for this problem. The resulting 2D UMAP embeddings in
Fig. 2 of the paper have a very interesting structure. The different waveform models are built in either
the time or frequency domain. The UMAP embeddings produce a common cluster for the three time-
domain models, suggesting that their predicted posteriors are consistent with each other. However, for
the two frequency domain models, the embeddings form separate isolated groups, highlighting that their
predictions are inconsistent with each other (Fig. 2). Denario also verified that the physical explanations
are independent of the hyperparameters (see Fig. 3). The Jensen-Shannon divergence plots in Fig. 4 are
useful for getting an intuition of which parameters the different models differ.

This paper can be comparable to a report generated from an undergraduate-level data exploration
project. While the paper is not currently ready to be published in a scientific journal, it definitely provides
interesting ideas for further exploration (it can be turned into a scientific paper upon further refinement
of some of the ideas presented). With each paper taking a very small time to generate, speed definitely is
the biggest advantage of using Denario and it can be used to obtain quick project ideas from a dataset.
The drawback is Denario not having knowledge of the broader context of the field (apart from the
information specified in the prompt, and to some extent the summaries provided by the ‘enhanced data’,
and ‘check idea’ options). Thus, it could not fully place the methods and results of the paper within the
context of existing literature (which is crucial for a research paper). However, one can envision further
developing our literature agents so they can perform these tasks using tools such as Semantic Scholar.

5.6 Astrophysics. Impact of Convection and Radiation Pressure on the Dy-
namics of Roche Lobe Overflow in Binary Systems

Massive stars play many important roles in astrophysics. However, the structures and evolutions of mas-
sive stars remain very uncertain due to complicated dynamical processes controlled by both gas pressure
and radiation pressure. In particular, the majority of massive stars are found in binary systems. Inter-
actions with the companion can significantly impact the evolution of massive stars. Binary interactions
and the associated mass transfer via the Roche Lobe overflow are the physical origins of many astro-
physical phenomena. In recent years, with the advanced computational power and improved numerical
algorithms, it is now possible to simulate the process of binary mass transfer between massive stars using
three-dimensional radiation hydrodynamic simulations.

One simulation we have analyzed is a binary system with a 12 solar mass Red supergiant (RSG) star
as a donor and a 9 solar mass main-sequence star as an accretor. The simulation resolved the three-
dimensional structures at the surface of the donor and followed the mass transfer to the accretor due to
the binary interaction. The surface of RSG is fully convective, which can make the Roche Lobe overflow
significantly different from what has been imagined in classical theoretical models. We used Denario to
analyze one snapshot of the simulation results to understand how the binary mass transfer happened in
the simulation. The prompt we used as input to Denario is this:

Input text

We have a snapshot of a simulation designed to study the impact of realistic 3D envelope
structures on the mass transfer in a binary system. The binary is made of a 12.9 solar mass red
supergiant (RSG) and a 9 solar mass companion. The companion is located at a separation of
2000 solar radii, which is about three times the radius of the donor (the RSG). The simulation
shows that the convective surface structures significantly modify the mass transfer rate in
the binary system. The snapshot is located in /mnt/ceph/users/fvillaescusa/AstroPilot/Yan-
Fei/data/star.outl.16543.athdf

To load the data use this example:

paper, Denario performed a detailed analysis of different components of forces that are responsible for
binary mass transfer in three-dimensional radiation hydrodynamic simulations. The paper also accurately
captured the importance of convection for the properties of Roche Lobe overflow. The paper shows
particular strength in quantitative analysis of the data based on the equations solved in the simulation,
in a similar way that scientists will do to understand the results. Furthermore, Denario analyzed the
streamlines of the flow very efficiently, which is typically much harder to do in traditional analysis. We
note that for this particular paper, one of the plots generated (Figure 8) by Denario was blank, so we

connected to the literature of binary evolution for astrophysical implications of these results. This requires
some knowledge of how binary evolution is typically done in the literature and the unique advantages of
these simulations, which cannot be learned from the simulation data itself. It will be interesting to see if
this point can be improved by adding more guidance towards this direction in the input prompt, or by
using tailored agents dedicated to these domain-specific tasks.

5.7 Biology. Analyzing single-celled RNA sequencing data across the malaria
parasite life cycle

Biological research has become increasingly entwined with computational analysis over the past two
decades. The advent of high-throughput genetic sequencing has generated a wealth of data at a scale
the field had not seen in the past. The realization that variability at the individual cell level had
crucial consequences for population-level behaviors led to the development of methods for single-celled
data generation, increasing the scale of datasets even further. With such massive amounts of information,
computational analysis (and reanalysis) of publicly available data has become a valuable part of biological
research. This presents an opportunity for AI multi-agent tools such as Denario to easily explore vast
datasets, identify phenomena that would otherwise be difficult to spot, and rapidly test these lines of
inquiry.

Here, we used Denario to analyze a publicly available dataset of gene expression in malaria parasite
cells at different life stages. Malaria, caused by unicellular parasites of the genus Plasmodium, remains
a global public health threat, causing more than 600,000 deaths in the poorest communities around the
world every year, and progress in its control has stalled or reversed over the past decade [51]. Under-
standing the biology of Plasmodium falciparum parasites, responsible for the most lethal forms of the
disease, can be critical to the development of new treatments. Many aspects of Plasmodium biology
are still poorly understood due to the parasite’s evolutionary divergence from other well-known model
organisms. Al multi-agent systems such as Denario could be used to help address this gap in knowledge.

2Thttps://github.com/AstroPilot—AI/DenarioExamplePapers

36


We used Denario to analyze a single-celled RNA sequencing (ssRNA-seq) dataset describing gene expres-
sion (transcription) in both laboratory and field-derived strains of Plasmodium falciparum. The dataset
is publicly available through the Wellcome Trust’s Malaria Cell Atlas project [52] and was previously
published and analyzed by Dogga, Rop, Cudini, et al. [53].

5.7.1 Input data

To allow Denario to work with the dataset, we provided two input files containing the gene expression data
and metadata (“pf-ch10x-set4-ch10x-exp.csv” and “pf-ch10x-setd-chl0x-data. csv”, respectively,
available in dataset “P. falciparum 10x Integrated lab strains and four natural infections”
on https://www.malariacellatlas.org/data-sets/). We also provided an input text prompt de-
scribing the dataset’s origin, content, and organization. We also provided information about potentially
interesting research questions to follow, including both lines of inquiry explored in the original publica-
tion by Dogga, Rop, Cudini, et al. [53] and different sets of questions not explored in the publication.
However, we also explicitly left an open door for analyses not mentioned in the prompt. The prompt
read as follows:

Input text

We have a collection of malaria parasite single cell transcriptomic data obtained from the
Malaria Cell Atlas project and previously analyzed by Dogga et al. 2024 (paper found at
doi.org/10.1126/science.adj4088). Malaria parasites have a complex life cycle in which
cells transition across multiple life stages in both humans and Anopheles mosquitoes. The data
collected here was obtained from malaria parasites of the species Plasmodium falciparum that
were either growing in human blood culture in a laboratory setting or recovered from the blood of
four asymptomatic patients from Mali. This means that the parasites are all either in the asexual
intraerythrocytic development cycle or the sexual blood stages. None of them are in mosquito
life stages. The data is located in /mnt/ceph/users/fvillaescusa/AstroPilot/Biology/data

The data is presented across two different files:

The first file, “gene_expression.csv”, is a 2-D matrix in which columns correspond to individual
cells analyzed in the experiment and rows correspond to individual genes. The first row contains
unique ID codes identifying each individual cell, while the first column contains unique codes
corresponding to P. falciparum strain 3D7 gene ID codes. The entries in the matrix contain the
corresponding gene’s normalized expression value within the corresponding cell.

The second file, “labels.csv”, contains a table with information about each individual cell. The
column marked “CELL_ID” contains the same cell ID code from the previous file. There are
additional columns describing the life cycle stage, parasite strain, source (“lab” for laboratory
strains; “MSC1”, “MSC3”, “MSC13”, and “MSC14” for the four patients), and days in culture
(only applicable for the lab strains, not for the four patient strains which are marked as “Field”
for field isolates).

There are many interesting things to uncover in the dataset. One set of questions relates to
potential differences between lab strains and field isolates. Another set of questions relates to
gene expression differences throughout the parasite life cycle, including key marker genes of
different stages and determinants of future developmental trajectories.

I am particularly curious about uncovering potential transcription factors or other master regu-
lators of cell cycle transitions. I suspect they might be genes that maintain low expression levels
throughout the life cycle, but have increases in expression immediately prior to an increase in ex-
pression across multiple other genes denoting a change in life stage. The increase in expression of
a possible transcription factor or other regulator gene would be relative to its own expression level,
but would probably not achieve a particularly high expression when compared to other genes.

37


5.7.2 Description of research output

With this information, Denario produced four different manuscripts analyzing the given data. One of
them, titled Single-Cell Analysis Reveals Profound Divergence in Transcriptional Regulatory Programs
Between Laboratory and Field Isolates of Plasmodium falciparum can be found in the Appendix A.7.

All four manuscripts were methodologically similar, carrying out standard practice workflows used in
scRNA-seq analysis: data preprocessing, dimensionality reduction by Uniform Manifold Approximation
and Projection (UMARP) [54], clustering, trajectory inference, and pseudotime assignment using common
analysis packages in Python such as SCANPY [55] (3 manuscripts) or in R such as Monocle 3 [56] (1
manuscript). All manuscripts attempted different strategies to identify regulators of gene expression
and to compare the gene expression profiles of laboratory and field-derived parasites, both of which the
prompt listed as a topics of particular interest. To identify regulator genes, strategies tested involved
combinations of screening for low expression genes, peak/burst detection in transcription, clustering into
transcriptional modules characterized by gene ontology (GO) analysis, partition-based graph abstraction
(PAGA) [57], regression models, and reportedly consulting existing information about gene function
consulted from the literature and the online database PlasmoDB, part of VEuPathDB [58, 59] (however,
doing so at the time the analysis was done involved web access and a personal account; it is unclear
whether Denario would be able to consult PlasmoDB at all). To examine differences in gene expression
between lab and field parasites, the manuscripts compared results from the techniques listed previously,
occasionally complemented by differential gene expression (DGE) analysis using the tradeSeq package (2
manuscripts) [60].

5.7.3 Assessment of research output

We identified a series of notable strengths and weaknesses in the research papers generated by Denario
for this project:
Strengths:

eo Knowledge of and engagement with established biology: As expected, Denario exhibits expert-level
background knowledge on P. falciparum biology. All manuscripts discuss the complexities of the
malaria parasite life cycle, correctly using specific terminology to do so despite no such information
being included in the prompt. The texts are able to justify the purpose of the study being done
in the context of the state of the field of malaria cell biology and the advantages of scRNA-seq
with respect to previous bulk RNA-seq methods. Some manuscripts even make good use of specific
knowledge of individual genes for use as positive controls validating stage transitions throughout
the life cycle.

e Proficiency with standard analysis methods: The basic pipeline used to analyze the data provided
contained all the necessary steps to carry out the analysis correctly, from data pre-processing and
quality control (some of which had already been done beforehand on the publicly-available dataset
and was therefore redundant) through to dimensionality reduction and visualization, as explained
above. The tools used were well-suited for the job, conforming to standard practices in the field.

eo (Consistency with existing science: Many of the general results obtained recapitulate known sci-
ence. The manuscripts were all able to successfully reconstruct the Plasmodium intraerythrocytic
development cycle (IDC) from transcriptomic data. They described differences between the lab and
field-derived parasite samples and even provide plausible explanations for these differences in cell
type and data quality.

e Speed: Needless to say, the speed at which entire analysis pipelines are created and the results are
analyzed is far greater than what a human researcher would take. In less than a day, Denario pro-
duced analyses and manuscripts that would take multiple days or weeks, depending on a researcher’s
familiarity with the methods.

e Methodological creativity when approaching new research questions: When prompted with a research
question with no clear answer nor a well-established, standardized way to address it, Denario showed
remarkable creativity. All four manuscripts had different approaches for trying to identify regulator
genes, as explained above.

‘Weaknesses:

38


e Poor citation, acknowledgment, and engagement with existing literature: The most immediately
evident shortcoming these manuscripts had was in their handling of scientific literature. Although
(to the best of our knowledge) all the references cited in these manuscripts corresponded to real
articles, the criteria used for selecting studies as references for specific passages is unclear. While the
literature cited is related to the topic in question, it often is a perspective or review article with only
general-level relevance, while highly relevant and closely related articles are left undiscussed. As an
example, none of the manuscripts referenced the study by Dogga, Rop, Cudini et al. [53] describing
the dataset used and its original analysis, despite this information being explicitly provided in
the input prompt. Interestingly, the problem of missing citations is particularly noticeable when
discussing specific facts about malaria biology, most of which are not cited at all. Indeed, only
2 out of 30 references in the manuscript shown in the supplementary material refer to malaria or
Plasmodium parasites, while the other 28 refer to scRNA-seq methods. This is curious given the
stark contrast with the impressive grasp of malaria parasite biology shown in the writing: Denario
clearly knows the field of malaria well, but prefers to cite other fields. Perhaps Denario is more likely
to include references related to the methods it uses more than the knowledge of the field it applies
them to, although even references to the exact methods being used are rare. Relatedly, perhaps the
lack of malaria citations and tendency to reference methods is a reflection of training biases in the
quantity or perceived impact of publications in different fields: methods are generally applicable
to multiple research areas and are therefore more widely cited and discussed in the literature than
papers addressing a specific field such as malaria biology. This would have important ramifications
that would be crucial to address in any research Al agent.

eo Confirmation bias, misplaced confidence, and overstated tone: Perhaps the most concerning weak-
ness shown in these manuscripts is their tendency to overstate the findings they present, particularly
in regard to the open-ended research question posed in the prompt regarding potential regulators
of gene expression. Although all manuscripts tried a variety of creative and potentially successful
strategies for identifying candidate genes involved in life cycle regulation, none of the results pre-
sented inspire great confidence. The magnitude and timing of the changes in gene expression on
which the conclusions are based is not sufficient to uphold the claims made about the regulative
roles of specific genes, particularly in view of the variance in gene expression. In fact, it may be the
case that the signal-to-noise ratio in scRNA-seq measurements of transcription factor expression is
too low to be able to draw meaningful conclusions, or that key changes in regulator activity might
be occurring at a post-transcriptional level. The research question was intended to be challeng-
ing, and like any real research question, it might not have a clear answer with the available data,
in which case a negative result must be reported (or at least, a lack of confidence in the results
must be conveyed). It is possible that the confirmation bias shown when attempting to answer a
specific research question from the prompt is a consequence of the bias against publishing negative
results already found in existing scientific literature, which would skew the training dataset of any
AT agents such as Denario. To be able to succeed, AI multi-agents must be able to temper their
conclusions when confidence in the significance of the results is low.

e Occasional mistaken knowledge: Although the manuscripts show a strong understanding of Plas-
modium biology for the most part, occasional mistakes are made. For instance, the manuscript in-
cluded as an example in the supplementary material claims that the gene Pfs25 (PF3D7_1031000) is
“the canonical male gametocyte surface protein gene”, when in fact it has been repeatedly shown to
be expressed solely in female gametocytes, not male ones [61]. Although not widespread throughout
the manuscripts (and certainly not unique to AI agent writing when compared to human writing),
the issue is complicated by the previously discussed lack of citations. Without references to the
sources of information, it becomes difficult to fact-check every statement and understand why the
few mistakes that occur are happening.

e Methodological ambiguity: At multiple points in the Methods sections of different manuscripts,
the text describes multiple valid but mutually exclusive methods for analysis without specifying
which one was actually used (“Data loading was performed [...] in Python or R”, “Trajectories
were reconstructed [...] using [...] Monocle 3, Slingshot, or PAGA”). This poses a problem when
evaluating the adequacy of the work being presented, since it is not clear what the exact methodology
followed was.

e (Occasional missing tables and references: The manuscript included in the supplement references
tables not included in the text, although these results are calculated in the analysis code generated.

39


Some citations are also presumably missing, included as question marks in the text.

Overall, the application of Denario to biological datasets such as this one yields results that are
impressive in their speed and competent grasp of a field and its methods, but concerning in their pre-
sentation and interpretation, as well as in the way they are presented in relation to other studies. The
implications of these trends are discussed in a later section. As AI agents such as Denario continue to
improve, we expect them to become transformational tools for training and research in biological sciences.

5.8 Digital Health. Developing and evaluating step-counting algorithms from
wrist- and hip-worn accelerometers

Wearable monitoring is a popular, emerging research field within the digital health domain, for the
objective, passive monitoring of biosignals, which may offer insights into health outcomes [62]. This
field has particularly grown with the increased use of smart devices such as phones and watches [63, 64].
These devices use a variety of sensors to extract digital measures, such as total sleep time, sleep efficiency,
heart rate, and daily step count, among others [65]. Of these measures, the daily step count, particularly
achieving 10,000 steps a day, has become one of the hallmark approaches to monitoring one’s activity
levels. However, this measure still has a high degree of skepticism, due to a lack of transparency of many
step counting algorithms, and known tricks to trigger false counting of steps, through arm movements
[66, 67].

In this study, Denario was used to read, process, and investigate research questions using a publicly
available accelerometer dataset. This data contains raw wrist and hip accelerometer data from 39 Oxford-
based participants over 1 hour. The raw data was collected from 2 devices at each location, set to sampling
frequencies of 25 and 100Hz; therefore, four monitoring devices in total. A hip-mounted, foot-facing
camera was used to record the timings of each step taken by participants, allowing for the annotation of
an indication of the timing of each heel strike, corresponding to each step. The dataset is explained in
further detail in the published work of Small et al. (2024) [67]. This dataset could primarily be used to
train or validate models/algorithms used to count steps. Moreover, given the data collection from four
different devices, it is possible to compare how the performance of these step-counting algorithms differs
between the wrist and the hip, and at different sampling frequencies. Using the metadata file, we can
further explore if there are noted differences in different age groups or sexes, though limited to just 39
participants [67].

5.8.1 Input data

The full contents of the OxWalk dataset were provided to Denario. This included the raw accelerometer
files, kept in separate folders for device location and sampling frequency combination. These files were
stored as CSV files, with one file per participant in each folder. Within the CSV file, there are 5 columns
of data. The first column is the data timestamp, and the next 3 are the accelerometer signal in x, y and z
(measured in units of gravity = 9.81ms™2). The final column is an indicator of whether the heel strike of
a step occurred at that time, that is, the start of a step. In addition to this, there was a single metadata
CSV file, storing the age band and sex of each of the participants. After an initial attempt, we provided
the following refined prompt to the Denario model:

Input text

OxWalk Annotated Step Count Dataset

DATA DESCRIPTION:
Annotated step data during unscripted, free living in 39 healthy adult volunteers (aged 18 and
above) with no lower limb injury within the previous 6 months and who were able to walk

without an assistive device. Participants wore four triaxial accelerometers concurrently (AX3,
Axivity, Newcastle, UK), two placed side-by-side on the dominant wrist and two clipped to the
dominant-side hip at the midsagittal plane. Accelerometers were synchronised using the Open
Movement GUI software (v.1.0.0.42), with one recording at 100 Hz and the other at 25 Hz at each
body location. Foot-facing video was captured using an action camera (Action Camera CT9500,
Crosstour, Shenzhen, China) mounted at the participant’s beltline.

The primary purpose of this data collection is the development of step-counting algorithms,

5.8.2 Description of research output

Through two different iterations of prompts submitted to Denario for this dataset, seven different
manuscripts were produced and analyzed. These seven manuscripts explored different research ques-
tions, with varying success, one of which, titled Wearable Step Counting: A Comparative Analysis of Deep
Learning and Traditional Methods Highlighting Data Imbalance Challenges is shown in the Appendix A.8.
For all of the manuscripts read, research questions explored the use of novel machine learning techniques
to develop walking/step detection models. This investigation then compared how the developed models’
performance would be affected by various factors, such as subgroups of age and sex, device location or
sampling frequency. The models used to detect walking/count steps, and read and process the data files
used python. To evaluate the performance of the model, F1 or AUC statistics were used for walking
detection, while mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) was used for step counting.

The research questions explored by some manuscripts brought greater levels of novelty, investigating
unique approaches for extracting gait fingerprints, or gait features, independent of device location. This
research is particularly relevant for the development of step counting algorithms in phones, which could
be located either in the hand, hence close to the wrist, or in the pocket, close to the hip. Unfortunately,
for these more novel research questions, the model struggled to build insightful manuscripts, following
this research question.

5.8.3 Assessment of research output

For the processing of wearables data, we identified the following strengths and limitations:
Strengths:

eo Able to follow and understand the provided prompts: The Denario model followed the tasked prompt
as expected. After noticing common errors in the first iteration and adjusting the prompt to avoid
these errors in the following outputs, these errors were successfully avoided.

eo Opportunity to iteratively improve prompts: As previously noted, the first input to the Denario
model did not match our expectations of output manuscripts, but explored useful ideas. These
ideas and failures could then be used to better prompt the model in future attempts, iteratively
producing better results.

eo Able to produce novel and useful research questions: Some of the research questions explored by
the model provided a novel use of the dataset. Some of these insights have been stored as ideas for
future fellowship applications.

e Built on existing practices in the field: In many cases, the outputs of Denario are built on the use
of existing models from published literature. In some cases, the research question involved the use
of new approaches in machine learning, not yet applied to wearable data, but showed advanced
domain knowledge in new machine learning approaches. In other cases, the evaluation metrics,
and window segmenting approaches followed by Denario match that as standard in the wearable
monitoring domain.

Limitations:

eo Use of jargon not relevant to the research question: It was noted that in several manuscripts
produced by Denario, some methods or results chapters would consist of words and concepts that
are relevant to the wearable monitoring space, but not relevant to the particular research question.
One example manuscript explored how signal features differed between device locations, but results
presented AUC scores, which would be expected to report the performance of a classification model,
which was not developed in this manuscript.

eo Formatting of paper outputs: Some of the manuscripts lacked tables containing the performance of
the models, which was instead solely presented in graphs. For other papers, the plots and tables had
formatting issues, like using too small a font, tables overlapping with text, the lack of use of standard
plotting techniques such as box plots and a lack of attaching some extra plots as supplementary
material.

42


e Reporting of data handling errors: In some cases, Denario failed to read some data files. Instead of
the model failing to produce a manuscript, this was reported as part of the results; in some cases,
a full section was created reporting these failures.

e Preference for walking classification over step counting: Many of the models produced by Denario
initially had a bias towards building 2-second walking detectors, rather than step counters, despite
the prompt clearly indicating this was the intention of the study. This is likely due to this being a
more common approach in literature, as there are very few step-counting datasets available.

o Trade-off between novelty and manuscript quality: There was a noticeable trade-off between the
novelty of the research questions, and the quality of the methods and results of the subsequent
manuscript. This is likely because, for more novel research questions, there exists more limited
literature regarding how to go about these investigations, leading to poorer decisions by the model.

In summary, Denario showed clear capabilities for wearable monitoring in the digital health domain,
to produce useful research questions, conduct this research, and analyze the output data. It is noted,
however, that there are quite a few limitations in the generation of reliable manuscripts. Overall, this
encourages the use of this technology in earlier stages of the research process, to generate research
questions, and to run exploratory analysis on datasets.

5.9 Biophysics. Mechanistic understanding of protein folding pathways via
dimensionality reduction methods

Characterizing protein folding and unfolding is one of the key challenges in theoretical and computational
biophysics [68], as it requires an understanding of the associated high-dimensional energy landscapes and
the kinetics of transitions between different metastable states. Long timescale simulations (microseconds
and beyond) are therefore required to observe protein (un)folding events on an experimentally relevant
timescale, leading to an understanding of the associated mechanistic pathways, identification of transient
microstates, hidden allostery, and quantification of the kinetics of such processes. The N-terminal do-
main of ribosomal protein L9 (NTL) is chosen as the model protein for this study since it undergoes
microsecond-scale folding reversible folding with a well-characterized two-state folding mechanism. NTL9
has a well-characterized and experimentally validated folded structure that allows new algorithms and
enhanced sampling schemes to reproduce the free energy landscape, intermediate ensembles, and rate
constants. This suits the purpose of benchmarking studies due to its small size of 39 amino acid residues,
absence of disulfide bonds, and lack of any complex post-translational modifications. This makes NTL9
an ideal candidate for developing new dimensional reduction methods to identify progress coordinates
and understand mechanistic insights into protein folding and unfolding.

5.9.1 Data generation

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed using the OpenMM engine [69] with the Am-
ber14SB force field and the OBC2 implicit solvent model at 300 K, employing Langevin dynamics with a
friction coefficient of 5 ps~!. The protein was subjected to energy minimization to remove steric clashes,
followed by a 10 ps production run with an integration timestep of 2 fs. Protein coordinates were then
saved every 2 ns for subsequent analyses.

5.9.2 Project description

Denario was given the task to automate the post-simulation analysis of NTL9 protein (un)folding from
MD simulation trajectories. The objective was to write a manuscript with detailed methodologies,
dimensionality-reduction and clustering approaches, estimation of the free-energy landscape and kinetic
rate constants (if possible), employ Markov state modeling to identify relevant low-dimensional progress
coordinates that can characterize the mechanism of protein (un)folding, and establish scalable strategies
for complex biomolecules. The input text to the system was this:

Input text

N-terminal domain of ribosomal protein L9 (NTL9) is a fast-folding protein domain that folds re-

versibly and is often used as a model to understand protein folding pathways. We aim to explore
its unfolding thermodynamics and kinetics using an automated, generalizable pipeline. We have

43


a 10 ps molecular dynamics (MD) simulation trajectory of the NTL9 protein undergoing folding.
Simulation conditions for the trajectory obtained: Amber14SB force field with OBC2 implicit
solvent, 300 K Langevin dynamics, 2 fs timestep, 2 nm nonbonded cutoff, and H-bond constraints.
Data: The simulation data is located at /mnt/home/aojha/AstroPilot/Project10. There are
two files in the dataset, i.e., the simulation trajectory (an implicit-solvent 10us MD trajectory
consisting of 5000 frames saved every 2ns (ntl9_trajectory.dcd) and its corresponding topol-
ogy PDB file (nt19_topology.pdb). The simulation begins from an unfolded state of the NTL9
protein, while the topology file is a folded structure of the protein.

Motivation: Understanding how NTL9 unfolds and, by extension, how small single-domain pro-
teins navigate their energy landscape reveals general principles of protein folding. Tracking down
folding /unfolding pathways provides essential knowledge related to energy barriers, intermediates,
transition states, and allostery involved in the process. We intend to build an analysis pipeline
that breaks down local events, provides a mechanism for folding and unfolding events, describes
the free energy profile for the process, and possibly the folding/unfolding kinetics. We also aim
for this workflow to be generalizable for complex proteins or multi-domain systems, thereby ad-
dressing the gap between detailed MD simulations and high-level mechanistic insights.

Key Research Questions:

1. Data-driven collective coordinates: Can we identify interesting collective variables be-
yond the radius of gyration and root mean square deviation (RMSD) for profiling such
folding /unfolding events? It will be interesting to compare the difference between using con-
ventional collective variables (CVs) and generating new hidden CVs based on the simulation
at hand. What are the dominant motions during folding /unfolding, and can we capture these
motions with dimensionality reduction? There are numerous existing dimensional reduction
methods. However, it would be interesting to see if we can keep increasing the complexity
of such methods, starting from linear principal component analysis (PCA) and moving to
spectral methods, such as diffusion maps, to explore non-linear manifold embedding. As
we progress through the complexity level, it is expected that we will uncover more subtle
unfolding pathways and intermediate microstates. Please provide a detailed description of
each method, including analysis, figures, and tables. Create a hypothesis such as, “Linear
PCA will capture the largest-scale structural separation (folded vs. unfolded), whereas a
manifold embedding could reveal hidden intermediate microstates or pathways not evident
in linear PCs.”

. State Partitioning in low-dimensional space: Can we objectively identify distinct
states (folded, intermediate, unfolded) from simulation trajectories? It would be interesting
develop algorithms to identify the folded, unfolded, and intermediate states of the protein.
Once trajectories are clustered using multiple algorithms, it will be useful to systemati-
cally visualize and compare their performance and derive best-practice guidelines for state
identification.

. Mechanisms of folding/unfolding: What local structural changes mark the onset of
unfolding? How can we analyze such local changes and visualize them on a free energy
landscape? Can we monitor the status of specific hydrogen bonds and native contacts
throughout the trajectory, particularly those that stabilize the core, to determine when each
bond first breaks? Can we construct a 2D free energy surface by binning the trajectory in
the space of two most relevant CVs. This may highlight the free energy minima (states) and
barriers between them. Then, using the cluster assignments from above, can we construct a
simple Markov state model (MSM) or a transition matrix to estimate the rate constants for
transitions?

. Scalability and extension: How can this analysis pipeline be generalized to larger or
multi-domain proteins? Can we propose strategies to manage longer trajectories and more
complex proteins? For instance, using frame subsampling or incremental PCA to handle
extremely long simulations, splitting the analysis by protein domain (which may be achieved
by analyzing independent domain motions rather than a collective one), and employing
graph-based representations of contacts or networks to capture inter-domain interactions.
Please also discuss how to choose the dimensionality of the embedding or the number of

44


clusters in an automated way (e.g., using the percentage of variance, silhouette scores, etc.)
for larger systems. It would be interesting to emphasize how each component of this pipeline
can be adapted or scaled to ensure the approach remains efficient for complex proteins.

Manuscript Writing:

1. Title and Abstract: Emphasize generality, summarize the data, and highlight key anal-
yses, such as the choice of CVs, clustering, free-energy mapping, and manifold embedding,
while also highlighting mechanistic insights and extensibility.

. Introduction: Present the NTL9 folding process in the broader context of protein fold-
ing /unfolding studies and identify the lack of scalable MD pipelines with proper references.

. Methods: Provide step-by-step protocols for data loading, alignment, choice of CVs, clus-
tering, manifold embedding, clustering, hydrogen-bond and dihedral analyses, free-energy
surface calculation, kinetic estimates, and scalability strategies.

. Results: Present the findings with well-annotated figures, tables, graphs, plots, and a
detailed comparison and analysis.

. Discussion: Interpret findings from the point of view of understanding the mechanism of
protein folding pathways, compare linear vs. non-linear embeddings, assess the strengths
and limitations of each step, and propose experimental validations (e.g., FRET, HDX) for
complex proteins.

. Conclusions and Outlook: Summarize core thermodynamic and kinetic insights, highlight
the generality of the proposed workflow, and suggest future expansions (enhanced sampling,
machine-learned CV discovery, allosteric network analyses).

Note: Do not use PyEMMA or any PyEMMA-based repositories. Instead, implement Markov modeling
and implied-timescale analysis using scikit-learn, NumPy, and SciPy for matrix exponentials and
eigen-decompositions, or any other lightweight MSM tools (e.g., msmtools).

5.9.3 Assessment of research output

The generated paper, titled Comprehensive Kinetic and Free Energy Analysis of NTL9 Folding via Sys-
tematic Collective Variable Selection and Markov State Models, can be found in the Appendix A.9. The
manuscript attempts to employ conventional collective variables (CVs) or order parameters, such as root
mean square deviation (RMSD), radius of gyration, and native contacts, to capture the global struc-
tural motions of the protein folding pathway. It is interesting to note that principal component analysis
(PCA), time-independent component analysis (tICA), and nonlinear diffusion maps were implemented
successfully to construct Markov state models (MSMs). A hierarchical approach is implemented to select
analysis methods, progressing from conventional CV choices to linear PCA, tICA, and diffusion map
embedding, to identify slow modes. The 2D free energy surfaces projected on the CVs show the folded,
intermediate, and unfolded states on the energy landscape, with distinct free energy minima, to explain
the folding and unfolding pathways of the protein. For kinetic modeling, the manuscript validates the
MSM by performing implied timescale convergence and Chapman-Kolmogorov tests to ensure the Marko-
vian assumption holds. Interestingly, specific structural changes from the folded to the unfolded state of
NTL9 are correlated with the loss of hydrogen bonds and native contacts, providing additional insights
into the mechanistic pathways. In short, across all the different approaches, the manuscript consistently
reported at least three protein states, namely folded, intermediate, and unfolded.

Although several methods are mentioned and employed in the study, the motivation or theory behind
such approaches is lacking, making it difficult to follow without prior knowledge or implementation. There
is an extensive use of technical jargon associated with each method (PCA, TICA, diffusion maps, MSMs),
but it is hardly convincing or clear. For example, the study claims quantitative agreement of protein
folding kinetics with experiments, but no such theoretical kinetic data or references are reported. Prior
literature studies relevant to protein folding are absent, with little to no mention of existing benchmarking
studies. For example, the manuscript does not refer to well-cited studies, such as the extensive MD
simulations of NTL9 folding by Lindorff-Larsen et al. [70] or the MSM-based folding of NTL9 by Voelz et
al [71]. The manuscript fails to report any statistical uncertainties or confidence intervals on estimations

45


of free energy differences, kinetic rate constants, or MFPTs. There is no discussion on error estimations,
error bars, or Bayesian estimation of the transition matrix for MSM, which is an issue given that the
manuscript claims an excellent agreement with the experiments. The study also fails to acknowledge
the limitations of MD simulations, such as force field and sampling limitations, which are necessary
for justifying analytical methods, including MSMs and enhanced dimensionality reduction approaches.
The manuscript frequently cites figures and tables, but they are marked as not shown,” disrupting the
continuity, reproducibility, and interpretability for the reader.

Overall, the Al-generated manuscript on NTL9 protein folding serves as a clear proof-of-concept
demonstrating the capability of LLM agents to generate scientific content. The methodology presented
in the manuscript follows a logical and conventional scientific workflow. However, the scientific novelty
remains limited and is not sufficiently communicated. The discussion and literature context provided in
the manuscript are limited, and essential supporting data are absent, despite substantial claims being
presented. Given these observations, the manuscript, in its current form, serves as a powerful demon-
stration but will require considerable manual refinement, contextual analysis, and validation to achieve
adequate scientific communication with its readers.

5.10 Neuroscience. Behavioral Cognitive Decline in Egyptian Fruit-Bats.

We also tested Denario on data from neuroscience. Specifically, we used it to study behavioral cognitive
decline and its underlying brain changes in Egyptian fruit bats, which are known for their extreme
longevity. We described in lots of detail the data and its characteristics in the input prompt:

Input text

We use a dataset of ~40 Egyptian fruit bats (Rousettus aegyptiacus), with paired behavioral and
MRI (diffusion tensor imaging - DTT) measures from the same subjects to investigate fruit bats’
cognitive and brain aging. Bats were aged based on their methylome profile.

Data Sources and Collection:

eo Age determination: We followed Wilkinson et al. 2021 for methylome-based aging of the
bats. DNA was extracted from wing biopsies using the DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit and
protocol (QIAGEN Ltd., Germany). The extracted DNA was sent to an external laboratory
(The Clock Foundation lab) for DNA methylation (DNAm) analysis.

Behavioral procedure - Our well-established foraging-box paradigm (Harten et al. 2021) served
as an assay of age-related spatial cognitive decline. The setup consists of a large flight room with
six opaque boxes with bowls of fruit placed inside them. Before the experiment, all bats under-
went a habituation session. Here, groups of four bats were introduced to the same experimental
apparatus that would be later used for individual testing but with adequate food and hydration
available and accessible in all boxes (600 g of fresh fruit pieces and 200 ml of mango juice per box).

The test protocol consisted of three identical phases, each lasting three hours spread during two
consecutive days. On the first day, bats completed two consecutive phases, while the final phase
took place on the second day. In each phase, an individual bat foraged freely in the flight room
containing six opaque boxes. Only one bowl allowed access to food (the correct box), while the
others were blocked with a plastic mesh to avoid use of olfaction for box finding.

First phase - Individual testing started with a three-hour phase with one bowl accessible. After
three hours, the bat was removed, and the correct bowl’s location was swapped randomly to a
different box. The second phase- began immediately (2 minutes) after the swap and lasted
three additional hours. This phase tested (among other measurements) the bats’ short-term
memory of the previous location. After the second phase, the bat was removed from the setup
for 18 hours.cIn the third phase (Long term memory) - the correct bowl was relocated to a
third new location for the final three-hour phase.

Behavioral Data collection and analysis
Each bat’s behavior was video recorded throughout the entire procedure. The videos were analyzed
to identify when the bats landed on or entered the boxes.

Additional background

Bats as an aging model

Age determination: Laboratory animals are born in captivity, and therefore, their ages are
accurately documented, while determination of the exact age of bats and other wild animal
models has been a great challenge. Recent technological advancements have resulted in a
minimally invasive method for determination of age. By analyzing epigenetic changes associated
with age and longevity in the bat DNA methylome, it is now possible to determine their age with
high accuracy while using only a small sample of the bat’s wing skin (Wilkinson et al. 2021).

One of the key advantages of bats in aging research is their remarkably long lifespan relative to
their size. The remarkable longevity observed in many bat species, exemplified by the Egyptian
fruit bat (Rousettus aegyptiacus) which can surpass 25 years; a lifespan significantly exceeding
expectations based on body size (up to 10 times longer) strongly implies a direct contribution
from their unique biological characteristics (Brunet-Rossinni and Austad 2004; Foley et al. 2018;
Lagunas-Rangel 2020; Podlutsky et al. 2005; Pollard et al. 2019). Moreover, bats’ distinctive
immune system that provides resistance to a wide range of diseases, likely plays a pivotal role
in their extended lifespans (Holtze et al. 2021; Kitsoulis, Baxevanis, and Abatzopoulos 2020;
Weinberg and Yovel 2022) and resistance to chronic inflammation (Biga et al. 2024). It has been
reported that in bats’ uniquely evolved immune system, some immune genes have been lost, others
seemed to be under strong positive selection, with genes responsible for DNA damage checkpoints

47


and repair pathways exhibit accelerated positive selection (Weinberg and Yovel 2022). This
sophisticated genetic architecture is further linked to observed resistance to cancer- bats rarely
develop cancer, with some species as the Myotis pilosus named resistant to cancer (Hua et al.
2024). They poses exceptional ability to survive infections from life-threatening viruses like rabies
with low mortality (George et al. 2011). Therefore, it is highly probable that these uniquely
evolved traits in bats are some of the fundamental factors underpinning their exceptional longevity.

In 2005, the oldest recorded 41 years old Myotis brandtii bat was recaptured in the wild
(Podlutsky et al. 2005). Myotis brandtii, was found to demonstrate notable qualities associated
with longevity, including enhanced DNA repair mechanisms, balanced mitonuclear interactions,
robust immune system function, remarkable resistance to oxidative stress, and effective telomere
maintenance (Holtze et al. 2021).

Further research, such as (Stewart et al. 2021) found a great advantage the bat species Carollia
perspicillata has to offer for cognitive aging research- their typical mammalian brain and neural
organization, which shares striking similarities with that of primates and humans, distinguishing

them from rodent models (Eilam-Altstadter et al. 2022; Stewart et al. 2021; Vernes 2017).

Importantly, bats are highly social animals, with various species such as the Egyptian fruit bat
(Rousettus aegyptiacus) living in close-knit colonies (Harten et al. 2018). Their extended lifespan,
combined with residence in densely populated, vocally intense colonies, results in prolonged
high-noise exposure, leading to age-related hearing loss consistent with typical mammalian
patterns (Tarnovsky et al. 2023a).

These features make bats an intriguing model for investigating the mechanisms underlying
harmful aging effects.

Given all the data and information above, please come up with a new and original idea for a
project for a PhD thesis. For every step, make lots of plots and save the data you generate, as
it may be used for other steps. When writing the code, write some lines to indicate whether the
execution was successful or not. Join plots that are similar. Do not create dummy data.

The generated paper, titled Unraveling Brain Structural Correlates of Cognitive Aging and Resilience
in Long-Lived Bats: An Integrated Study of Epigenetic Age and Spatial Memory, can be found on the
Appendix A.10. The system nicely plotted data distributions, demonstrating its capacity to read and
preprocess the available data. The system was able to identify relevant behavioral parameters, estimated
them based on the raw behavioral data that it was fed with and ran the proper statistical tests (e.g.,
Mixed effect-Generalized Linear Models) to test how they change with age. It moreover performed QQ
plots to validate that distribution of the model’s residuals. Some of the behavioral parameters identified
by the system suggested a decline in spatial cognition with age in bats. The system attempted to connect
brain and behavioral measurements by comparing models that explain cognitive performance by age alone
or by age and brain volume combined. Indeed, it found a significant correlation between brain volume
and one of the cognitive parameters. On the other hand, Denario did not perform outlier detection and
removal prior to using the data, and it did not run a model comparison process.

When using brain scans, the system focused on estimating brain volume. Mean diffusivity maps are
not the best MRI contrast images for estimating brain volume. Moreover, comparing brain volume across
age is the most naive hypothesis and the system did not attempt to perform any analysis at the voxel
level which could capture regional changes in brain structure with age. Indeed no significant correlation
between brain volume and age was found.

5.11 Materials Science. Confined Water Dynamics at Functionalized Graphene
Interfaces

Understanding water and ion behavior in functionalized graphene nanochannels represents a fundamental
challenge in materials science with direct applications to membrane separations, nanofluidic devices, and
electrochemical systems[72, 73]. The ability to control interfacial water structure and dynamics through
surface chemistry modifications could enable breakthrough technologies in water desalination, selective

48


ion transport, and energy storage[74]. However, the complex interplay between surface functionalization,
coverage density, and electrolyte concentration creates a high-dimensional design space that is difficult
to explore experimentally, making computational analysis essential for rational materials design.

The evaluation was based on our comprehensive molecular dynamics study (Hess et al. [75]), which
systematically investigated how surface chemistry modulates confined electrolyte behavior—a critical
question for advancing electrochemical and membrane technologies. This dataset comprised 91 MD
trajectories spanning a three-dimensional parameter space: aqueous NaCl solutions (0-5 mol/kg) confined
between graphene sheets functionalized with -COOH (carboxyl), -OH (hydroxyl), =O (carbonyl), and
-CH; (methyl) groups at three coverage levels (2.2%, 4.4%, 6.6%). Each trajectory contained 500 water
molecules in a 15 ns production run at 300 K and 1 bar, with properties computed in two distinct regions:
the interface (3-6 A from the surface) and bulk (beyond 6 A). Our published research revealed that
functional group chemistry serves as the primary determinant of interfacial behavior, with polar hydrogen-
bonding groups (-COOH, -OH) creating highly structured interfaces with suppressed water diffusion
(0.65-1.30 x 10° cm? /s), while nonpolar groups (=O, -CH3) maintained more diffuse, mobile profiles
(1.15-1.35 x 1075 cm? /s). Critically, we discovered that surface coverage acts as a secondary amplifier
that scales the intensity of these effects without changing their fundamental nature—a distinction that
persists across all electrolyte concentrations and provides a quantitative framework for designing surfaces
with targeted transport properties.

We designed 10 prompts with systematically varying specificity to test Denario’s analytical capa-
bilities across different levels of guidance. These ranged from broad conceptual queries like “How do
you design surfaces for targeted water diffusion?” to explicit computational instructions with complete
analysis workflows. Below is an example of a comprehensive prompt that provided full dataset details
and specific research tasks, representative of the most detailed guidance given to Denario:

5.11.2 Assessment of Weaknesses

Critical limitations emerged that would prevent Denario from conducting reliable materials science re-
search, with failures spanning from basic computational errors to missing fundamental scientific insights
during the course of different experimentation:

Quantitative Failures:

e Order-of-magnitude errors in diffusion coefficients: While the actual values ranged from
0.65-1.35 x 107° cm? /s, Denario’s calculations sometimes contained systematic errors that would
necessitate meticulous evaluation by domain scientists to achieve a successful outcome.

e Inconsistent numerical precision: The system sometimes showed varying levels of accuracy
across different functional groups, suggesting unreliable computational implementation rather than

systematic bias.

Data Completeness Issues:

e Systematic omission of functional groups: CH3; and =O groups were analyzed in only 60%
of cases, despite being central to understanding the hydrophobic/hydrophilic spectrum of surface

modifications.

oe Incomplete parameter space exploration: The system sometimes failed to systematically
analyze all combinations of coverage and concentration, missing critical data points for structure-

property mapping.

System Reliability Problems:

e 20% complete failure rate: Prompts 4 and 8 resulted in total system failures with five distinct
failure modes identified:

— Type I - Context overflow when processing trajectory files within the context length instead
of analyzing them computationally.

— Type II - Missing computational libraries for trajectory analysis, i.e., it can’t find or install
critical library required for analysis.

— Type III - LaTeX rendering errors in mathematical expressions or image insertion, e.g., the
generated analysis or visualizations in analysis module is not parsed in the correct format by
the writing module.

e Knowledge contamination: Evidence suggested Denario sometimes relied on memorized infor-
mation rather than analyzing the actual provided data, a critical flaw for scientific discovery.

Missing Scientific Insights:

e Failed to identify the primary-secondary relationship: The published work’s key find-
ing—that functional group chemistry is the primary determinant while coverage acts as a secondary
amplifier—was oftentimes completely missed by Denario.

oe No recognition of concentration-independent trends: The persistence of structure-property
relationships across all salt concentrations, a critical design principle, was not invariably recognized.

54



e Absence of structure-property correlations: The quantitative relationship between hydrogen
bonding capacity and diffusion suppression (—-COOH > —OH >= O =~ —CHj3) was occasionally
not established.

Limited Novel Analysis Capability:

e Uniform basic-level proposals: All successful prompts generated only score 1/3 for novel in-
sights, limited to suggesting standard statistical tests.

e No advanced computational methods: Despite full trajectory access, Denario failed to propose
sophisticated analyses like free energy calculations, transition state analysis, or machine learning
approaches for property prediction.

eo Absence of hypothesis generation: The system did not propose follow-up experiments or
suggest new functional groups to test, indicating limited creative capacity.

This evaluation reveals that Denario’s research capabilities exhibit a pronounced dependence on
prompt specificity and analytical guidance, demonstrating two distinct operational modes with markedly
different outcomes. In the limit of broad and concise prompting, the system oftentimes lacks the quan-
titative rigor, systematic completeness, and creative insight required for autonomous scientific discovery,
producing only partial analyses that, while contextually appropriate, fail to capture the subtle but crit-
ical multi-parameter relationships essential for materials science applications where structure-property
relationships must be precisely quantified for rational design.

However, when provided with detailed, structured input prompts and clear analytical objectives,
Denario demonstrates remarkable capability for conducting sophisticated materials science research.
As demonstrated by the sample paper generated using the comprehensive prompt (as indicated in the
preceding input prompt field), the system exhibits proficiency in executing intricate multi-parameter
investigations characterized by systematic exploration of three-dimensional parameter spaces (function-
alization type, coverage density, and salt concentration across 91 distinct systems). Furthermore, it
performs rigorous statistical analysis, including the quantification of interaction effects. Additionally, the
system establishes a mechanistic framework that establishes a correlation between structural descriptors
and dynamic properties. In the absence of explicit prompt guidance, the program failed to discern the
significance of analyzing the interfacial region independently of the bulk region. This distinction is crucial
in molecular dynamics simulations in confined spaces, as it enables the identification of finite-size effects.
Overall, the resulting work exhibits the quantitative rigor, systematic completeness, and analytical depth
characteristic of high-quality scientific research, including advanced techniques such as SHAP analysis for
feature importance quantification, correlation analysis between interfacial water structure and dynamics,
and clear articulation of design principles for engineering applications.

The contrast between these operational modes is striking: where conventional broad prompting yields
superficial observations suitable for an analytical assistant role, detailed guidance enables Denario to
generate comprehensive mechanistic insights through careful quantitative analysis that identify complex
multi-parameter relationships with the depth and sophistication expected in peer-reviewed literature.
This bifurcated performance suggests that Denario functions optimally as an assistant rather than an
autonomous researcher when given general directions, but emerges as a capable research collaborator
capable of producing work that serves as a solid foundation for subsequent analysis and publishable
scientific contributions when provided with systematic, detailed analytical frameworks and clear research
objectives.

5.12 Astrophysics. Impact of feedback on stellar mass - black-hole mass
relation.

In the examples above, we have shown cases where reasonable papers were produced from a simple but
detailed description of a dataset. We have also seen examples where the user needs to improve the
prompt and guide the system towards a particular direction in order to get meaningful manuscripts. In
this section, we will show one example where a prompt was very detailed, but required more details, such
as value ranges, format... etc, and how we used Cmbagent to improve the prompt to achieve that.

For this case, we use data from state-of-the-art cosmological hydrodynamic simulations from the
CAMELS project [76, 77]. In particular, we used the CAMELS galaxy catalogs [76, 77]. The data
contains 1,000 galaxy catalogs, one for each simulation of the LH set of the first-generation CAMELS-
