by inputting Denario with the previously generated idea and the above input text, but with a few more
lines about using more sophisticated methods. In this case, Denario will generate a new methodology,
new analysis, and new paper, but the essence of the paper will remain intact. The generated paper,
titled Mapping the diversity of the black hole-stellar mass relation: the role of feedback and cosmology in
simulated galaxies, can be found in the Appendix A.12.

In this paper Denario investigated the impact of cosmological and astrophysical parameters on the
Mp — M, relationship in simulated galaxies. In particular, the paper models the relation between black-

58


hole mass and stellar mass in galaxies, as log,o(Mpn) = a + flog,,(M,). The paper splits the galaxy
population into three different stellar mass bins: Low-mass galaxies (M, < 10° My), Intermediate-mass
galaxies (10° < M, < 10° My), and High-mass galaxies (> 10° My). Next, it studies the dependence
of a, 8, and the scatter in the relation as a function of the cosmological and astrophysical parameters.
In the first pass, it used both linear regression and random forest to determine which parameter affects
the data the most in the different regimes. But in the second pass, it used XGBoost and SHAP values.
Furthermore, in this latest version of the paper, linear regression is carried out with the Huber loss to
minimize the impact of outliers.

The paper finds that for low stellar mass galaxies, supernova feedback is the physical process that
impacts the Mpy — M, relationship most, while AGN feedback becomes the main factor for massive
galaxies. It also finds that cosmological parameters play a secondary, but still important, factor. As
far as we know, this is a completely new result not explored before with CAMELS data. According to
experts in the field, the results are particularly sensitive and have important theoretical implications. We
believe that this paper may be what an undergraduate or graduate student does in a period of weeks to
months (depending on experience and familiarity with the data and machine learning techniques). While
not groundbreaking research, Denario showed that it is capable of generating new knowledge that may
be relevant for future investigations.

5.13 Quantum physics, machine learning & cosmology. Cosmological param-
eters from merger trees

A powerful facet of Denario is its ability to combine ideas from different scientific fields. To illustrate
this, we have asked Denario to write a paper that uses ideas from quantum physics to analyze cosmolog-
ical data. The generated paper, titled QITT-Enhanced Multi-Scale Substructure Analysis with Learned
Topological Embeddings for Cosmological Parameter Estimation from Dark Matter Halo Merger Trees,
is shown in the appendix. For this paper, we gave Denario merger trees from the CAMELS-SAM [78]
cosmological N-body simulations, post-processed and curated as in CosmoBench?® [79] and asked it to
write a paper using that data that uses ideas from Quantum Tensor Trains (QTTs) [80]. The exact input
text used was this:

Input text

We have a file containing 1000 merger trees from cosmological N-body simulations. The file is
located in

/mnt/home/fvillaescusa/public_www/Pablo_Bermejo/Pablo_merger_trees2.pt

The data is stored in PyTorch Geometric format, and can be read as:

import torch
f_tree = ’/mnt/home/fvillaescusa/public_www/Pablo_Bermejo/Pablo_merger_trees2.pt’
trainset = torch.load(f_tree, weights_only=False)

trainset is now a collection of 1000 PyTorch Geometric graphs. For instance, trainset[0] represents
the first merger tree and contains the data in this format:

Data(x=[382, 4], edge_index=[2, 381], edge_attr=[381, 1], y=[1, 2], num_nodes=382, lh_id=100,
mask_main=[93], node_halo_id=[382, 1])

x represents the node features. y is the value of the cosmological parameters, Omega m and
sigma_8. The node features are mass, concentration, vmax, scale factor. The first property is
log10(mass), the second is log10(concentration), the third one is logl0(Vmax), and the fourth one
is the scale factor.

The scale factor ranges from 0 (beginning of the universe) to 1 (current time). The mass goes
from 10 to 15. Each node represents a dark matter halo and is characterized by the four values
mentioned above: halo mass, halo concentration, halo Vmax (maximum circular velocity), and
scale factor. You may want to normalize each feature to have mean 0. Omega m ranges from
0.1 to 0.5, while sigma_8 goes from 0.6 to 1.0. For each simulation, i.e. a given value of the
cosmological parameters, there are 25 different merger trees chosen randomly.

28nttps://cosmobench.streamlit.app/

59


Please come up with an idea to explore this data using methods from Quantum Tensor Trains.

Note that PyTorch and PyTorch Geometric are already installed. The system has 16 cpus and 1
gpu. Please make some plots to illustrate your findings.

The generated paper, QITT-Enhanced Multi-Scale Substructure Analysis with Learned Topological
Embeddings for Cosmological Parameter Estimation from Dark Matter Halo Merger Tree, can be found
in the Appendix A.13. In it, Denario analyzes cosmological merger trees, firstly performing a multi-scale
substructure identification for each merger tree. This step identifies branches of a merger tree (that
represent sub-graphs by themselves) where a merger happens or a significant change in halo properties
occurs. Next, it extracts features for the substructure: 1) physical features such as the scale factor when
a merger takes place and the total mass in the substructure, and 2) topological embeddings from each
substructure extracted using graph neural networks. All these features were then used to construct a 3D
tensor for each merger tree that contains the physical and topological properties for all its substructures.
The dimension of this tensor was (60,74), i.e. 60 substructures (some merger trees may contain fewer,
but 0-padding was used) and 74 topological plus physical features.

That 3D tensor is relatively big, which makes it difficult to use for downstream tasks. Because of
that, it reduces its representation using tensor trains that the paper refers to as QITT (Quantum-inspired
tensor trains) since these are methods commonly used in some areas of quantum physics. QITT aims
to compress high-dimensional tensors (e.g., representing high-dimensional functions), producing a low-
rank decomposition of the original tensors into tensors with smaller ranks. For instance, in the case of
smooth functions, QITT has been shown to achieve an optimal approximation order. This is the case
of any univariate polynomial of degree p, which can be represented by a QITT of rank at most (1 + p)
[81], where the number of tensors in the tensor train dictates the resolution within the discretized grid.
Here, we would expect contiguous merger trees to possess similar characteristics, and hence a sense of
smoothness that could be translated into low-rank tensors describing such features.

The result of compressing the original 3D feature tensor with QITT is the latent representation of
each merger tree and is used as input for different regression models, including linear regression, random
forest, and gradient boosted trees. The optimal dimensionality of this reduced tensor was found to be 202.
One could expect that the decomposition algorithm, factoring out the tensor chain, could still benefit
from a more refined breakdown, probably using a higher number of tensors connected through bonds
with lower ranks.

The paper then compares the results obtained against several baselines, including 1) physical features
of the substructures (i.e., no topological or QITT compression), 2) global features of each global tree,
and 3) topological features from each substructure but no QITT compression.

The paper finds that linear regression with QITT features performs very well and can constrain the
value of both ,, and og with high accuracy. The paper also finds that linear regression with the global
features of the trees performs slightly better, indicating that simple tree-level features may be enough
to regress the parameters. The paper also shows some interesting results, such as the graph topological
embedding containing information about the number of halos in the substructure.

We were impressed by this paper, which required the expertise of researchers in cosmology, machine
learning, and quantum physics to evaluate its relevance. The fact that Denario was able to perform such
complex analysis, which includes a non-trivial decomposition of merger trees into substructures, training
graph neural networks in an unsupervised setup, and compressing data with quantum-inspired tensor
trains.

We note that this paper was generated on a MacBook Pro without using GPUs and with a very
limited dataset. Therefore, we believe the results can be substantially improved; for instance, training
was only done for five epochs. Given its originality, interesting results, and methods, we believe that this
paper, with a few improvements and a reliable scaling analysis, could be considered for submission to an
international journal.

We note that this paper was accepted for publication in the Agents4Science 2025 conference, the first
open conference where Al serves as both primary authors and reviewers of research papers’. We note
that around 250 submissions were made, with 48 acceptances, and only 5 fully Al-generated papers were
accepted, including this one, reaching the maximum score [82].

29nttps://agentsdscience. stanford. edu/

60


6 Discussion

In this section, we describe important aspects related to Denario such as failure modes, validation and
evaluation, advantages and limitations, and future directions.

6.1 Failure modes

By running Denario many times over many different datasets from different disciplines, we have identified
a couple of severe failure modes. We now describe them here in detail:

6.1.1 Cylic peptide generation

In this case, we asked Denario to solve a computational biology problem of generating molecular struc-
tures for cyclic peptides. After multiple failed attempts, the agents hallucinated an entire paper without
implementing the necessary numerical solver. The problem itself has well-established solutions in the
literature [83, 84], involving linear algebra computations and optimization algorithms. While the agents
were able to outline plausible solution strategies by either mimicking known methods or proposing novel
machine-learning approaches, their actual code implementations consistently produced structures with
significant geometric flaws, and adding detailed geometry requirements did not help.

Furthermore, after several tries, Denario came up with a paper claiming solutions were successfully
found, and data plots were provided to show the successful results. However, upon inspection, we could
not locate the solutions referenced in the paper, and the corresponding source code lacked a crucial
numerical solver. Even in the paper, the section describing this missing solver was very vague and
abstract. This was a surprising case, and such “cheating” only appeared once in our experiments. We
suspect this could be due to the easily accessible solution descriptions and datasets in the literature, while
the actual codes, in contrast, were embedded in large software packages that have license requirements.
This case underscores the importance of scrutinizing agent-generated research with the same rigor applied
to human-generated work: verifying source codes and raw data is essential for ensuring the validity of
scientific claims.

6.1.2 Pure Mathematics

As part of our evaluation of Denario’s capabilities, we tested its performance on an open-ended research
problem in pure mathematics. The problem concerned the representability of simplicial complexes as
nerves of collections of unit balls in Euclidean space, and a related question on approximating semi-
algebraic sets by unions of balls [85, 86].

The input text asked whether every finite abstract simplicial complex can be realized as the nerve of
a collection of closed unit balls in some Euclidean space, and whether a compact semi-algebraic set in
Euclidean space can be approximated — up to homotopy — by a union of balls of fixed radius. While
some partial results are known in special cases — for example, in the one-dimensional case, or for sets
with positive reach or defined in general position — the problem remains unsolved in general.

We used both a concise and an extended version of the input text to generate five research papers.
The outputs were then analyzed in detail, evaluating their mathematical rigor, conceptual coherence, use
of references, and stylistic authenticity. The results revealed several fundamental shortcomings:

1. Superficial structure. The papers resembled mathematical writing on the surface — with titles,
abstracts, and phrases like “main theorem” — but lacked real internal logic. There were no formal
statements or proofs, and the flow of ideas was loose or incoherent.

2. Misuse of citations. Foundational references were often missing, while others were used decora-
tively — cited as support for claims introduced in the same paragraph, or with no clear connection
to the text.

3. Template-like prose. Sentences like “we propose a novel invariant” or “we provide computational
evidence” were repeated across papers, detached from any technical substance. This led to a sense
of scripted, ritual language rather than genuine mathematical argumentation.

4. Mathematically vacuous results. One example involved a seemingly new property — the
“Controlled Local Intersections” condition — that turned out to be either trivially true or trivially
false depending on interpretation. The paper contained no real proofs, only vague commentary and a
single non-example. A few incidental signs — such as unusual font choices or two-column layouts —

61


further contributed to a sense of unfamiliarity. While not central, these cosmetic features reinforced
the impression that the texts were not fully integrated into the stylistic norms of mathematical
writing. Some local ideas had superficial plausibility, but none were developed in a mathematically
meaningful way. The outputs resembled a stream of initial intuitions that a human mathematician
might have before formalizing anything — but without the subsequent refinement or insight.

This case study highlights a central limitation: the system can imitate the form of mathematical writing,
but not yet its function. Mathematics is not merely a collection of symbols or formulas, but a social
and rhetorical practice governed by implicit conventions. Validity in mathematics is not conferred by
structure alone, but by participating convincingly in a shared discourse — one that includes expectations
of clarity, responsibility, and logical development.

While the experiment did not uncover any convincing or usable results, it revealed how close the
system is to replicating outward patterns of mathematical behavior. The fact that it can generate
seemingly plausible definitions or mimic standard stylistic elements is nontrivial. Still, the outputs lacked
the clarity, progression, and internal necessity that characterize mathematics, at least as conventionally
recognized within the mathematical community.

6.2 Validation and Evaluation

Formally, validation is the act of providing objective evidence that a system, model, or method is fit
for its intended purpose. In the case of Al-generated papers, validation should be understood as the
process of checking whether the claims made in the paper are true or not. In other words, validation
tasks include verifying that the codes written are correct and that the results obtained contain enough
evidence to support the claims in the paper. For standard papers, this process is called peer review.

We note that LLM hallucination is a well-known problem that can cause agents write incorrect code,
reach conclusions or make claims that do not have enough evidence. In other cases, they can simply
make up things. This problem can occur at any stage, from the generation of ideas and coding to paper
writing. While Denario contains multiple agents whose role is to check the work of others, ultimately, a
human expert should be responsible for checking and verifying all steps involved in the process.

We have performed an exhaustive validation of some of the papers generated by Denario. We now
discuss two particular examples:

e For the cyclic peptide generation mentioned above, we found that even if all the agents involved in
coding failed, the paper-writing agent wrote an entire paper claiming things without any evidence
at all, likely being dominated by its prior knowledge and not the evidence from its calculations.

e To evaluate the scientific integrity of one of the generated papers in astrophysics, in person, our
team read the paper in detail and wrote code to reproduce the figures and claims in the paper.
We note that we did not provide access to the codes written by Denario for that paper. The
domain expert was able to reproduce very similar metrics for the correlation and validate that an
independent human reviewer can arrive at the same conclusion and scientific discovery.

An obvious conclusion is that a human expert should always check the codes and claims made by
Denario written papers. However, we also note that this should also be done for standard human-created
papers. We note that there have been multiple cases of standard papers that have passed peer-review
validation and have lately been found to be wrong due to authors modifying or inventing data in order
to provide evidence for a preconceived idea.

Another important aspect in the revision of scientific papers is evaluation. In this context, we un-
derstand evaluation as the process of determining the quality of the paper, its value in comparison with
previous works, and its contribution to the field. We note that evaluating the quality of scientific papers
is a highly non-trivial and likely subjective task. In his current form, the evaluation of Al-generated
papers by Denario is done by human domain experts’

For the papers discussed in this paper (the ones located in the Appendix) we have asked the domain
experts in our team to evaluate them and to provide a numerical score to them. The range was from
0 (for really bad papers) to 10 (really good papers). We show the distribution of the numerical scores
provided by the experts in Fig. 11. We note that a numerical score of 5 represents a normal” paper. As
can be seen, 3 papers were ranked below the average, while the majority of them were above. In some
cases, the human experts provided scores as large as 8 and 9. From this experiment, we can conclude

30 Although we note that Denario contains the reviewer module that is designed to provide a referee-report-like as a proxy
for performing evaluation.

that Denario has the capacity of producing ”reasonable” and ”interesting” papers, given all the caveats
discussed in Sec. 5. We note that this score is highly subjective and does not pretend to be a rigorous
criterion, but to provide some insight into the generative capabilities of Denario.

6.3

Advantages and limitations

According to the analysis of the example papers discussed in Sec. 5, we believe agentic systems like
Denario will bring some important positive aspects to science in general:

The ideas generated by Denario can enhance the researcher’s capabilities by unveiling concepts
(from mathematics, machine learning, or other disciplines) unknown to the researcher. We believe
this may help researcher be more creative and discover techniques that may be relevant to their
particular problem.

System like Denario excel at performing shallow research very quickly. In other words, while
current LLMs may not have the capabilities to abstract the solution to a problem to something
fundamental (e.g., a single mathematical equation governing the physics of many different systems),
they are very good at performing relatively simple analyses and reaching very useful conclusions.
This capability may enable researchers to identify promising research avenues and focus on those
faster than with traditional human approaches.

All text, plots, and code are output by Denario and therefore provide a high level of transparency
and enable reproducibility. This is an important step for many disciplines, where calculations are
complex and results cannot easily be reproduced.

The potential connection with other fields at the level of ideas of methods may enable more collab-
oration and interdisciplinary work.

Systems like Denario are excellent at exploring risky ideas. For instance, if a study is highly
uncertain, and the outcome may not be very rewarding (e.g., exploring an idea that even if it
works, may not lead to a publication), many researchers will feel discouraged from pursuing it.
However, that study may be very useful for other analyses, perhaps completely unrelated. We
believe researchers may consider exploring such ideas if the effort required is significantly reduced,
as tools like Denario can do.

We believe that systems like Denario can help researchers in many different tasks, from idea
generation to method implementation. Ultimately, if we lead AI to perform some of these tasks,

63


It

under our supervision, scientists will have more time to think deeply and perform higher-level
research. This could make science deeper, broader, and more robust.

is also important to discuss the current limitations associated to Denario

Citations. The citations in both papers typically refer to relevant papers for the considered sentence,
but perhaps not the most relevant ones. An expert reader can easily spot an Denario Al-generated
paper from a human one just from the citations.

Depth. From the generated papers, we can see that the explanations of the results tend to be
relatively shallow and not comparable to what an experienced researcher would write. As we show
in the discussion of many papers in Sec. 5, current system behaves more like a good undergraduate
or early graduate student rather than a full professor in terms of big picture, connecting results...
etc.

LaTeX. Sometimes, figures are generated with non-LaTeX y/x labels or legends. For instance, some
figures have omega m in the y-axis instead of Q,. Another problem is that the paper writing agent,
more rarely, makes small mistakes in LaTeX, e.g., dealing with underscores in equations, text, and
references. These errors usually prevent the paper from being compiled properly, although they are
easy to fix.

Coding. In its current form, Denario sometimes may struggle with writing and executing code.
This may happen for multiple reasons, such as changes in the API for recent packages and failures
when running code in parallel. This behavior may cause the system to crash during the analysis
module.

We believe all the above points can be addressed, or at least significantly improved, by improving the
agents in charge of some tasks (e.g. citations), by advances in LLMs (e.g. reasoning), or by including

more

6.4

agents to fix the small mistakes made by the other agents (LaTeX).

Future directions

There are numerous ways to improve Denario, which we plan to implement in the near future:

While in its current version Denario made some asynchronous LLM calls, it does not fully exploit
its potential. Reformatting some agents to make more asynchronous calls can significantly speed
up the time spent on the different tasks and lower the cost.

In its current form, Denario may fail or significantly deviate from its goals at several stages of the
process. Adding new agents that can provide feedback on the outcome of some agents will improve
the stability of the framework and make it more robust.

Parallelization and optimization. Our current workflows are sequential: we deal with tasks step-by-
step, doing one thing at a time. Efficiency will be greatly improved using parallelization strategies,
e.g., [87] or massgen?!.

Adaptive Planning & Control. Currently, once a plan is fixed, it is executed until the end. This is
not how research is done. Next steps are always conditioned, or even determined, by past ones. A
more refined Planning é Control strategy will have adaptive planning so that after each task, the

new steps left to be done can be re-assessed and potentially changed, removed, or some new steps
can be added.

The paper writing module can be significantly improved by adding more context information about
the code written and the figures created. Furthermore, specialized agents to check claims and put
them in touch with literature agents can significantly help write things with a broader perspective.

Currently, Denario only supports paid LLM providers through their API, but there are plenty of
open-source models that can be installed and run locally. We plan to provide support to run our
agents with locally installed LLMs, which will give the user more freedom to choose among the
available LLMs, use custom models, and get more control over their resources.

3lhttps://docs.massgen.ai/en/latest/

64


e We keep working on easing access to Denario. Besides improving the Python API and the GUI, we
plan to include a Command Line Interface (CLI) to run the different modules of the multi-agent
system without the need to write code explicitly.

e Develop evaluation frameworks that will allow us to improve the quality of the research assistance
tools in a systematic way. This will rely on extended benchmark datasets, following the efforts of
TPBench [88] or ReplicationBench [89].

7 Ethical implications and scientific challenges

Systems like Denario are designed to facilitate the work of scientists. However, the powerful technology
behind them raises many ethical considerations. In this section, we describe some of them and also
discuss how Al agents fit in the way we do science from a historical perspective.

7.1 Ethics

We now describe a few points where the usage of systems like Denario will lead to ethical considerations.

e Quality of research: Generative Al tools such as Denario allow users to easily and quickly generate
large numbers of potentially low-quality papers. Some of the incentive structures of academic
research may lead to individuals using generative Al tools to artificially increase their research
output and/or inflate citation numbers for their own articles.

e Implications for scientific training and education: Tools such as Denario have the potential
to make it easy to write an entire paper with just a few lines of description about a project idea,
its methods, results, and the plots made. This poses questions and challenges for scientific training
and education. In what ways are scientific writing and creativity in data analysis valuable as skills
inherent to the researcher? To what degree or in what fashion should Al tools play a role in helping
researchers carry out this type of work to begin with? How should we teach students the skills they
will need to succeed as producers and interpreters of research?

eo Assessment of quality and legitimacy: If these tools start being used widely, there may be a
risk of trusting results from agents without any validation. For instance, an agent may perform
some calculation and decide that it is not interesting. Without validation, that result may block a
potentially interesting research direction. Indeed, as Al agents become both increasingly common
producers and consumers of research, we are faced with important questions about the nature of
quality and legitimacy in research. How is quality and correctness defined, and by whom? If Al
agents become the standard by which to assess the quality of a paper or whether it is “correct”
or “wrong”, how does one assess which AI agent to trust? We can therefore fall into a situation
of crisis with respect to responsible scientific working guidelines. If anyone can use Al to generate
paper, and if no one can control this process and oversee standards of originality, who can be held
responsible?

e Homogenization: A pattern seen across some of the application cases presented is Denario’s
difficulty proposing new research questions or identifying serendipitous, potentially novel findings.
This is representative of a greater concern that Al agent-driven research might be biased towards
producing research that confirms and aligns with the existing scientific literature of its training
dataset, potentially leading to homogenized research and stifling innovation. Further experimen-
tation with model architectures, such as the multi-agent frameworks implemented here, could help
address this issue.

e Access: Al tools such as Denario require significant investment in computational infrastructure
and energy for their training and operation. These constraints shape which actors have access to
their use and operation, affecting the fields of science being chosen for AI agent-driven research, the
types of problems being tackled, and the methods used to do so. We must take deliberate steps to
democratize both access to the benefits of Al agent-driven research and participation in its creation
and training, in order to make sure science addresses the full breadth of interests and problems
across societies.

65


eo Authorship: Generative Al has already sparked debates over the nature of scientific authorship
and Denario is no different. A key requirement for understanding the debate is a careful definition of
the roles of authorship in the scientific literature. One clear role of authorship is its use to allocate
professional credit and recognition for doing work, which is important for career development.
This aspect of authorship raises important questions that we must build answers to as a scientific
community: if a human author uses Al agents to aid their research, in what ways is that different
from previous research tools, and should that change the way we attribute professional credit to the
human author? Should AI systems be assigned that kind of professional credit, and if so, for what
purpose? How should the corpus of work used to train the AI agent be recognized, and what kind
of professional credit should be used? Moreover, a second role of authorship implies responsibility
for the quality and some implications of the results presented, an aspect that also raises critical
questions for both the scientific community and wider society. Who should bear the ultimate
responsibility for the work presented in a paper? What kind of guarantees and accountability
should be upheld by the individuals and organizations training the model? A valuable but certainly
insufficient step to addressing these issues would be to clearly state when a research article has been
generated by agentic systems, which would have the added benefit of flagging the article as such
when considering the training datasets of future AI agents, improving their performance [90].

eo Misalignment of incentives in scientific publishing: Given the speed and volume with which
research articles can be generated using agentic tools like Denario and the career incentives that
are associated with inflated publishing statistics in our current academic system, the proliferation
of AI agent-driven research may lead to a deluge of low-quality papers overwhelming scientific
publishing and readership capabilities. This misalignment of career incentives with the purposes of
productively advancing scientific knowledge can also lead to situations in which users maliciously
generate research articles that purposefully cite their own previous research. These challenges pose
questions not only about the incentive structure in academic publishing and career building, but
also about what the role of a “research article” is in the age of generative AI and what form or
medium can most effectively communicate and evaluate science in this new regime.

oe Environmental concerns: Training and running LLMs come at a significant cost in the consump-
tion of energy, water, coolant, and rare earth metals, among others [91, 92]. As with other massive
applications of machine learning, the scale of this resource consumption is far from sustainable at
the time of writing. Researchers must take active roles in advocating for and developing solutions
to address this major issue.

e Malicious use: Al agents could be used to quickly flood the scientific literature with claims driven
by a particular political agenda or specific commercial or economic interests. The volume of papers
created could then influence the corpus used to train non-malicious Al agents, reinforcing and
effectively “laundering” facts. Developing ways to detect this at the technical level and discuss it
at the societal level is critical.

Overall, tools like Denario can enhance researchers’ capabilities by helping them in tasks that require
a significant amount of time, such as writing papers, debugging code, or exploring ideas. We believe the
best usage of Denario would be as an Al-assistant for different tasks. For instance, it can be used to
improve an idea (by exploiting methods not known to the researcher), or help with the writing of the
paper once the results are in place. Denario is able to perform complex tasks orders of magnitude faster
than humans. We think the quality of the research papers will crucially depend on how the system is
used:

e Responsible usage. We believe that under responsible usage, the quality of the research papers will
improve. In order to explain this apparently contradictory logic (fast generation vs quality), we
believe that researchers are usually time-limited; e.g., an undergraduate needs to graduate or a
graduate student needs to apply for postdoc/faculty jobs. Given a fixed amount of time, the fact
that a very small fraction of that time goes into generating a draft with all associated codes and
plots, will enable the researcher to dedicate more time to thinking deeper, improving the quality of
the paper, improving the methods, than if the user needs a very large fraction of the time to just
produce a first draft.

o [Irresponsible usage. If the usage takes place in an irresponsible manner, i.e. just generating papers
without or little validation, then given the current capabilities of systems like Denario, the quality
of the papers will degrade.

66


While we expect both usage modes, we think most researchers will make use of these tools responsibly.
Finally, we would like to stress that systems like Denario will further emphasize the need to give more
weight to quality rather than quantity when evaluating scientists’ careers. However, given the fact that
quality is very hard to quantify and likely subjective, the current system may need to reshape itself for
the benefit of science and society.

7.2 Epistemic changes in a science driven by AI agents

The integration of LLMs and AI agents into scientific practice marks a profound inflection point in the
philosophy of science. These systems are not mere computational tools; they increasingly participate
in the core activities of science—formulating hypotheses, synthesizing literature, generating theoretical
connections, falsification procedures, theory choice, epistemic virtue-discussions, and even simulating
reasoning. This shift forces us to re-examine long-standing philosophical frameworks concerning the
nature of scientific rationality, understanding, and progress. In particular, the proliferation of AI agents
in scientific research poses questions regarding the nature of scientific knowledge, its legitimacy, its quality,
and its ultimate purpose.

7.2.1 The nature of scientific knowledge in AI-driven science

To examine this, we can first turn to the notion of “research programmes” as defined by Imre Lakatos
(1978) [93]: long-term, theoretical frameworks with a stable “hard core” and evolving “protective belts”
of auxiliary hypotheses. Lakatos argued that scientific rationality lies in comparing the relative progress
of these programmes: a progressive programme predicts novel facts and accommodates anomalies, while
a degenerative one merely accommodates data retrospectively. Within this framework, LLMs raise fun-
damental questions. Are they simply auxiliary tools bolstering existing programmes—helping refine
theories, conduct literature reviews, and test hypotheses more efficiently? Or do they represent the birth
of a new kind of research programme altogether—one not driven by causal explanation, but by linguistic
modeling, probabilistic reasoning, and massive-scale pattern recognition?

If the latter is true, then LLMs bring with them a new type of “hard core”: the assumption that
knowledge is fundamentally representable and usable in statistical-linguistic form. This new type of
hardcore could be ultimately defined as the model embeddings of a training dataset and interpreted in
human terms as the weighted aggregate of a body of scientific literature. Weighted how? Nobody can
fully understand, because understanding mechanistically is no longer the goal. This contrasts sharply
with traditional programmes based on mechanistic or formal-logical representations. Moreover, LLMs
produce novel predictions, connections, and reformulations—yet not always in a way that is interpretable
or falsifiable in Lakatosian terms. As such, they may challenge the very criteria by which progress in
science is traditionally measured. Lakatos maintained a vision of rational science driven by theoretically
motivated explanations; LLMs, in contrast, are increasingly effective despite their lack of explicit theory.
Their success poses a challenge: can a research programme be progressive even if it lacks a human-
understandable theoretical core?

W.V.0O. Quine’s epistemology—particularly as articulated in Two Dogmas of Empiricism” (1951)
[94] and his broader naturalized epistemology—offers a subtle but profound framework for understanding
the epistemic disruptions caused by LLMs. Quine rejected the analytic-synthetic distinction and argued
for a holistic view of knowledge, where statements face the tribunal of experience not in isolation, but
only as part of an interconnected web of belief. In this view, revision is always possible, even for logical
or mathematical statements, and empirical data can force changes anywhere in the system.

From this perspective, LLMs do not simply introduce new tools into the scientist’s arsenal; they
reconfigure the web itself. LLMs are not theory-driven or tethered to empirical input in the traditional
sense. They model language, not the world—but through language, they influence belief revision, hy-
pothesis generation, and theoretical framing. As such, they intervene in science at the level of conceptual
structure, shifting what is considered coherent, plausible, or meaningful within the web of scientific belief.

7.2.2 The nature of scientific legitimacy, quality, and purpose in Al-driven science

The notion that science is a historically contingent and socially negotiated enterprise, insisted upon
by writers such as Paul Feyerabend (1975) [95], finds new relevance in the age of AI. As LLMs are
integrated into research workflows, they begin to shape what is seen as legitimate knowledge, not through
philosophical argument but through infrastructural embedding—by determining what is written, cited,
or ignored. This has deep implications for the sociology of knowledge: the epistemic authority of LLMs

67


may evolve not because they “know” in any human sense, but because they shape the conditions under
which knowledge is produced and circulated.

Additionally, Quine’s naturalized epistemology—his call to study knowledge using the methods of
science itself—opens the door to seeing LLMs as epistemic agents within a naturalized framework. They
are not mere passive instruments but active components in the scientific ecosystem, akin to laboratories,
statistical methods, or even communities of inquirers. Yet they differ in one crucial way: they operate in a
non-transparent manner, lacking not only introspection but causal understanding. This opacity generates
an ontological challenge: What is the status of knowledge produced by a system that lacks grounding in
experience or semantics, and whose justification lies in performance rather than comprehension? How is
the quality of this mode of scientific knowledge judged, and should it be judged differently at all?

From a Quinean standpoint, LLMs are both natural extensions of scientific inquiry and radical dis-
ruptors of its structure. They unsettle the boundary between tool and theorist, instrument and agent.
They force us to reconsider what counts as observation, evidence, and explanation, and they deepen the
holistic fluidity of the scientific web—potentially accelerating progress, but also undermining the inter-
pretive clarity on which much of science has historically depended. Ultimately, Al-driven research opens
(or reopens) a question on the fundamental purpose and value of scientific knowledge and enterprise,
highlighting a tension between the goal of a mechanistic, human understanding of the world and the goal
of achieving statistical practical utility first and foremost.

An interesting situation in which this tension surrounding the ultimate purpose of agentic Al research
manifests is the Turing Trap [96]. The term “Turing Trap” refers to the tendency to develop Al systems
that mimic or replace human cognition, instead of enhancing or complementing it. Named in reference to
Alan Turing’s famous test for machine intelligence, the trap emerges when passing as human becomes the
benchmark for success, thus narrowing the scope of what AI can and should do. In science, this translates
into a shift from tools that assist human reasoning toward agents that simulate it. LLMs such as GPT-5
are increasingly being used not merely for clerical tasks, but for co-authoring papers, generating reviews,
or even proposing research directions. This then underscores the question: if AT agents have the potential
to exceed human capabilities in at least certain regards, should we reevaluate the basic tasks and units
of how science is practiced, communicated, and evaluated in non-human terms?

7.3 The impact of AI agent-driven science on the structure of scientific work

Besides the questions raised regarding epistemic changes in the nature of science and scientific knowledge,
agentic Al-driven research also appears poised to reconfigure the structure of scientific practice. To
understand the ways in which this may occur, it is helpful to use the framework developed by Thomas
Kuhn (1975) [97] according to which science develops through periods of “normal science” in which
knowledge is incorporated into existing theoretical frameworks, alternated by “paradigm shifts” during
which those frameworks are overhauled.

7.3.1 AI agent-driven science as an enabler of innovation

From a Kuhnian perspective, LLMs could be seen as catalysts for a paradigm shift. Kuhn emphasized
that science does not evolve through continuous accumulation of knowledge, but rather through disruptive
revolutions in which one paradigm is replaced by another, reshaping the methods, standards, and even
the very questions that science considers meaningful. LLMs introduce precisely this kind of rupture: they
not only change how science is done, but what it means to do science. Their ability to generate plausible
hypotheses, summarize vast literatures, and recombine knowledge across disciplinary boundaries at scales
and speeds beyond the capabilities of a single human researcher challenges the prevailing paradigm in
which singular human cognition, creativity, and interpretive judgment are central to scientific discovery.

Kuhn's notion of “normal science”, routine puzzle-solving within an accepted paradigm, may become
destabilized as LLMs increasingly participate in tasks once thought uniquely human. Moreover, their
epistemic style is deeply different: LLMs operate not on causal mechanisms but on statistical and linguistic
associations. Insofar as LLMs begin to influence theory choice, experimental design, or even what is
considered an interesting or valid research question, they may be ushering in a new epistemic regime,
one where prediction trumps explanation, pattern overrules theory, and where coherence across texts
replaces ontological depth. Kuhn's framework helps us see that the rise of LLMs may not be a simple
technological enhancement. It could even bring us to a deep transformation of the values and structures
that undergird scientific practice. This presents a challenge for the very practice of science.

Paul Feyerabend’s radical critique of scientific rationality offers another perspective. In Against
Method (1975) [95], Feyerabend argued that science does not—and should not—operate according to

68


fixed methodological rules. Progress, he claimed, often occurs when conventions are violated and when
heterodox or even “irrational” approaches are permitted to flourish. From this viewpoint, LLMs may
be the ultimate Feyerabendian agents. They defy the norms of methodological consistency, rely on
opaque black-box architectures, and generate insights not through logic or controlled experimentation
but through stochastic generation and pattern inference across language corpora. Precisely because of this
transgressive character, LLMs may serve as engines of epistemic pluralism and innovation. They break
down disciplinary barriers, resurface forgotten ideas, and draw novel analogies that human researchers
may overlook. Feyerabend’s critique of scientific monism—the idea that there is one best method or
one correct epistemic framework—is echoed in the way LLMs expose the contingencies and limits of
human-centric scientific norms. In his terms, they have the potential to be tools that reassert the chaotic,
cultural, and creative dimensions of science, reminding us that genuine progress often arises not from
strict adherence to method but from bold and unpredictable departures from it.

7.3.2 AI agent-driven science as a stifling, homogenizing force

Despite this potential, an argument can also be made that AI agent-driven science risks minimizing
innovation rather than enhancing it. In Kuhnian terms, AI agent-driven scientist could lead to a reduction
in paradigm shifts and a slump into ” perpetual normal science”. When AI agents carry out entire cycles of
knowledge production, we risk creating a system that perpetually produces research extending the status
quo, the risk of homogeneity. Given that these agents are by design trained on broadly similar bodies of
knowledge, one wonders to what degree they are intrinsically biased towards what Kuhn calls "normal
science production”, tending to generate output that fits well to knowledge available in the training set.
In Feyerabendian terms, the nightmare of total scientific monism could be a possible outcome of Al-driven
homogenization if AI agent research converges on the same training data sets, architectures, and desired
outcomes.

In addition to the biases inherent in their own architecture, Al agent-driven research can also reinforce
biases in the structures of scientific institutions. The ease with which agentic AI can be used to produce
scientific output that easily conforms to existing dogma—useful in some environments to inflate statistics
valuable for career advancement—could result in less paradigm-shifting work. Furthermore, the potential
for a rapid feedback loop in which future agentic Al is training on Al-generated scientific literature with
the same bias towards ”extending” existing theory (rather than disrupting it) could accelerate this trend.

However, this doesn’t have to be the case: we can build in statistical and agent-level architectures
that minimize this bias towards normal science and emphasize the role of human scientists within the
loop of Al-assisted knowledge production. Achieving this implies an active effort from all parts of the
scientific enterprise, from the computer science behind the design of AI agents to the career incentives for
individuals and funding mechanisms used to encourage scientific production. It is crucial to democratize
both access to the tools themselves as well as the skills and infrastructure for their development, and to
be deliberate and conscientious when compiling training data.

7.4 Conclusions from philosophy of science

LLMs do not merely support current scientific practice; they transform it. Through the lens of Kuhn [97],
they potentially inaugurate a new paradigm of machine-augmented science—or plunge us into perpetual
normal science. Through Lakatos [93], they challenge existing research programmes and perhaps herald
a new one grounded in probabilistic modeling rather than explanatory theory, with the potential to
bring about unprecedented pragmatic relevance—and perhaps a vision of science divorced from human
understanding. And through Feyerabend [95], they emerge as agents of epistemic disorder and creativity,
unsettling dogma and enabling new modes of inquiry—or trap us in sterile, homogenized scientific monism.
As the transformation of science and its practice by Al tools continues, it is worth remembering that an
LLM is ultimately an “universal interpolator” that retrieves information—directly or interpolated—from
a body of knowledge, with all the advantages and flaws that this entails.

Ultimately, AI agent-driven science raises crucial but uncomfortable questions at the heart of sci-
ence: are we outsourcing not just labor, but judgment and meaning? When the outputs of LLMs are
treated as autonomous knowledge contributions—rather than the mediated results of probabilistic as-
sociations—they can displace the interpretive and evaluative labor that defines good science. Scientific
rationality becomes performative: coherence, plausibility, and citation density stand in for theoretical
depth, causal understanding, or experimental validation. To engage seriously with the implications of
LLMs, we must therefore go beyond technical or instrumental perspectives and grapple with the philo-
sophical foundations of science itself. What counts as knowledge, explanation, or progress may no longer

69


be what it once was—and it is only by revisiting and reevaluating previous frameworks of science that
we can begin to navigate this new epistemic terrain.

8 Summary and Conclusions

In this work, we have introduced Denario, an AI multi-agent system designed as a research assistant.
Denario is built in a modular way, and can perform many different tasks, such as

e Generate novel or refine existing research ideas

Check the literature to determine whether an idea is new and its potential interest

Develop detailed research plans

Write and execute code, make plots, and summarize results
e Draft a scientific paper
e Review a scientific paper

Denario can also perform end-to-end scientific research by running all the above modules sequentially.
Different modules require different inputs and produce different outputs (see Table 1). When run in
end-to-end mode, the system only requires an input text containing general instructions to the system
(e.g., describing the data to be used). We emphasize that the goal of Denario is not to automate science,
but rather to serve as a powerful tool to help researchers across disciplines accelerate scientific discovery.

In Section 2, we described the different components needed for creating multi-agent systems, from
Large Language Models (LLMs) to agentic orchestration. In Section 3, we presented in detail the different
modules in Denario and the tasks they carry out. We have illustrated the capabilities of Denario in
Section 5 by evaluating papers generated by it in many different scientific disciplines, from astrophysics
to biology. From the expert evaluation of these manuscripts, we conclude that the generated papers are
at the level of what a good undergraduate or early graduate student could achieve after weeks or a few
months of work. In comparison, it took Denario around 30 minutes per paper and a cost of around $4.
We have discussed the failure modes, the importance of validation and evaluation, and the advantages
and limitations of Denario in Sec. 6. Finally, in Sec. 7 we discussed the ethical considerations that
agentic systems like Denario lead to and discussed how these technological advances could be perceived
from a philosophy of science perspective.

We note that we have not discussed important aspects related to Al agents such as benchmarking
[98] and risks [99]. However, these are active areas of research.

We conclude by stating that Denario represents one more example that the latest advances in deep
learning, in particular in large-language models and AI agents, may help scientists with their work [5, 8].
As we mentioned above, the papers that Denario can generate right now do not have the breadth and
reach of those written by the more experienced researchers in the field. Whether future LLMs or more
sophisticated systems with more specialized agents can achieve that remains an open question.

We believe that tools like Denario can open up new ways of doing science. Traditionally, researchers
focus deeply on a small set of questions, since tasks such as coding, reviewing the literature, and learning
new concepts or tools require significant time and effort. By contrast, Denario excels at rapidly exploring
a broad range of ideas, albeit at a more superficial level. These approaches are highly complementary:
AI can scan widely and highlight promising directions, while human experts can select the most relevant
ideas and pursue them in depth to achieve a deeper understanding.

Geometric Structure of PINN Latent Space for Burger’s Equation: Low-Dimensional Manifolds and

Initial Condition Encoding

AsTROPILOT!

! Anthropic, Gemini € OpenAl servers. Planet Earth.

ABSTRACT

Understanding how Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) encode complex physical systems
and the influence of parameters like initial conditions within their latent representations is crucial for
interpretability and application. This study investigates the geometric structure of the 10-dimensional
latent space generated by a PINN solving the 2D Burger’s equation across 25 different initial con-
ditions. Using Principal Component Analysis and subspace similarity measures, we analyze the set
of latent vectors for each initial condition as a potential low-dimensional manifold embedded in R!©,
comparing and contrasting these structures across the dataset of simulated solutions. The analysis
reveals a highly organized latent space; globally, the latent vectors occupy an effectively 6-dimensional
subspace capturing over 99% of variance. For each individual initial condition, the latent vectors form
a distinct, approximately 3-dimensional affine manifold, a structure remarkably consistent across all
tested conditions. Crucially, the primary effect of changing the initial condition is encoded as a trans-
lation of this 3D manifold along a nearly one-dimensional path within the 10-dimensional latent space,
strongly aligned with the global principal component. Furthermore, these 3D manifolds are remark-
ably parallel to each other, exhibiting an average subspace similarity exceeding 0.98, with only subtle,
low-dimensional variations in their orientation. These findings demonstrate that the PINN learns a
highly structured and efficient parameterization where initial conditions select specific, geometrically
simple, and highly related low-dimensional structures within the overall latent space, offering valuable
insights into the network’s internal encoding mechanisms and suggesting potential avenues for model
interpretation and compression.

Keywords: Neural networks, Computational astronomy, Principal component analysis, Astronomy data

analysis, Computational methods

1. INTRODUCTION

Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) represent
a significant advancement in solving partial differential
equations (PDEs) by embedding the governing physical
laws directly into the neural network architecture and
training objective.

This approach offers compelling advantages, such as
the ability to handle complex geometries and scenarios
with limited observational data, providing a mesh-free
alternative to traditional numerical techniques. How-
ever, despite their successes, PINNs, like many deep
learning models, often function as “black boxes,” ob-
scuring the precise mechanisms by which they learn and
represent the underlying physical phenomena. Under-
standing how these networks encode complex solution
landscapes and incorporate the influence of problem pa-
rameters, such as initial and boundary conditions, is

paramount for enhancing their reliability, interpretabil-
ity, and facilitating downstream applications like model
compression or transfer learning.

A central element within many neural network ar-
chitectures, including PINNs, is the latent space.
This intermediate representation layer compresses high-
dimensional input data into a more abstract, often
lower-dimensional, form. In the context of a PINN solv-
ing a PDE, the latent space typically holds a learned
encoding of the physical state of the system at specific
points in space and time (x,t).

Investigating the structure of this latent space pro-
vides a window into how the network perceives and pro-
cesses the physics. A fundamental challenge lies in deci-
phering how the latent representation varies across the
physical domain (x,t) and, critically, how this variation
changes in response to modifications in the problem’s
parameters, such as the initial condition. The difficulty


2

is compounded by the potentially high dimensionality
of the latent space (10 dimensions in this study) and
the unknown, potentially complex non-linear geometric
structures formed by the collection of latent vectors cor-
responding to a given physical solution. For a specific
initial condition, the set of latent vectors {L(z,t)} sam-
pled over a grid of (x,t) points forms a point cloud in
this 10-dimensional space, whose intrinsic structure and
relationship to other such point clouds generated by dif-
ferent initial conditions are not a priori understood.

This study focuses on dissecting the geometric struc-
ture of the 10-dimensional latent space generated by a
PINN trained to solve the 2D Burger’s equation. The 2D
Burger’s equation is a canonical non-linear PDE widely
used as a simplified model for complex fluid dynamics
phenomena like turbulence and shock formation, known
for its rich dynamic behavior highly sensitive to initial
conditions. We specifically examine how the PINN’s
latent representation of the solution changes across 25
distinct initial conditions. For each initial condition, we
treat the collection of latent vectors {L(z,t)} sampled
across a discrete grid of (x,t) points as a dataset forming
a point cloud in RY. Our primary objective is to analyze
the geometric properties of these point clouds, charac-
terizing their effective dimensionality, shape, and how
these characteristics compare and contrast across the
ensemble of 25 initial conditions. We hypothesize that
despite the complexity of the Burger’s equation and the
high dimensionality of the latent space, the network may
learn a structured and perhaps simple encoding where
the latent point clouds exhibit low-dimensional geomet-
ric properties and are related across initial conditions by
simple transformations.

To achieve this, we employ a suite of geometric analy-
sis techniques. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is
utilized extensively to quantify the dominant directions
of variation and determine the effective low dimensional-
ity of the latent vector point clouds, both for the global
collection of all latent vectors across all initial condi-
tions, and for the point cloud corresponding to each
individual initial condition. Furthermore, we employ
subspace similarity measures to quantitatively compare
the orientations of the principal subspaces learned for
different initial conditions. By systematically analyzing
the centroids of these point clouds and the relationship
between their principal components and the global la-
tent space structure, we aim to build a comprehensive
picture of how the PINN encodes the effect of varying
initial conditions within its learned representation. This
approach allows us to test whether changes in initial
conditions correspond to simple, predictable geometric

transformations, such as translations or rotations, of a
fundamental latent structure.

Our analysis reveals a highly structured organization
within the latent space. We find that, while the latent
space is 10-dimensional, the entire collection of latent
vectors across all initial conditions occupies an effec-
tively 6-dimensional subspace, capturing over 99% of the
total variance.

Strikingly, for each individual initial condition, the
corresponding set of latent vectors forms a distinct, ap-
proximately 3-dimensional affine manifold. This 3D
structure is remarkably consistent in its intrinsic dimen-
sionality and variance distribution across all 25 tested
initial conditions. Crucially, the primary effect of chang-
ing the initial condition is encoded as a translation
of this consistent 3D manifold. These manifold cen-
troids trace a nearly one-dimensional path within the
10-dimensional latent space, strongly aligned with the
dominant global principal component. Moreover, the
orientations of these 3D manifolds are exceptionally sim-
ilar, exhibiting an average subspace similarity exceeding
0.98, indicating they are nearly parallel with only sub-
tle, low-dimensional variations in their alignment. These
findings demonstrate that the PINN learns a highly effi-
cient and structured parameterization where initial con-
ditions select specific, geometrically simple, and highly
related low-dimensional structures within the overall la-
tent space, offering valuable insights into the network’s
internal encoding mechanisms and suggesting potential
avenues for model interpretation and compression.

2. METHODS

The objective of this study is to dissect the geomet-
ric structure of the 10-dimensional latent space gen-
erated by a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN)
trained to solve the 2D Burger’s equation. We investi-
gate how the latent representations corresponding to dif-
ferent initial conditions are organized within this space
and how their structure relates across an ensemble of
25 distinct initial conditions. Our methodology involves
data preparation, applying Principal Component Anal-
ysis (PCA) to characterize the dimensionality and vari-
ance distribution of latent vector sets, and employing
subspace similarity measures to compare the orienta-
tions of principal subspaces across different initial con-
ditions.

2.1. Latent Space Data Preparation

The data used in this analysis originates from a pre-
trained PINN solving the 2D Burger's equation over a
specified spatiotemporal domain. The data was pro-
vided as a NumPy array data_bundle with dimensions


(101,103, 25,13). These dimensions correspond to spa-
tial grid points (a-coordinate), time steps (t), initial con-
dition index, and features, respectively. The spatial grid
consists of 101 points along the z-axis, and the temporal
domain is discretized into 103 time steps. The dataset
includes solutions and latent space representations for 25
different initial conditions. The features dimension (size
13) contains the predicted solution components (e.g.,
velocity fields uw and v) and the 10-dimensional latent
vector output by an intermediate layer of the PINN for
each spatial point (x) and time step (¢) under a specific
initial condition.

The 10-dimensional latent space data was extracted
from the last 10 components of the features dimen-
sion. This resulted in a tensor latent_space_data
with dimensions (101,103,25, 10). Each element
latent_space_datali, j, k, :] represents the 10-
dimensional latent vector L(z;,t;,ICy) corresponding to
the spatial point x;, time t;, and the k-th initial condi-
tion IC. For each initial condition k, the set of latent
vectors {L(x;,t;,ICy)} over all i = 0..100 and j = 0..102
forms a collection of 101 x 103 = 10403 points in the 10-
dimensional latent space R'°. This collection is treated
as a point cloud representing the PINN’s latent encoding
of the physical solution for initial condition ICy.

2.2. Geometric Analysis Techniques

To analyze the structure of these point clouds and
their relationships, we employed Principal Component
Analysis (PCA) (Ferreras et al. 2006; Ugwoke et al.
2023; Nandi & Pandey 2025) and subspace similarity
measures.

2.2.1. Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

PCA is a statistical procedure that uses an orthogo-
nal transformation to convert a set of observations of
possibly correlated variables into a set of values of lin-
early uncorrelated variables called principal components
(Ferreras et al. 2006; McGurk et al. 2010). This trans-
formation is defined in such a way that the first prin-
cipal component has the largest possible variance (that
is, accounts for as much of the variability in the data as
possible), and each succeeding component in turn has
the highest variance possible under the constraint that
it is orthogonal to the preceding components (Ferreras
et al. 2006). The principal components are the eigen-
vectors of the data’s covariance matrix, and their corre-
sponding eigenvalues represent the variance along those
directions (Ferreras et al. 2006; McGurk et al. 2010).

In this study, PCA was applied in several contexts:
(Paraficz et al. 2016; Hatipoglu 2022; Cretignier et al.
2022; Sharma & Jassal 2024)

3

e Global PCA: PCA was applied to the en-
tire collection of latent vectors across all spatial
points, time steps, and initial conditions. The
latent_space_data tensor was reshaped into a
2D matrix of size (101 x 103 x 25,10), effectively
treating all 10403 x 25 = 260075 latent vectors as a
single dataset in R19. This global PCA reveals the
overall dimensionality and dominant directions of
variation within the latent space spanned by all
observed states. The eigenvalues were used to cal-
culate the percentage of total variance explained
by each principal component and the cumulative
variance, providing an estimate of the effective
global dimensionality.

e Per-Initial Condition PCA: For each of the 25
initial conditions, PCA was applied independently
to the set of 10403 latent vectors {L(x;,t;,I1Ck)}
corresponding to that specific initial condition k.
For each IC k, the data latent_space_datal:,
:, k, :] was reshaped into a 2D matrix of size
(10403, 10). This per-IC PCA characterizes the
intrinsic dimensionality and shape of the point
cloud associated with a single physical solution.
The centroid (mean vector) Cy, of the point cloud
for IC k was calculated, and the eigenvalues and
eigenvectors (principal components) of its covari-
ance matrix were obtained. The eigenvalues in-
dicate the variance along the principal directions,
and the eigenvectors form an orthonormal basis for
the principal subspace capturing the data’s varia-
tion. The cumulative variance explained by the
principal components for each IC was analyzed to
determine the effective intrinsic dimensionality of
the manifold for that specific initial condition.

« PCA on Centroids: The centroids C}, for each
of the 25 initial conditions are 10-dimensional vec-
tors. These 25 centroid vectors were collected into
a 2D matrix of size (25,10). PCA was applied to
this matrix to analyze the geometric arrangement
of the manifold centroids in the latent space. This
reveals whether the variation in initial conditions
primarily translates the latent manifold along a
low-dimensional path or occupies a more complex
structure in the latent space.

For all PCA applications, the data was centered by
subtracting the mean before computing the covariance
matrix and performing the eigenvalue decomposition
(Hatipoglu 2023; Cakir & Buck 2024).

2.2.2. Subspace Similarity Measures


To compare the orientations of the principal sub-
spaces identified by the per-IC PCA, we employed sub-
space similarity measures. For each initial condition
k, the per-IC PCA yields a set of principal compo-
nents {vk 1,Vk,2,-.., Vk 10} ordered by their correspond-
ing eigenvalues. Based on the cumulative variance ex-
plained, we determined an effective intrinsic dimension-
ality d;.. for the individual manifolds (e.g., the number of
components capturing 95% of variance) (Ferreras et al.
2006; Nandi & Pandey 2025). The principal subspace
for IC k is then approximated by the span of its first d;.
principal components, span{vi 1, ..., Vk d;. }-

To quantify the similarity between the principal sub-
spaces of two initial conditions k£ and j, we com-
pared their sets of principal vectors {vg 1, ..., vx 4, } and
{vj1,...,0j4,.}. A quantitative measure of subspace
similarity is given by the principal angles between the
two subspaces. Alternatively, for small d;., the similar-
ity can be approximated by comparing corresponding
principal vectors. For instance, the alignment of the
primary direction of variation is measured by the abso-
lute dot product |vg 1 - v;,1]. A value close to 1 indicates
strong alignment, while a value close to 0 indicates or-
thogonality. We computed these measures for pairs of
corresponding principal vectors (e.g., vg 1 vs Vj1y Vk2
VS vj 2) across all pairs of initial conditions to assess the
consistency in manifold orientation.

A high average subspace similarity across all pairs of
ICs indicates that the principal directions of variation
for the latent manifolds are largely parallel, implying
that the manifolds are primarily translated versions of
each other.

2.3. Analysis Workflow

The analysis was structured in a sequence of steps to
progressively reveal the geometric structure of the latent
space (Shukla et al. 2021; Rissaki et al. 2024) and the
encoding of initial conditions:

2.3.1. Initial Exploratory Data Analysis

We began by performing global PCA on the entire
collection of latent vectors to understand the overall dis-
tribution and effective dimensionality of the combined
dataset (Ferreras et al. 2006; Nandi & Pandey 2025).
Concurrently, we performed per-IC PCA for each of
the 25 initial conditions to obtain individual centroids
and principal components, characterizing the typical in-
trinsic dimensionality and variance structure of a single
manifold (Damiano et al. 2019). Finally, PCA was ap-
plied to the set of 25 centroids to understand how the
mean positions of the manifolds are organized (Nandi &
Pandey 2025).

2.3.2. Characterization of Individual Manifolds

Based on the per-IC PCA results, we determined the
effective intrinsic dimensionality d;. for the latent point
cloud of each initial condition. We approximated each
point cloud as an affine subspace defined by its centroid
Cy, and the span of its first d;. principal component vec-
tors Vi = [Uk.1,...,Vk4,.] (Ferreras et al. 2006; Dami-
ano et al. 2019; Nandi & Pandey 2025). The eigenval-
ues associated with these vectors provided insight into
the extent of the manifold along each principal direction
(Ferreras et al. 2006; Nandi & Pandey 2025).

2.3.3. Comparative Analysis Across Initial Conditions

We systematically compared the characterized man-
ifolds across the 25 initial conditions. The analysis
of centroids (PCA on {Ci}) revealed the structure of
the path traced by the manifold centers as the initial
condition changes (Nandi & Pandey 2025). Subspace
similarity measures were computed for pairs of princi-
pal subspaces span(V}) to quantify how similarly ori-
ented the manifolds are (Ferreras et al. 2006; Nandi &
Pandey 2025). By combining the information from cen-
troid locations and manifold orientations, we assessed
whether the primary effect of changing the initial condi-
tion is a simple translation, a rotation, or a more com-
plex transformation of a fundamental latent structure
(Nandi & Pandey 2025). We also specifically analyzed
the set of first principal vectors {vg 1} across all ICs us-
ing PCA to see if the dominant direction of variation
for individual manifolds exhibits a structured, possibly
low-dimensional, variation across ICs (Nandi & Pandey
2025).

2.3.4. Relation to Global Latent Space Structure

Finally, we related the local structures (individual
manifolds) to the global structure identified by the
global PCA. We projected the centered latent vectors
(Lx — Cy) for each IC k onto the dominant subspace
identified by the global PCA to see how much of the
per-I1C variance is aligned with the global principal di-
rections. We also examined the alignment between the
per-IC principal subspaces span(V},) and the global prin-
cipal subspace span(Uyiop).-

2.3.5. Synthesis

The findings from these analyses were synthesized to
provide a comprehensive geometric description of the
PINN’s latent space (Clemente et al. 2025,7). We de-
scribed the typical intrinsic dimensionality of the latent
representation for a single solution, the extent to which
these representations form affine manifolds, how these
manifolds are related across different initial conditions


(e.g., by translation along a low-dimensional path, by
consistent orientation), and how these local structures
relate to the overall structure of the latent space. This
synthesis allowed us to draw conclusions about how the
PINN efficiently encodes the initial condition within its
internal representation (Cuomo et al. 2022).

3. RESULTS

The objective of this study was to investigate the geo-
metric structure of the 10-dimensional latent space gen-
erated by a PINN solving the 2D Burger’s equation, fo-
cusing on how different initial conditions are encoded
within this space. Using Principal Component Analysis
(PCA) and subspace similarity measures, we analyzed
the latent vectors corresponding to 25 distinct initial
conditions.

3.1. Global structure of the latent space

We began by analyzing the overall structure of the la-
tent space by performing PCA on the entire collection
of latent vectors generated across all spatial points, time
steps, and the 25 initial conditions. This global analysis,
as described in the Methods, treats all 101 x 103 x 25 =
260075 latent vectors as a single dataset in R'?. The
variance explained by each principal component (PC)
provides insight into the intrinsic dimensionality and
dominant directions of variation within the aggregated
latent representation.

The results of this global PCA reveal a significant
concentration of variance in the leading principal com-
ponents. As shown in the scree plot in Figure 1, the
first principal component (PC1) alone captures 60.12%
of the total variance. The second (PC2) and third (PC3)
components capture an additional 23.44% and 12.93%,
respectively. Cumulatively, the first three global PCs
account for 96.48% of the total variance. Including the
fourth (1.30%), fifth (1.17%), and sixth (0.76%) com-
ponents brings the cumulative variance explained to
99.72%. The remaining four components individually
explain less than 0.3% of the variance each.

This strong concentration of variance within the first
six principal components demonstrates that the entire
collection of latent vectors, despite residing in a 10-
dimensional space, effectively occupies a much lower-
dimensional subspace. The vast majority (>99%) of the
variability observed in the latent representations across
all tested physical states and initial conditions is cap-
tured by a 6-dimensional linear subspace. This sug-
gests that the PINN learns an overall efficient encoding,
where the complex dynamics across different conditions
are constrained to a relatively low-dimensional manifold
within the full latent space.

3.2. Intrinsic dimensionality of per initial condition
manifolds

Next, we investigated the structure of the latent space
corresponding to individual initial conditions. For each
of the 25 initial conditions (ICk, k =0,...,24), we per-
formed PCA independently on the 101 x 103 = 10403
latent vectors {L(x;,t;, IC}y)} associated with that spe-
cific condition. This analysis aims to characterize the
intrinsic dimensionality and shape of the latent point
cloud representing the PINN’s encoding of the solution
for a fixed initial state.

The results show a remarkable consistency across all
25 initial conditions. As shown by the average scree
plot in Figure 2 and the intrinsic dimensionality distri-
bution in Figure 3, for every single IC, precisely 3 prin-
cipal components were sufficient to explain over 95%
of the variance within its corresponding latent point
cloud. Quantitatively, the average cumulative variance
explained by the first three per-IC principal components
is 97.48%, with a very low standard deviation (0.15%).
The average variance explained by the first, second, and
third per-IC PCs were 59.61%, 23.72%, and 14.15%, re-
spectively. The variance captured by the fourth per-IC
PC and beyond drops sharply, with the average variance
for the fourth PC being below 2%.

These findings strongly suggest that, for any given ini-
tial condition within the tested set, the PINN’s latent
representation of the spatiotemporal solution {L(z,t)}
forms an effectively 3-dimensional structure embedded
in the 10-dimensional latent space. The high percentage
of variance captured by the leading three components in-
dicates that these structures are well-approximated by 3-
dimensional affine manifolds (shifted linear subspaces),

3.3. Geometric arrangement of manifold centroids

To understand how the latent representations differ
across initial conditions, we analyzed the geometric ar-
rangement of the centroids Cy of the per-IC latent point
clouds. Each centroid C}, is a 10-dimensional vector rep-

resenting the mean position of the latent manifold for
initial condition IC}. We collected these 25 centroid
vectors and performed PCA on this (25 x 10) matrix.

The results of this centroid PCA are striking, as shown
in the scree plot in Figure 4. The first principal compo-
nent of the centroids (CPC1) explains an overwhelming
99.86% of the total variance in the centroid positions.
The second component (CPC2) explains only 0.10%,
and the third (CPC3) explains 0.02%.

in the mean position of the learned solution manifold.

across initial conditions. For each IC}, the per-IC PCA
yields a set of principal vectors {vk1, Vk2, Vrs} spanning
the approximate 3D affine manifold. We compared these
principal subspaces across different initial conditions.

This indicates that the variations in the orientations of
the principal axes of the 3D manifolds are themselves
highly structured and change in a low-dimensional man-

ner, effectively tracing out nearly one-dimensional paths
in the space of orientation vectors as the initial condition
