3.4. Catalog-to-catalog variations, uncertainties, and
outlier analysis

The existence of significant catalog-to-catalog varia-
tion across the 1,000 simulations is a central finding
of this study. This variation is a direct consequence
of exploring a wide range of cosmological and feedback
parameters. As discussed in Section 3.2.1 and illus-
trated by Figure 1 and Figure 2, the low-mass bin ex-
hibits the greatest diversity in the fitted parameters «
and (3, with a substantial number of catalogs classified
as outliers according to our IQR-based method. This
highlights the sensitivity of the Mpy—Mjgia, relation in
dwarf galaxies to the specific feedback implementations
and strengths (as further demonstrated by Figure 3).
The intermediate-mass bin, in contrast, shows remark-
able uniformity with very few outliers, suggesting a more
stable and universally established relation in this mass
range across the explored parameter space. The high-
mass bin shows intermediate levels of variation and out-
liers.

The bootstrap resampling procedure, applied to each
per-catalog, per-mass-bin fit, provided robust estimates
of the uncertainties for «, 8, and scatter. The consis-
tently high bootstrap success rates (approximately 100

The small number of mass bins (9 for fitting, 8 for
occupation fraction) that did not meet the minimum
sample size criterion (Npgso > 10) were flagged and
excluded from the fitting analysis, ensuring that our re-
sults are based on statistically robust per-catalog esti-
mates. The vast majority of catalog-mass bin combina-
tions (2,991 out of 3,000) provided reliable data points
for the subsequent mapping analysis.

The observed catalog-to-catalog variation underscores
that the Mpp—Mga, relation is not a single, universal
relation in these simulations, but rather a family of re-
lations whose specific properties are determined by the
underlying physical parameters.

3.5. Comparison with observational constraints and
physical interpretation

Comparing our simulation results with observational
constraints provides a crucial test of the physical pro-
cesses included in the simulations. The median slopes
derived in the intermediate-mass (~ 1.06) and high-mass
(~ 1.22) bins are broadly consistent with the slopes re-
ported in observational studies of the Mpy—Mgiar rela-
tion for massive galaxies (e.g., Kormendy & Hu 2013;

McConnell & Ma 2013). The intrinsic scatter in these
bins (median ~ 0.30 — 0.40 dex) also aligns well with
observed scatter values. The black hole occupation frac-
tion is near unity in the high-mass bin, consistent with
observations.

However, our simulations predict greater diversity
in the Mpu—Mgtar relation, particularly at low stellar
masses, than is currently constrained by observations.
The shallower median slope (~ 0.76), significant scat-
ter, and lower occupation fraction (~ 0.84) in the low-
mass bin are consistent with recent observational efforts
focusing on dwarf galaxies, which suggest incomplete
black hole occupation and potentially different scaling
relations compared to massive galaxies (e.g., Greene et
al. 2020). The large catalog-to-catalog variation in the
low-mass bin (as seen in Figure 1 and Figure 2, and illus-
trated by Figure 3) implies that the Mpy—Mjgtar relation
in dwarf galaxies might be highly sensitive to the spe-
cific feedback physics, potentially explaining some of the
scatter and apparent diversity in observational samples.

Physically, our findings support a mass-dependent pic-
ture of black hole and galaxy coevolution driven by feed-
back, as quantified by the machine learning analysis and
shown in the partial dependence plots (e.g., Figure 5,
Figure 15, Figure 17).

o In low-mass galaxies with shallow potential wells,
supernova feedback (Agni) is the dominant reg-
ulator. Strong SN feedback can expel gas, in-
hibiting both star formation and black hole accre-
tion. This leads to a shallower Mpg—Mgiar relation
and a lower black hole occupation fraction. The
stochastic nature of SN feedback in these systems
contributes significantly to the scatter (Figure 7).

e In intermediate-mass galaxies, deeper potential
wells retain gas more effectively. AGN feedback
(Aagn1) becomes the primary driver, regulating
both star formation and black hole growth (Fig-
ure 13, Figure 14). The strong correlation between
Aagni and the slope suggests that AGN feedback
in this regime helps establish the tight scaling re-
lation, potentially by channeling gas flows towards
the central black hole.

« In high-mass galaxies, the deepest potential wells
are less susceptible to stellar feedback. AGN feed-
back (Aagni) continues to dominate (Figure 20),
but its role may shift towards self-regulation and
quenching. The potential for AxgNy to negatively
impact the slope in this regime (Figure 17) sug-
gests that very strong AGN feedback can suppress
further black hole accretion, limiting their growth
and contributing to the increased scatter as some


black holes grow faster before quenching. The
high occupation fraction reflects the near-universal
presence of black holes in these massive systems.

Cosmological parameters (),,, og) modulate these pro-
cesses by influencing the cosmic assembly history and
the availability of matter, thereby affecting the timing
and environment of galaxy and black hole growth, which
can subtly alter the normalization and scatter of the
scaling relations, particularly at higher masses (e.g., Fig-
ure 19, Figure 21).

3.6. Comparison with previous methodologies and new
insights

This study significantly advances upon previous anal-
yses of Mpu—Mstar relations in simulations, including
our own prior work, primarily through a more sophis-
ticated and robust methodological framework. Earlier
studies often relied on simpler linear regression and ba-
sic statistical descriptions of the relation. Our current
approach incorporates several key enhancements:

¢ Robust Regression and Uncertainty Quan-
tification: The use of Huber loss for robust re-
gression makes the fitting less sensitive to outliers
within a given catalog, providing more reliable es-
timates of @ and 8. Bootstrap resampling provides
rigorous, per-catalog uncertainty estimates, which
were previously less systematically quantified.

e Comprehensive Parameter Space Explo-
ration: Leveraging 1,000 catalogs spanning a
wide range of six key parameters allows for a much
more thorough exploration of the parameter space
than previous studies, which typically varied only
a few parameters or focused on a single simulation
suite.

e Advanced Machine Learning for Mapping:
The application of ensemble methods (Random
Forest, Gradient Boosting) and interpretability
tools (Permutation Importance, SHAP values,
Partial Dependence Plots) provides a powerful,
non-linear mapping from the input parameters to
the output relation properties. This goes beyond
simple linear correlations, allowing us to iden-
tify the relative importance of parameters even in
complex, interacting systems (e.g., Figure 4, Fig-
ure 14) and visualize non-linear dependencies (e.g. ,
Figure 5, Figure 17).

These methodological improvements yield several new
insights that were not apparent from simpler analy-
ses. We have been able to clearly and quantitatively

13

demonstrate the distinct mass-dependent roles of SN
(Agni) and AGN (Aagni) feedback, showing a clear
transition in dominance around Mg, ~ 10° — 1019 M,.
The potential sign reversal in the influence of Axgny on
the slope at high masses, indicative of quenching (Fig-
ure 17), is a subtle but important finding enabled by
the detailed analysis of parameter dependencies. Fur-
thermore, the robust quantification of catalog-to-catalog
variation (Figure 1, Figure 2) and the identification of
mass bins with high outlier rates provide direct evidence
for how stochastic processes and parameter choices con-
tribute to the diversity of the Mpy—Mgtar relation. The
use of partial dependence plots specifically allows us to
visualize how, for instance, the slope changes as a func-
tion of Axgni, averaged over all other parameters, re-
vealing the overall trend and potential non-linearities.

In summary, the refined methodology has provided a
much more detailed and nuanced understanding of how
cosmological and feedback physics shape the Mpup—Mstar
relation and its diversity across different mass scales in
simulations.

4. CONCLUSIONS

In this paper, we conducted a comprehensive study
to quantify the diversity of the black hole-stellar mass
(Mpu—Mstay) relation and its physical drivers across
a large parameter space of cosmological and feedback
physics. Understanding this diversity is critical for ad-
vancing models of galaxy and black hole coevolution, but
the complex interplay of physical processes has made
systematic investigation challenging. We addressed this
by analyzing 1,000 simulated galaxy catalogs at redshift
zero, each characterized by a unique combination of six
global parameters: matter density (€,,), density fluctu-
ation amplitude (og), and supernova (Agni, Asnz) and
active galactic nucleus (Aacgni, Aacne) feedback effi-
ciencies.

Our methodology involved robustly fitting the Mpp—
May relation and calculating the black hole occupation
fraction within three stellar mass bins for each catalog,
employing bootstrap resampling to estimate uncertain-
ties. We then leveraged a suite of advanced statistical
and machine learning techniques, including hierarchi-
cal linear modeling, random forest regression, gradient
boosting, permutation importance, SHAP values, and
partial dependence plots, to map the derived relation
properties (slope, normalization, intrinsic scatter) and
occupation fractions to the six input parameters. This
allowed us to identify the dominant drivers and quantify
their mass-dependent effects.

Our results reveal substantial diversity in the Mpp—
My. relation across the explored parameter space, with


14

properties varying significantly between catalogs and
stellar mass bins. We found a clear mass-dependent
transition in the primary drivers of this diversity.

At low stellar masses (< 10° M,), supernova feed-
back, particularly Agni, is the dominant factor shap-
ing the relation’s slope, normalization, scatter, and the
black hole occupation fraction. Stronger SN feedback
generally leads to shallower slopes, lower normalizations,
increased scatter, and significantly suppressed occupa-
tion fractions. This is consistent with SN feedback effec-
tively expelling gas from shallow potential wells, hinder-
ing both star formation and black hole growth in dwarf
galaxies. Cosmological parameters play a secondary role
in this mass range. The low-mass bin exhibits the largest
catalog-to-catalog variation and the highest number of
outlier relations, highlighting its sensitivity to feedback
physics and potentially stochastic growth processes.

In the intermediate stellar mass range (10° < Mgtar <
1019 My), active galactic nucleus feedback, specifically
AagN1, becomes the overwhelmingly dominant driver.
Aagni strongly influences both the slope and normal-
ization of the relation, with stronger AGN feedback gen-
erally leading to steeper slopes. This suggests a regime
where AGN feedback plays a crucial role in establishing
the tight Mgp—Mga, correlation, possibly by regulating
gas flows that fuel both star formation and black hole
accretion. This mass bin shows remarkable uniformity
across the 1,000 catalogs, with almost no outliers in the
scaling relation parameters, indicating a more robustly
established relation less sensitive to the specific param-
eter choices within the explored range.

At high stellar masses (> 10° My), AGN feedback
(Aagn1) remains the most important driver. However,
the analysis suggests a potential shift in the nature of
its influence on the slope, with very strong Axgni1 po-

tentially leading to a flattening or even a negative cor-
relation with the slope, consistent with self-regulation
and quenching of black hole growth in massive galaxies.
Cosmological parameters (£2,,, og) have a more notice-
able modulating effect on the normalization and scatter
in this regime. The intrinsic scatter is highest in this
bin, and the black hole occupation fraction is near unity,
showing minimal dependence on the input parameters.

Comparing our results to observations, the simula-
tions broadly agree with the slopes and scatter observed
for massive galaxies. Crucially, the simulations predict
greater diversity and lower occupation fractions at low
stellar masses, aligning with recent observational find-
ings for dwarf galaxies and suggesting that the Mpp—
Mi., relation in this regime is more sensitive to the
specific physical conditions and feedback strengths.

This study provides a detailed, quantitative mapping
of how the properties of the Mpy—Mga, relation and
black hole occupation fraction are shaped by underly-
ing cosmological and feedback parameters. We have ro-
bustly demonstrated the critical, mass-dependent roles
of SN and AGN feedback, transitioning from SN dom-
inance at low masses to AGN dominance at higher
masses. The systematic analysis using advanced ma-
chine learning techniques allowed us to uncover and
quantify these complex, often non-linear, dependencies
across a wide parameter space. Our findings offer a de-
tailed framework for interpreting the observed diversity
in black hole scaling relations and underscore the neces-
sity of accurately modeling feedback processes across dif-
ferent mass scales for realistic simulations of black hole-
galaxy coevolution. The substantial diversity predicted,
especially at low masses, highlights the challenges and
opportunities for future observational campaigns aiming
to constrain the physical mechanisms driving black hole
growth in the smallest galaxies.

QITT-Enhanced Multi-Scale Substructure Analysis with Learned Topological Embeddings for

Cosmological Parameter Estimation from Dark Matter Halo Merger Trees

AsTROPILOT!

! Anthropic, Gemini € OpenAl servers. Planet Earth.

ABSTRACT

Estimating cosmological parameters from dark matter halo merger trees is a crucial task. We in-
troduce a novel approach that leverages Quantum-Inspired Tensor Trains (QITT) on multi-scale sub-
structure features, incorporating learned topological embeddings, for enhanced cosmological parameter
estimation. We identify substructures within merger trees from a dataset of 1000 trees based on mass
accretion rates and significant changes in halo properties. For each substructure, we extract physical
features and learn a topological embedding using a Graph Neural Network (GNN). These features
are then organized into a tensor, and QITT decomposition is applied to compress this information.
The resulting QITT cores serve as input features to regression models, including Linear Regression,
Random Forest, and XGBoost. Our results demonstrate that QITT-based models achieve competi-
tive performance, with QITT-XGBoost significantly outperforming models using flattened combined
features, highlighting the benefit of QITT decomposition for feature compression and representation.
However, a simple baseline using global aggregate tree features achieves the best performance for
Omega,,, suggesting that global properties are highly informative for this parameter. The combination
of learned topological embeddings and QITT decomposition offers a promising avenue for extracting
complex information from merger trees, with potential for advancing data-driven cosmology.

Keywords: Stellar evolution, Cosmological parameters, Astronomical simulations, Solar system, Ob-

servational astronomy

1. INTRODUCTION

Estimating cosmological parameters, such as the mat-
ter density of the Universe (€2,,) and the amplitude of
the matter power spectrum (og), is a cornerstone of
modern cosmology. These parameters dictate the for-
mation and evolution of large-scale structures, including
the ubiquitous dark matter halos. These halos, the grav-
itational homes of galaxies and galaxy clusters, assem-
ble hierarchically over cosmic time, leaving a detailed
record of their formation history encoded within their
merger trees. These merger trees, representing the an-
cestry of dark matter halos, offer a rich source of infor-
mation about the underlying cosmology. Extracting this
cosmological information effectively from merger trees,
however, remains a formidable challenge.

The primary hurdle lies in the inherent complexity of
dark matter halo merger trees. Their intricate branching
patterns, reflecting the hierarchical nature of structure
formation, make it difficult to discern the most salient
features relevant for cosmological parameter estimation
(Parkinson et al. 2007; Jiang & van den Bosch 2013).

Traditional approaches often resort to using global prop-
erties of the trees, such as total mass or average concen-
tration, or simple summary statistics of halo properties
(Jiang & van den Bosch 2013). While computationally
efficient, these methods risk overlooking crucial informa-
tion encoded in the detailed substructure and merger
history of individual halos (Benson et al. 2012; Jiang
et al. 2025D).

Identifying and characterizing these substructures
across multiple scales is not only computationally de-
manding but also requires sophisticated techniques ca-
pable of navigating the high-dimensional parameter
space (Angel Chandro-Gémez et al. 2025; Jiang et al.
2025b). Furthermore, capturing the complex topological
relationships within these merger trees is a non-trivial
task, as these relationships can be both intricate and
high-dimensional, defying simple characterization (An-
gel Chandro-Gémez et al. 2025; Jiang et al. 2025b).

To address these challenges, we introduce a novel ap-
proach that leverages Quantum-Inspired Tensor Trains
(QITT) on multi-scale substructure features, incorpo-
rating learned topological embeddings, for enhanced


2

cosmological parameter estimation from dark matter
halo merger trees (Parkinson et al. 2007; Jiang &
van den Bosch 2013). Our method begins by identify-
ing significant substructures within merger trees based
on both mass accretion rates and significant changes in
halo properties such as concentration and maximum cir-
cular velocity (Jiang & van den Bosch 2013). For each
identified substructure, we extract physically motivated
features, such as mass ratios and merger times, captur-
ing key aspects of their formation history (Parkinson
et al. 2007; Jiang & van den Bosch 2013). Crucially, we
also learn a topological embedding for each substructure
using a Graph Neural Network (GNN). This GNN, pre-
trained on a large ensemble of graphs, is designed to
capture the essential topological characteristics of the
substructure, providing a low-dimensional representa-
tion of its connectivity and overall structure (Jiang &
van den Bosch 2013; Jiang et al. 2025Db).

These physical features and topological embeddings
are then organized into a tensor, representing the collec-
tion of substructures within each merger tree. We apply
QITT decomposition to compress this tensor, effectively
extracting the most important information while simul-
taneously reducing dimensionality. The resulting QITT
cores, encapsulating the compressed representation of
substructure features and topology, serve as input fea-
tures to various regression models, including Linear Re-
gression, Random Forest, and XGBoost, to predict cos-
mological parameters. By leveraging the power of QITT
to compress and represent complex data, we aim to im-
prove the accuracy and efficiency of cosmological param-
eter estimation.

To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we train
and evaluate our QITT-based models on a dataset of
1000 merger trees extracted from cosmological simula-
tions (Tweed et al. 2009; Han et al. 2017; Rangel et al.
2020). We compare their performance against several
carefully chosen baselines, including models using ag-
gregate graph-level features, raw substructure features
without topological information, and graphlet counts, a
measure of basic topological structure. We assess the
performance of each model using Root Mean Squared
Error (RMSE) and R-squared, and we perform statis-
tical tests to determine the significance of any perfor-
mance differences. By demonstrating that our QITT-
based models achieve competitive or superior perfor-
mance compared to these baselines, we aim to establish
the potential of our approach for advancing data-driven
cosmology and unlocking the wealth of information en-
coded within dark matter halo merger trees.

2. METHODS

This section details the methodology employed to
investigate the relationship between dark matter halo
merger trees and cosmological parameters (£2,,, og) us-
ing Quantum-Inspired Tensor Trains (QITT) enhanced
with learned topological embeddings. Our approach ad-
dresses the challenges of extracting cosmological infor-
mation from the complex branching patterns of merger
trees, as highlighted in the introduction, by focusing on
multi-scale substructure analysis and advanced feature
representation techniques.

2.1. Data loading and preprocessing

The dataset consists of 1000 dark matter halo merger
trees, each represented as a PyTorch Geometric ‘Data’
object. These trees were extracted from cosmological
simulations (Parkinson et al. 2007; Han et al. 2017). The
dataset was loaded using the following code:

import torch
import numpy as np

(Elahi et al. 2019; Nadler et al. 2023; Jung et al. 2024;
Porter & Scaife 2023; Do et al. 2024)

Prior to model training, the data underwent several
preprocessing steps to ensure optimal performance (Ichi-
nohe et al. 2018; Li et al. 2024; Tak et al. 2024).

2.1.1. Node feature normalization

Each node in the merger tree is characterized
by four features: log;o(mass), log;,(concentration),
log19(Vimax), and the scale factor (Robles et al. 2019;
Tang & Ting 2022). To mitigate the impact of differing
scales and distributions, each feature was normalized to
have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1 (Tang
& Ting 2022). The mean and standard deviation were
computed across all nodes in the entire training dataset
to ensure consistent normalization (Tang & Ting 2022).
The normalization was performed as follows:

Tr — fg
Ox

Tnormalized =

where x represents the original feature value, pu, is the
mean of the feature across all nodes in the training set,
and o, is the standard deviation of the feature across
all nodes in the training set.

2.1.2. Target variable handling

The target variables, €2,, and og, represent the matter
density of the Universe and the amplitude of the matter
power spectrum, respectively. These variables were used
directly for regression without further transformation,
as their ranges are well-defined and physically meaning-
ful (Thing & Koksbang 2024).


2.1.3. Data splitting

The dataset was partitioned into training, validation,
and testing sets to facilitate model training, hyperpa-
rameter tuning, and unbiased performance evaluation
(Zuo et al. 2024). A 70-15-15 split was employed, re-
sulting in 700 trees for training, 150 trees for validation,
and 150 trees for testing. To prevent data leakage due to
potential correlations between trees originating from the
same cosmological simulation, all 25 trees from a given
simulation were kept within the same split (Buchner &
Fotopoulou 2025). This ensured that the model was
evaluated on unseen cosmological parameters. Given the
1000 trees come from 40 unique simulations, we assigned
28 simulations for training (700 trees), 6 for validation
(150 trees), and 6 for testing (150 trees).

2.2. Multi-scale substructure identification

A key aspect of our methodology is the identifica-
tion of significant substructures within each merger tree
(Robles et al. 2019; Angel Chandro-Gémez et al. 2025).
This allows us to capture the detailed formation history
of dark matter halos, addressing the limitations of tra-
ditional approaches that rely on global tree properties
(Robles et al. 2019; Angel Chandro-Gémez et al. 2025).
A substructure is defined as a branch of the merger tree
originating from a merger event or a significant change in
halo properties, extending down to its leaf nodes (Robles
et al. 2019; Angel Chandro-Goémez et al. 2025; Gannon
et al. 2025).

2.2.1. Traversal

Each merger tree was traversed starting from the main
root halo, defined as the halo at the scale factor closest to
1 (Nadler et al. 2023; Jung et al. 2024; Angel Chandro-
Goémez et al. 2025). The ‘edge_index‘ attribute of the
PyTorch Geometric ‘Data’ object defines the parent-
child relationships within the tree, enabling efficient
traversal (Jespersen et al. 2022; Jung et al. 2024).

2.2.2. Identifying merger events

Merger events were identified as halos with multi-
ple direct progenitors (Pearson et al. 2024). These
events mark the confluence of multiple branches within
the merger tree, indicating significant accretion events
(Pearson et al. 2024).

2.2.3. Substructure definition

Substructures were defined based on two criteria:
mass accretion rates (Lucia et al. 2003; Soltis et al. 2024)
and significant changes in halo properties (Yencho et al.
2006; Soltis et al. 2024).

3

« Mass accretion rate: The mass accretion rate
for each progenitor branch leading into a merger
was calculated as:

Mgescendant - Mprogenitor

SFiescendant - SFprogenitor

where M represents the mass and SF rep-
resents the scale factor (Soltis & Garrison

2024). We also considered the mass ratio
logo (Mprogenitor/Mdescendant) (Soltis & Garrison
2024).

e Significant changes in halo properties:
Changes in normalized log; (concentration) and
log19(Vmax) were monitored along each branch.
A significant change was defined as a deviation
greater than a dynamically determined threshold.

oe Adaptive thresholds: Thresholds for iden-
tifying significant mass accretion or property
changes were determined dynamically based
on the distribution of these quantities within
each tree. For example, major mergers
were defined as those where the mass ratio

(Mprogenitor/Miess_massive_progenitor at merger) fell
within the top X-percentile within each tree.

2.2.4. Substructure graph creation

Each identified substructure was represented as a sep-
arate PyTorch Geometric ‘Data’ object, inheriting node
features and connectivity from the original tree (Garuda
et al. 2024). The root of the substructure graph was de-
fined as the halo immediately preceding its merger into
a more massive branch or the halo where a significant
property change was initiated (Garuda et al. 2024; Ma
et al. 2025).

2.3. Feature extraction for substructures

For each identified substructure, we extracted two
types of features: physical features (Lisanti et al. 2015;
Ruiz-Lara et al. 2022) and learned topological embed-
dings (Tsang et al. 2024). These features capture com-
plementary aspects of the substructure’s formation his-
tory and internal structure.

2.3.1. Physical features

The following physical features were extracted for each
substructure: (Mondino et al. 2020; Ruiz-Lara et al.
2022; Tsang et al. 2024)

oe Mass ratio: For substructures originating from

mergers, logy (Mj ubstructure_ root /Mmain_branch_at_merger )

was calculated.


oe Merger scale factor: The scale factor at which
the substructure’s root halo merges into a larger
branch was recorded.

e Property differences: The difference in normal-
ized log, (concentration) and log; (Vmax) between
the substructure’s root and its parent in the main
branch at the time of merging was calculated.

¢ Substructure intrinsic properties: Aggregate
properties of the substructure itself were com-
puted, including its total mass, average concen-
tration of its halos, and the range of scale factors
it spans. The mean and standard deviation of the
normalized node features within the substructure
were also calculated.

These features were combined into a fixed-length fea-
ture vector (e.g., 5-10 dimensions) for each substructure
(Fagin et al. 2024; Ma et al. 2025).

2.3.2. Learned topological embeddings

To capture the topological characteristics of each sub-
structure, we employed a Graph Neural Network (GNN)
to generate learned topological embeddings (Roncoli
et al. 2024; Zhu et al. 2024; Ma et al. 2025).

« GNN architecture: A GraphSAGE model was
used for its inductive capabilities and efficiency in
generating node embeddings by sampling and ag-
gregating features from a node’s local neighbor-
hood. The model consisted of 2-3 GraphSAGE
layers with ReLU activations and mean aggrega-
tion. The output dimension of the GNN for each
node in the substructure graph was set to 64.

e GNN application: The GNN, pre-trained on a
large ensemble of graphs, was applied to each sub-
structure graph. The input features for the GNN
were the same four normalized halo features used
for the node features in the merger trees.

« Graph-level embedding: A graph-level embed-
ding for each substructure was obtained by ap-
plying a global mean pooling layer to the node
embeddings generated by the GNN. This resulted
in a fixed-size vector (64 dimensions) representing
the topology and properties of the substructure.

2.4. Tensor construction

To represent the collection of substructures within
each merger tree, a 3D tensor was constructed (Zhou
et al. 2025; Jiang et al. 2025a). This tensor captures
both the physical features and topological embeddings
of each substructure (Chittenden et al. 2025).

2.4.1. Feature concatenation

For each substructure, its physical feature vector and
topological embedding vector were concatenated. If the
physical feature vector had P dimensions and the topo-
logical embedding had 7" dimensions, each substructure
was represented by a vector of P+T dimensions (Kiigler
et al. 2015; Horta et al. 2025).

2.4.2. Tensor dimensions

The tensor for each tree had dimensions (Ngub, Dreat )s
where Ngup is the number of substructures identified in
that tree and Dye = P + T is the dimensionality of
the combined feature vector per substructure (Jermyn
2019).

2.4.3. Padding strategy

Since Ng}, varies across trees, a padding strategy was
employed to ensure a consistent tensor shape for batch
processing and QITT input (Wu & Jespersen 2023). The
maximum number of substructures, max_ Ngu1,, was de-
termined across the training set based on the 95th per-
centile of substructure counts. For trees with fewer
than max_ Ng, substructures, padding was applied us-
ing a learned embedding from a "padding graph.” This
"padding graph” was a single node with average feature
values, and its embedding was generated by the same
pre-trained GNN (Jagvaral et al. 2022). Zero vectors
were used for its physical features. This combined vec-
tor was used for padding, ensuring that all tensors had
a shape of (max_ Ngub, Dieat )-

2.6. Regression models

The concatenated and flattened QITT cores served as
input features to various regression models to predict
Q,, and og (Villaescusa-Navarro et al. 2021; Balla et al.
2024; Makinen et al. 2024).

2.6.1. Models

The following regression models were employed:
(Stoppa et al. 2023; Jing & Li 2024; Martin & Mort-
lock 2024; Narkedimilli et al. 2024; Martin & Mortlock
2024)

« Linear Regression: As a baseline to understand
linear relationships.

« Random Forest Regressor: To capture non-
linear relationships and feature importances.

« Gradient Boosting Regressor (e.g., XG-
Boost): For high performance, capable of han-
dling complex interactions.

2.6.2. Training and hyperparameter tuning

Each model was trained on the training set (features
derived from QITT cores). Hyperparameters for each
model (e.g., number of trees, depth for Random Forest;
learning rate, n_ estimators for Gradient Boosting; TT-
ranks for QITT decomposition) were tuned using k-fold
cross-validation (e.g., k=5) on the training set, optimiz-
ing for Mean Squared Error (MSE) or R-squared on the
validation folds (Buchner & Fotopoulou 2025). The fi-
nal QITT rank was selected based on the performance of
the downstream regression task on the main validation
set (Soo et al. 2023).

2.7. Comparison with baselines

The performance of the QITT-based models was com-
pared against several baselines (Wynne & Schechter
2018; Schechter & Wynne 2019; Witt et al. 2022).

2.7.1. Aggregate graph-level features

2.7.2. Raw substructure features (no QITT, no topology
embedding)

Only the physical features extracted from substruc-

concatenated up to max_ Ng, (with padding for phys-

of size max_ Ngyp xX P. Regressors were then trained
on these flattened raw physical substructure features

CHG AR hCREPf ger tree, the frequency of small graph

on these graphlet count vectors.

2.7.4. Model with topology embedding but no QITT

The concatenated physical features and GNN-derived
topological embeddings for each substructure were used
(Farsian et al. 2022; Wu & Jespersen 2023). This
(max_ Ngub, Dteat) tensor per tree was flattened, and
regressors were trained directly on these flattened com-
prehensive substructure features (Garuda et al. 2024).

2.8. Evaluation metrics and statistical significance

Performance was primarily evaluated using Root
Mean Squared Error (RMSE) (Lue et al. 2025) and
R-squared (coefficient of determination) for both Qm
and 8 on the held-out test set. Paired t-tests (or non-
parametric equivalents like the Wilcoxon signed-rank
test if normality assumptions were violated) were per-
formed on the prediction errors from different models on
the test set to assess whether performance differences
were statistically significant, using a p-value threshold
of 0.05.

This comprehensive methodology allowed us to rig-
orously evaluate the efficacy of using QITT-enhanced
multi-scale substructure features, including learned
topological embeddings, for cosmological parameter es-
timation (Fluri et al. 2021; Mediato-Diaz & Handley
2025).

3. RESULTS

This section presents the results of applying the
Quantum-Inspired Tensor Train (QITT) enhanced
multi-scale substructure analysis, incorporating learned
topological embeddings, for cosmological parameter es-
timation from dark matter halo merger trees. We eval-
uate the performance of this approach against several
baseline methods and delve into the interpretation of
the learned representations and QITT components.

3.1. Data Processing, Substructure Characterization,
and Feature Engineering Summary


The initial dataset consisted of 1000 merger
trees. Node features (log, (mass), log, (concentration),
log; (Vinax), scale factor) were normalized based on the
statistics derived from the training set (700 trees). For
instance, the original mean log, (mass) was 11.14 and
scale factor was 0.37, which were transformed to have
zero mean and unit standard deviation for subsequent
processing.

Substructures were identified within each merger tree
by traversing from merger events and applying an
adaptive threshold based on the 20th percentile of
log; (Msub_ progenitor/Mmain_ progenitor) within each tree.
This resulted in an average of 47.45 substructures per
tree, with a median of 32 and a range from 2 to 563
substructures. For each substructure, a 10-dimensional
physical feature vector was extracted, capturing prop-
erties such as mass ratios, merger scale factors, dif-
ferences in normalized halo properties (concentration,
Vinax) between merging progenitors, and intrinsic prop-
erties of the substructure branch (e.g., mean normalized
concentration / Via, scale factor span, number of halos).
The num_ halos_ in_ branch feature, for example, had a
mean of 21.4 and a standard deviation of 54.0 across all
identified substructures.

A GraphSAGE-based autoencoder was trained on all
substructures from the training set (33,759 substruc-
tures) in a self-supervised manner to reconstruct node
features. The encoder part, consisting of two SAGE-
Conv layers (input 4 features — 128 hidden — 64
output), was then used to generate a 64-dimensional
topological embedding for each substructure graph via
global mean pooling of its node embeddings. The GNN
training achieved a final average loss of approximately
0.00014 after 5 epochs.

For each merger tree, the physical features and the 64-
dimensional topological embedding for each of its sub-
structures were concatenated, forming a 74-dimensional
feature vector per substructure (Dfeat combined = 10 +
64). These lists of substructure feature vectors
were then padded or truncated to a fixed length of
MAX_N_SUB = 60 substructures per tree. Padding
was achieved using a canonical null substructure repre-
sentation (zero physical features and the GNN embed-
ding of a single null node). This resulted in a tensor of
shape (60, 74) for each merger tree.

3.2. QITT Decomposition and Feature Generation

The (60, 74) feature tensor for each tree was then
prepared for Quantum-Inspired Tensor Train (QITT)
decomposition using the TensorLy library (backend:
NumPy). The 74-dimensional feature space per sub-
structure (Dfeat combined) Was reshaped into two factors

(2, 37), resulting in a 3rd-order tensor of shape (60, 2,
37) for each tree.

Tensor Train (TT) decomposition was applied to this
3rd-order tensor. The TT-ranks were selected via cross-
validation on the validation set (150 trees) by optimizing
the sum of RMSEs for (2, and og prediction using a
Ridge regression model. The candidate internal ranks
r1 (connecting mode 0 of size 60 to mode 1 of size 2)
and ry (connecting mode 1 of size 2 to mode 2 of size
37) were swept through values [2, 4, 6, 8]. The optimal
ranks were found to be ry = 2 and ry = 2, yielding a full
TT-rank tuple of (1, 2, 2, 1). This rank configuration
achieved the best sum RMSE of 0.0925 on the validation
set during rank search.

The TT-cores resulting from this decomposition were
flattened and concatenated to form a single feature vec-
tor for each merger tree. With the optimal ranks (1,
2, 2, 1) and tensor dimensions (60, 2, 37), the re-
sulting QITT feature vector had a dimension of 202
(60x24+2x2x242x37x1=1204+8+74 = 202). This
QITT-derived feature vector served as the input for the
final regression models.

3.3. Cosmological Parameter Estimation Performance

The efficacy of the QITT-derived features was eval-
uated by training Linear Regression, Random Forest,
and XGBoost models to predict €2,, and og. These were
compared against four baseline feature sets:

« B1_ Aggregate: 11 global aggregate features per
tree (e.g., total mass, mean normalized node fea-
tures).

« B2_ RawSubPhys: Flattened raw physical fea-
tures from substructures (60 substructures * 10
physical features /substructure = 600 features).

« B3__GraphletCounts: (Skipped due to imple-
mentation complexity in the automated pipeline).

« B4_FlatCombined: Flattened combined physi-
cal and topological features from substructures (60
substructures * 74 features/substructure = 4440
features), without QITT decomposition.

All input features were standardized before train-
ing. Hyperparameters for Random Forest and XGBoost
models were tuned using 5-fold cross-validation on the
combined training and validation sets (850 trees), op-
timizing a custom scorer based on the negative sum of
RMSEs for (2, and og. The test set performance of all
models is summarized in Table 1.

3.3.3. Comparison with Baselines

« B1_Aggregate (Aggregate Features): The
B1_Aggregate_ LinearRegression model achieved
the overall best performance for ©, (RMSE
0.0155, R? 0.9696) and very strong performance
for og (RMSE 0.0654, R? 0.6257). This indicates
that simple global properties of the merger trees
are highly informative, especially for €,,. The
QITT_ LinearRegression model is competitive but
does not surpass this simple baseline.


« B2_ RawSubPhys (Raw Substructure Phys-
ical Features): This baseline performed poorly.
The B2_RawSubPhys_LinearRegression model
yielded negative R? values, indicating it performed
worse than a mean predictor. While Random
Forest and XGBoost improved upon this, their
R? values (e.g., XGBoost: ,, R?=0.6109, og
R?=0.3042) were substantially lower than those
achieved by QITT-based models or B1/B4. This
highlights the difficulty of directly using high-
dimensional, potentially noisy raw substructure
features without further processing like topolog-
ical embedding or QITT.

« B4_FlatCombined (Flattened Combined
Physical and Topological Features): This
baseline uses the same per-substructure in-
formation as the input to the QITT pro-
cess (physical features + GNN topological
embeddings) but simply flattens them into
a very high-dimensional vector (4440 fea-
tures). The B4 FlatCombined XGBoost
model (RMSE ,,=0.0377, R?>=0.8194; RMSE
05=0.0817, R?=0.4159) performed worse than
the QITT__XGBoost model. This suggests that
the QITT decomposition provides a more ef-
fective and compact representation of the (60,
74) tensor than simple flattening, leading to bet-
ter generalization for the XGBoost model. The
B4_FlatCombined_ LinearRegression model also
struggled, especially with og (R?=-0.9339), likely
due to the high dimensionality and multicollinear-
ity.

3.3.4. Statistical Significance
Paired t-tests were performed on the squared errors of
the test set predictions to compare the QITT _XGBoost

model (as a representative advanced QITT model)
against the XGBoost models from key baselines.

e QITT_XGBoost vs. B1_ Aggregate. XGBoost:

— OQ: p-value = 0.9537. No significant differ-
ence.

— og: p-value = 0.1734. No significant differ-
ence.

This suggests that for XGBoost, the QITT fea-
tures do not offer a statistically significant im-
provement over simple aggregate features, which
are already very powerful.

— Q,,,: p-value = 1.8866e-08. QITT_XGBoost
is significantly better.

— 0g: p-value = 2.8041e-05. QITT_XGBoost
is significantly better.

This confirms that the feature engineering pipeline
(including GNN embeddings and QITT) signifi-
cantly improves upon using raw physical substruc-
ture features.

e QITT_XGBoost vs. B4_ FlatCombined_ XGBoost:

— Q,,: p-value = 0.0104. QITT_XGBoost is
significantly better.

— og: p-value = 0.0014. QITT_XGBoost is sig-
nificantly better.

This is a crucial result, indicating that the QITT
decomposition provides a statistically significant
advantage over simply using the flattened high-
dimensional feature tensors that include topolog-
ical information. The QITT method effectively
compresses and structures these features.

3.3.5. Predicted vs. True Values

The scatter plots of predicted versus true values for
Q,, and og using the QITT__XGBoost model are shown
in Figures 3 and 4, respectively. These plots provide a
visual assessment of the model’s predictive accuracy and
potential biases.

For ,,, the predictions align closely with the y=x
line, reflecting the high R? value of 0.8834. The scatter
is noticeably larger for og, consistent with the lower R2
of 0.5577, indicating greater difficulty in constraining
this parameter with the current feature set and models.
No strong systematic biases are apparent in these plots,
though the variance in og predictions is higher.

3.4.2. QITT Core Analysis

The QITT decomposition transforms the (60, 2, 37)
tensor for each tree into three cores with shapes deter-
mined by the optimal ranks (1, 2, 2, 1): Core 0: (1, 60,
2), Core 1: (2, 2, 2), Core 2: (2, 37, 1). The distribution
of magnitudes of the elements within each of these three
cores for an example tree tensor from the training set is
shown in Figure 6.

« Core 0 (Shape: (1, 60, 2)): The magnitudes
are relatively concentrated around zero, with a
range from approximately -0.16 to 0.65. This core
interfaces the ‘max _N_ sub‘ dimension (60 sub-
structures) with the first internal TT bond rank

2).

o Core 1 (Shape: (2, 2, 2)): This small internal
core also shows values mostly near zero but with
some elements approaching 1.0. Its values range
from approximately -0.03 to 1.0.

Figure 6. Distribution of element magnitudes within the
three Tensor Train cores for an example merger tree, af-
ter Quantum-Inspired Tensor Train (QITT) decomposition.
The element values of these cores are flattened and concate-
nated to form the QITT-derived features used for cosmolog-
ical parameter estimation.

e Core 2 (Shape: (2, 37, 1)): This core ex-
hibits the widest range of magnitudes, from ap-
proximately -66.6 to 302.3. It connects the second
internal TT bond rank (2) to the last dimension
of the reshaped features (size 37). The presence of
large magnitude values suggests that certain com-
binations of features along this dimension, as me-
diated by this core, are particularly significant.

The distributions suggest that the TT representation
is not excessively sparse for these low ranks, but Core 2
clearly carries elements with larger leverage. The flat-
tened and concatenated elements of these cores form the
202 features used by the regression models.

Feature importance plots for QITT_RandomForest
(Figure 7) and QITT_XGBoost (Figure 8) show the top
20 most important features out of the 202 QITT-derived
features. For comparison, feature importances for the
B4_FlatCombined models (Figures 9 and 10) are also
provided, which operate on a much larger, uncompressed
feature space. A direct physical interpretation of indi-
vidual QITT features is challenging because each feature
is an element from one of the TT-cores, representing a
complex, compressed interaction term. However, these
plots demonstrate that the models rely on a subset of
these compressed features. Future work could involve
attempting to deconstruct the high-importance QITT
features back to understand which original substructure
properties or interactions they represent.

3.5. Discussion
3.5.1. Efficacy of the QITT-Enhanced Approach

The primary goal was to assess if a QITT-enhanced
multi-scale substructure analysis, incorporating learned
topological embeddings, could effectively estimate cos-
mological parameters. The results present a nuanced
picture.

11

os (p=0.0014). This highlights the benefit of the QITT
decomposition in creating a more compact and effective
feature representation from the high-dimensional per-
substructure data (physical + topological features). The
QITT approach compresses 4440 features (60 substruc-
tures * 74 features/substructure) down to 202 features
while improving, or at least maintaining, predictive
performance for non-linear models.

However, the very simple B1__Aggregate_ LinearRegression

model, using only 11 global tree features, achieved the
highest R? for Q,, (0.9696) and was highly competitive
for og (R? 0.6257). This suggests that for the current
dataset and feature engineering, global properties of the
merger trees are extremely informative, especially for
Q,,. While the QITT approach processes much richer,
fine-grained substructure information, it did not, in its
current implementation, surpass this simpler baseline in
terms of raw predictive accuracy on the test set. The
QITT XGBoost model was not statistically different
from the B1_ Aggregate. XGBoost model.

3.5.2. Role of Topological Information and Substructure
Analysis

The inclusion of GNN-derived topological embeddings
was intended to capture complex structural information
beyond simple physical features of substructures. The
t-SNE visualization in Figure 5 indicated that these em-
beddings do capture aspects related to substructure size
(number of halos).

The significant outperformance of QITT_XGBoost
over B2_ RawSubPhys XGBoost (which uses only
physical substructure features, without topological em-
beddings or QITT on the combined set) strongly sug-
gests that the combination of topological embeddings
and the subsequent QITT processing is beneficial. The
B2 baseline, relying on 600 raw physical features, strug-
gled significantly, indicating that these features alone
are either too noisy or not sufficiently expressive without
further abstraction or combination. The GNN embed-
dings provide this abstraction for the topological aspect.

The comparison between QITT XGBoost and
B4_ FlatCombined XGBoost (both use topological em-
beddings) isolates the effect of QITT. The superior per-
formance of QITT_XGBoost indicates that the tensor
decomposition is a more effective way to handle the

The QITT-based models, particularly QITT _LinearRegressi¢thax_ N_ sub, D_ feat combined) structure than sim-

and QITT XGBoost, demonstrated strong predictive
power, achieving R? values for 2, up to 0.9231 and for
os up to 0.6206 (see Table 1 and Figures 1, 2). Crucially,
the QITT_XGBoost model significantly outperformed
the B4 FlatCombinedXGBoost model (which uses
the same input information prior to QITT but in a flat-
tened, uncompressed form) for both €,,, (p=0.0104) and

ple flattening, especially for subsequent non-linear mod-
els.

3.5.3. Interpretation of Model Performance Differences

The strong performance of B1__ Aggregate  LinearRegression,

especially for €,,, implies that (2, imprints a strong,
relatively simple signal on the global characteristics of


12

merger trees (like total mass, average node properties, or
tree size). og, which relates to the amplitude of matter
fluctuations, might be expected to influence more subtle
aspects of substructure and merger histories, potentially
explaining why it is generally harder to constrain (lower
R?2 values across most models).

The QITT_ LinearRegression model's surprising
strength compared to QITT_RandomForest/XGBoost
could imply that the QITT features (with ranks
(1,2,2,1)) are already in a space where linear relation-
ships to cosmological parameters are dominant, or that
the non-linear models were not able to exploit further
non-linearities effectively within this 202-dimensional
QITT feature space without more extensive tuning or
different architectures. The LinAlgWarnings during
Ridge regression for rank cross-validation and some ill-
conditioning/singularity warnings during some model
fits suggest potential multicollinearity or numerical sta-
bility issues with some feature sets/ranks, which might
affect model training and interpretation.

3.5.4. Limitations

e Interpretability of QITT Features: While
QITT provides effective compression, the resulting
features are elements of TT-cores and lack direct
physical interpretability. Understanding precisely
which physical interactions are captured requires
further investigation. The distributions of the TT-
core element magnitudes for an example merger
tree are shown in Figure 6.

e GNN Training: The GNN was trained for a lim-
ited number of epochs (5) for pipeline efficiency.
More extensive training or different self-supervised
objectives might yield even more informative topo-
logical embeddings.

e Substructure Definition: The definition of sub-
structures and the choice of physical features,
while physically motivated, are not exhaustive.
Other definitions or features might capture differ-
ent aspects of merger tree evolution. An illustra-
tion of the diversity in size and temporal extent of
substructures is shown in Figure 11.

e Dataset Size: While 1000 trees provide a good
starting point, larger datasets could enable the
training of more complex models and potentially
reveal more subtle relationships.

e Computational Cost of Baselines: Baseline
B3 (Graphlet Counts) was skipped. A full compar-
ison would ideally include it. Some baselines in-
volve very high-dimensional feature spaces, which

can be computationally intensive for certain model
types.

3.6. Summary of Results

In summary, this work presents a novel approach
for cosmological parameter estimation using QITT-
enhanced multi-scale substructure analysis with learned
topological embeddings. The QITT decomposition ef-
fectively compresses high-dimensional substructure in-
formation, leading to statistically significant improve-
ments over models using flattened features. However,
a simple baseline using global aggregate tree features
achieves the best performance for 2,,, suggesting that
global properties are highly informative for this param-
eter. The QITT-based approach shows promise for cap-
turing more subtle effects related to og and other cos-
mological parameters. Future work should focus on en-
hancing the interpretability of QITT features, exploring
more advanced GNNs, and applying this framework to
larger datasets and a wider range of cosmological and
astrophysical applications.

4. CONCLUSIONS

This paper addresses the challenge of extracting cos-
mological information from the complex structure of
dark matter halo merger trees, specifically focusing on
estimating the matter density of the Universe (£2,,) and
the amplitude of the matter power spectrum (og). The
proposed solution leverages Quantum-Inspired Tensor
Trains (QITT) to compress multi-scale substructure fea-
tures, incorporating learned topological embeddings ob-
tained through Graph Neural Networks (GNN).

The study utilized a dataset of 1000 dark matter halo
merger trees extracted from cosmological simulations.
Substructures within these trees were identified based on
mass accretion rates and changes in halo properties. For
each substructure, physical features were extracted, and
a GNN was employed to generate a topological embed-
ding. These features were then organized into a tensor,
which was subsequently decomposed using QITT. The
resulting QITT cores served as input features for several
regression models, including Linear Regression, Random
Forest, and XGBoost. The performance of these models
was compared to baselines that used aggregate graph-
level features, raw substructure features, and flattened
combined features.

The results demonstrated that QITT-based models
achieved competitive performance in estimating cosmo-
logical parameters. Notably, the QITT-XGBoost model
significantly outperformed the baseline model that used
flattened combined features, highlighting the effective-
ness of QITT decomposition for feature compression and


representation. However, a simple Linear Regression
model using global aggregate tree features achieved the
best performance for €2,,,, suggesting that global proper-
ties are highly informative for this parameter. Statistical
significance tests confirmed that the QITT-enhanced ap-
proach significantly improved upon using raw physical
substructure features and provided a more effective rep-
resentation compared to simply flattening the combined
physical and topological features.

From the results, we learned that QITT decomposi-
tion offers a promising avenue for extracting complex in-
formation from merger trees, with potential for advanc-
ing data-driven cosmology. The combination of learned

13

topological embeddings and QITT decomposition en-
ables the capture of intricate relationships within the
merger trees, leading to improved performance in cos-
mological parameter estimation compared to methods
that rely on raw substructure features or flattened rep-
resentations. However, the study also highlighted the
importance of global tree properties, particularly for es-
timating €,,,, and suggested that future research should
focus on further enhancing the interpretability of QITT
features and exploring more advanced GNN architec-
tures to capture even more nuanced information from
merger trees.
